Narrative: Spiny mice (Acomys) are the only mammals known to regenerate full-thickness skin — including hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and arrector pili muscles — without scarring. When threatened by a predator, they shed large patches of skin (autotomy) and regrow it completely, something no lab mouse can do. The regeneration extends beyond skin: Acomys can regenerate ear hole punches (including cartilage), kidney tissue after ischemia-reperfusion injury, and spinal cord tissue after injury — all with minimal fibrosis compared to Mus musculus. Gusev's group at Kazan Federal University (Filatov 2024) revealed a distinctive hemostasis phenotype: spiny mouse blood forms stronger hemostatic seals with elevated clottable fibrinogen, denser fibrin-rich clots, and superior plasma clot stiffness. This robust hemostasis may be an adaptation that enables the risky strategy of shedding skin — you need reliable clotting before you can afford to lose tissue. The molecular drivers are still being mapped: Acomys wounds show reduced TGF-beta signaling, a macrophage response biased toward pro-regenerative rather than pro-fibrotic polarization, and Wnt pathway activity resembling embryonic patterning rather than adult scarring. No single gene has been identified as the master switch — this appears to be a systems-level rewiring of the wound response. The challenge for translational work is moving from descriptive -omics to causal gene targets.
Short Description: Skin punched clean through heals back whole—hair follicles, glands, and cartilage regrow instead of scarring, driven by low TGF-beta signaling and clot-forming blood 2-3x stronger than a lab mouse's. A 4mm ear hole closes in about 60 days with full structure restored, versus permanent scarring in Mus. This exists only in the Cairo spiny mouse—no transgenic transfer into mice attempted. No master gene runs it: TGF-beta, macrophage signaling, and Wnt patterning would need rewiring together.
Mechanism: Systems-level wound response: reduced TGF-beta/fibrotic signaling; pro-regenerative (M2-like) macrophage polarization; Wnt pathway activity resembling embryonic patterning; distinctive hemostasis with elevated fibrinogen and denser fibrin-rich clots (Filatov 2024). Regeneration includes hair follicles, sebaceous glands, cartilage, and potentially kidney and spinal cord tissue.
Achievements (effect sizes): Seifert 2012 Nature: Acomys regenerated 4mm ear punches with cartilage, hair follicles, and sebaceous glands in ~60 days (Mus scarred). Brant 2015: full-thickness dorsal skin wounds healed without fibrosis. Filatov 2024 IJMS: Acomys blood formed 2-3× stronger fibrin clots vs Balb/c mice. Okamura 2021 (iScience, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2021.103269) reported that spiny mice activate unique transcriptional programmes after severe kidney injury and regenerate organ function without fibrosis. An earlier version of this record credited this finding to "Simkin 2017" with a DOI belonging to a mouse digit-tip macrophage study in Development, which does not concern Acomys kidney injury. Matias Santos 2023: ear regeneration involves blastema-like structure with Wnt/beta-catenin signaling.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (multiple mammalian organ systems) + T6 (replicated across independent labs)
Translational Gaps: No single master-switch gene identified; systems-level program likely requires multiple coordinated interventions; no transgenic experiments transferring Acomys wound program to Mus; no human-cell studies; hemostasis-regeneration link is correlative, not causally demonstrated.
Key References (DOIs): Seifert Nature 2012 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature11499 | Filatov IJMS 2024 https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms252312867 | Brant Wound Repair Regen 2015 https://doi.org/10.1111/wrr.12385 | Okamura iScience 2021 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2021.103269
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: NOT a single-gene candidate — included as a systems-level enhancement program. Translating Acomys regeneration may require rewiring TGF-beta signaling, macrophage polarization, and Wnt patterning simultaneously. Hemostasis connection (Filatov 2024) is from Gusev's lab but causal relationship between clotting phenotype and regeneration is unproven. Acomys are small rodents; whether the program scales to larger mammals is unknown. Some regenerative capacity (ear punch) may be shared with other Acomys species that differ in autotomy ability, suggesting the programs are separable.

Manipulation: overexpression (root-specific promoter in a heterologous plant host)
Narrative:
Chinese brake fern, Pteris vittata, grows on mine tailings and does something no flowering plant can do: it draws arsenic out of the soil and stockpiles it in its fronds at more than one percent of its dry weight (https://doi.org/10.1105/tpc.109.069773). That is a load that would be lethal in almost any other tissue. The trick is a transporter. Arsenate entering the root is reduced to arsenite on the way up, and PvACR3 — an arsenite efflux permease sitting in the membrane of the vacuole rather than in the cell surface — pushes that arsenite out of the cytosol and into the vacuole, where it is simply stored. The cell never detoxifies the metalloid. It puts it in a box and shuts the lid.

The evolutionary detail is what makes the gene worth exhibiting. ACR3 is present in mosses, lycophytes, other ferns and gymnosperms, and it has been lost in every angiosperm — which includes every crop we eat. Flowering plants threw the machinery away. Putting it back is therefore not the enhancement of an existing capability but the restoration of a discarded one, and in 2025 a group did exactly that: rice transformed with PvACR3 under a rice root-specific promoter became an arsenic pump, hauling the metalloid out of flooded paddy soil and into its own shoots (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eehl.2025.100168).

That result is a gift for soil cleanup and a disaster for dinner. The transgenic rice inverts the wild-type distribution of arsenic in the plant: wild type keeps most of its arsenic below ground, while the transgenic lines have significantly less in the root and hundreds of milligrams per kilogram in the shoot. For remediation that is the whole point, because the arsenic can be walked off the field in a wheelbarrow. For food it is fatal, because the shoots have to be harvested and disposed of as hazardous biomass before grain filling. Nobody has put this gene into an animal, and the first obstacle is anatomical rather than technical: animal cells have no vacuole to put anything into.
Short Description: A membrane pump moves arsenic out of the cytoplasm and locks it inside the vacuole, so a body can carry a dose of arsenic that would otherwise kill it — over one percent of its dry weight — without being poisoned. Rice given the fern's transporter under a root-specific promoter piled 452-557 mg/kg of arsenic into its shoots, 19 to 24 times more than wild type, and stripped 23.5 times more arsenic out of the same contaminated paddy soil. The fern itself is already planted in the field for arsenic phytoremediation; the transgenic rice exists only in hydroponics and pots, and no animal has ever been given the gene. The catch is that the transporter relocates arsenic upward rather than destroying it, so the shoots must be cut and hauled away as hazardous biomass before the grain fills and the plant can never be eaten. In an animal the same logic holds: the arsenic is still inside you, held in a compartment, and it leaves only when that compartment does.
Mechanism: Arsenate entering the root is reduced to arsenite before or during its journey to the frond. PvACR3 is a roughly 379-amino-acid, 41.6 kDa permease with ten predicted transmembrane helices, a member of the ACR3/ArsB family of arsenite efflux carriers. Its location is the point. In yeast the equivalent protein sits in the plasma membrane and throws arsenite out of the cell, whereas PvACR3 localises to the vacuolar membrane and instead moves arsenite from the cytosol into the vacuole, where the fern keeps it as free arsenite rather than as a glutathione or phytochelatin complex. Pteris vittata carries a duplicated pair of these genes, ACR3 and ACR3;1, and only ACR3 is arsenic-inducible in the tissues that contact soil. The family occurs in mosses, lycophytes, other ferns and gymnosperms but has been lost from every angiosperm lineage, which is the structural reason no flowering plant hyperaccumulates arsenic without help.
Achievements (effect sizes): Characterisation of the transporter in its native fern established both the phenotype and the causal link. “Gametophytes of the fern Pteris vittata can accumulate and tolerate more than 1% of their dry weight as arsenic”, and RNA interference against ACR3 — but not against its duplicate ACR3;1 — made those gametophytes arsenite-sensitive, while PvACR3 rescued the arsenic-sensitive phenotype of a yeast strain lacking its own ACR3 (Indriolo 2010, https://doi.org/10.1105/tpc.109.069773). Transferred into rice under the root-specific promoter pLsi1, the same gene turned a staple crop into an arsenic pump: in hydroponic culture “pLsi1::PvACR3 lines exhibited 37.1-50.3-fold and 19.2-23.7-fold higher shoot As concentrations than WT under 5 uM (268-364 mg/kg) and 20 uM (452-557 mg/kg) treatments, respectively (p < 0.05)”, against wild-type shoot concentrations of only 7.24 and 23.5 mg/kg (Zhu 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eehl.2025.100168). The same lines were then grown in flooded pots of moderately arsenic-contaminated paddy soil, where the transgenic rice “removed 23.5 times more As from the same paddy soils” than wild-type rice, reaching 45.9-80.3 mg/kg arsenic in the shoot and almost completely depleting arsenic from the soil pore water when the shoots were harvested before grain filling (Zhu 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eehl.2025.100168).
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (native loss-of-function in the source fern plus heterologous gain-of-function in a crop, demonstrated in both hydroponics and contaminated soil, by multiple laboratories)
Translational Gaps: No animal has ever received this gene, and the reason is anatomical before it is technical. Mammals handle arsenic by a different route entirely: arsenite methyltransferase (AS3MT) methylates arsenite, and the methylated products leave the body in bile and urine, so mammalian detoxification is chemical modification followed by export rather than storage. Animal cells also have no vacuole, so a mammalian version of this card would have to retarget the transporter to the lysosome, and nobody has attempted that experiment. There is no experimental structure either: the fold of ACR3-family permeases is known only from homology modelling and AlphaFold prediction, so the ten-helix architecture described here is a prediction rather than a measurement. Even within plants the evidence stops at hydroponics and pot trials, and the question of what happens to arsenic-loaded biomass after harvest has not been answered experimentally.
Key References (DOIs): Indriolo The Plant Cell 2010 https://doi.org/10.1105/tpc.109.069773 | Zhu Eco-Environment & Health 2025 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eehl.2025.100168 | Ma Nature 2001 https://doi.org/10.1038/35054664
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The discovery paper for the hyperaccumulation phenotype is Ma 2001 in Nature (https://doi.org/10.1038/35054664). Its DOI resolves, but the full text could not be retrieved while this record was prepared, so no number in this entry is taken from it and it is listed as a reference only. The commercial picture is unusual for this library: Pteris vittata itself is already planted deliberately for arsenic phytoremediation, so the wild-type version of this enhancement is in field use, while the transgenic rice exists only in laboratory hydroponics and pot experiments (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eehl.2025.100168). Field deployment has documented limits — Wan and colleagues report that soil texture and climate constrain where fern-based phytoremediation actually works (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhazmat.2022.129151). The transporter was isolated and characterised in the Banks laboratory at Purdue University, which also localised it to the vacuolar membrane and showed the gene is absent from all angiosperms (https://doi.org/10.1105/tpc.109.069773). The reference sequence is UniProt E3URE9 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/E3URE9); there is no Protein Data Bank entry, so any structural image is a model. There are no clinical trials, and it is worth saying plainly why that is appropriate: this gene concentrates a carcinogenic metalloid rather than eliminating it.

Narrative: Fish in Arctic and Antarctic water sit below the freezing point of their own body fluids and do not freeze, because their blood carries proteins that bind the faces of nascent ice crystals and arrest their growth. The interesting question for an enhancement project is not whether the trick works in a fish but whether it works in mammalian tissue, and the answer so far is a qualified yes with a clear ceiling. Supplementing standard mouse-ovary vitrification medium with 20 mg/mL of type III antifreeze protein raised the proportion of morphologically intact follicles from 28.9% to 44.7% (https://doi.org/10.3349/ymj.2015.56.3.778), which is a large effect in a field where a few percentage points is a publishable gain. The same group went on to compare three different antifreeze proteins head to head and found that the bacterial-derived LeIBP outperformed both a fungal protein and fish type III, reducing DNA double-strand breaks in the warmed tissue (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0126252). Whole organs followed. Korkut Uygun's group at Harvard supercooled human donor livers to -4 degrees Celsius without freezing them, extending the organ's viable time outside a body by roughly 27 hours, and then pushed further into genuinely subzero territory with partial freezing at -10 to -15 degrees Celsius (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-019-0223-y, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-31490-2). A synthetic antifreeze analogue has already been used on human transplant material: a completed phase 1 trial at the Clinical Islet Transplant Program bathed donor islets in 3 mg/mL of the glycopeptide PKX-001 during isolation before transplanting them into recipients (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03073577). In a human body carrying the gene rather than the purified protein, the promise would be tissue that tolerates deep cold; the unresolved problems are what chronic exposure to a fish protein does to the immune system, and the fact that more antifreeze protein is not simply better.
Short Description: These proteins find microscopic ice crystals the moment they nucleate and clamp onto the crystal faces, so ice stops growing and the tissue around it survives being frozen. Adding type III antifreeze protein at 20 mg/mL to mouse-ovary vitrification medium raised the intact follicle ratio from 28.9% in controls to 44.7%, and cut apoptotic follicles from 26.6% to 12.6%. A synthetic antifreeze mimic has already been through a completed phase 1 islet-transplant trial in people with type 1 diabetes, and a Harvard team supercooled whole human donor livers to -4 degrees Celsius, buying about 27 extra hours of viable storage. The dose-response curve is not monotonic, though: push the concentration higher and the protein templates long ice needles that damage the tissue it was added to protect.
Mechanism: Antifreeze proteins depress the freezing point non-colligatively, which means they do it without contributing the osmotic load that a chemically equivalent amount of salt or glycerol would. Instead of altering the bulk solution, they adsorb directly onto specific faces of an ice crystal. Because the ice front must then bulge outward between the bound proteins to keep growing, the local curvature raises the energy cost of adding water molecules and growth stalls. The measurable consequence is thermal hysteresis: the solution's melting point stays where it was, while its freezing point drops, opening a temperature window in which ice neither grows nor melts. A second and separately useful activity is ice-recrystallisation inhibition, which matters during warming rather than cooling. Small ice crystals in vitrified tissue would otherwise coalesce into a few large damaging ones as the sample passes back through intermediate temperatures, and antifreeze proteins block that coarsening. Some family members additionally stabilise membranes and ion channels at low temperature, which is thought to contribute to cell survival independently of any effect on ice. The therapeutic reagents span several structural families that share function without sharing ancestry: alanine-rich alpha-helical type I, the disulfide-bonded 14 kDa type II, the compact globular type III used in most of the cryopreservation work, and glycosylated antifreeze glycoproteins.
Achievements (effect sizes): Transgenic Atlantic salmon carrying a winter flounder antifreeze gene inherited it stably and expressed it on a seasonal cycle. The line was characterised across a programme of work spanning 1991-99, whose definitive report is the 1999 paper (https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1008900812864). Hew and colleagues integrated the genomic clone 2A-7 encoding the liver-type gene wflAFP-6, produced an F3 generation carrying a single copy at a unique integration site, and found antifreeze mRNA restricted to the liver, with serum protein levels highest in November and lowest in May and sera producing the hexagonal ice-crystal morphology that marks genuine antifreeze activity (https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1008900812864). The concentrations reached were nonetheless far below what a fish needs to avoid freezing in seawater, so the transgene conferred the molecule without conferring the phenotype. Plant work told the same story more starkly. Kenward and colleagues expressed type I antifreeze protein in tobacco and found that it accumulated only after the plant was held at 4 degrees Celsius for 24 hours, making expression cold-specific (https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00029012); when they later targeted type II protein to the cytosol and apoplast, active protein reached 2% of total apoplast protein and matched wild-type fish protein in thermal hysteresis activity and ice-crystal morphology, yet field-trialled plants showed no difference in frost resistance from wild type during early autumn frosts (https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1008886629825). Insect antifreeze proteins expressed in Drosophila likewise enhanced cold survival, though I could not resolve that result to a specific paper and it is recorded in this entry without an attribution. In mammals the transgenic line worked better. Bagis and colleagues produced mice carrying the ocean pout type III antifreeze gene, showed stable transmission and transcription with hypothermic storage of transgenic tissues (https://doi.org/10.1002/mrd.20601), and confirmed protein expression in the seventh generation in skin, oviduct, lung, kidney and liver tissue and in serum, though not in heart (https://doi.org/10.1002/jez.455); cryopreserved ovaries and testes from these animals retained function, and orthotopic ovary transplants yielded live offspring. The strongest dose-response data come from mouse ovary vitrification. Working with 182 ovaries from 4-week-old ICR mice and type III antifreeze protein at 0, 5 or 20 mg/mL in the vitrification solution, Lee and colleagues recorded intact follicle ratios of 28.9%, 42.3% and 44.7% respectively, with apoptotic follicle rates falling from 26.6% to 18.7% to 12.6%, and the 20 mg/mL advantage persisted after autotransplantation of the warmed ovaries (https://doi.org/10.3349/ymj.2015.56.3.778). A companion study compared three antifreeze protein types at 0.1, 1 and 10 mg/mL across 5,790 scored follicles from 5-week-old B6D2F1 mice and found the 10 mg/mL LeIBP group best protected, with fewer TUNEL-positive follicles and reduced gamma-H2AX and Rad51 staining indicating fewer DNA double-strand breaks (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0126252). Organ preservation scaled the idea up. Amir, Rubinsky and colleagues preserved rat hearts in University of Wisconsin solution at -1.3 degrees Celsius with antifreeze protein I or III present at 15 mg/cm3: hearts held at -1.3 degrees Celsius without antifreeze protein froze and died when nucleation was initiated, while those with it did not freeze and survived (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cryobiol.2004.02.009), and in a heterotopic transplant series spanning 104 and 58 animals across two protocols, hearts preserved for 18, 21 and 24 hours with type III protein showed superior viability scores, better fractional shortening on echocardiography and less TUNEL-positive apoptosis than hearts held at 4 degrees Celsius (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.healun.2004.11.003). Antifreeze proteins are supplied at clinical grade for oocyte vitrification, and a synthetic small-molecule replica, the antiaging glycopeptide PKX-001, completed a phase 1 islet-transplantation trial in which it was added at 3 mg/mL to CMRL-1066 islet preservation medium during isolation, with washed islets then transplanted intraportally into recipients (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03073577). Finally, human whole organs: de Vries and colleagues supercooled human livers to -4 degrees Celsius after homogeneous preconditioning with protective agents during machine perfusion, extending viable ex-vivo time by 27 hours and showing that the livers withstood simulated transplantation by normothermic reperfusion with blood (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-019-0223-y). The same group then entered high subzero temperatures of -10 to -15 degrees Celsius by partial freezing, extending rat liver storage five-fold (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-31490-2) and subsequently to ten days with an optimised protocol using higher polyethylene glycol and bovine serum albumin concentrations (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-76674-6).
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (human ex-vivo organs, IVF cells) + T5 (Tg mice with functional tissue cryopreservation)
Translational Gaps: No supercooled human liver has yet been transplanted into a recipient. The 27-hour extension was demonstrated on organs that were then rewarmed and tested by normothermic machine reperfusion with blood, which is a strong surrogate for viability but is not a transplant (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-019-0223-y). Immunogenicity under chronic exposure is the second gap, and it separates the two use cases sharply: adding a fish protein to a preservation solution for hours is a different proposition from a human body expressing that protein continuously, and no chronic-exposure immunogenicity data exist. The transgenic-animal precedent shows the third gap concretely. Salmon and mice both inherited and expressed the gene, but neither reached serum concentrations approaching what the source fish achieves, so the gene alone did not deliver the trait (https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1008900812864, https://doi.org/10.1002/jez.455). The clinical foothold that does exist uses a synthetic peptide added to a dish, not a gene in a patient: PKX-001 was chosen precisely because full-size antifreeze proteins are too large to pass from capillaries into interstitial tissue and reach target cells (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03073577).

Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The dose-response relationship is not monotonic, which is the most practically important caveat in this record. Below the useful concentration the protein does nothing; above it, the same ice-face binding that arrests crystal growth instead templates long ice needles, or spicules, that mechanically damage the tissue. In the mouse ovary series the benefit was still rising at 20 mg/mL (28.9% to 42.3% to 44.7% intact follicles), so the turn has to be established per tissue and per protein rather than assumed (https://doi.org/10.3349/ymj.2015.56.3.778). Transgenic frost tolerance has been inconsistent, and one result is a clean negative that deserves to be stated plainly: type II antifreeze protein accumulated in transgenic tobacco to 2% of total apoplast protein, was indistinguishable from wild-type fish protein in thermal hysteresis activity and ice-crystal morphology, and still conferred no frost resistance in field trials (https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1008886629825). That matters because it decouples the molecule from the phenotype: expressing a functional antifreeze protein at high level in the right compartment was not sufficient, which implies the limiting factor lies in where ice actually nucleates in an intact organism rather than in how much protein is present. It is also worth correcting a common misattribution. The commercially approved AquAdvantage salmon owes its fast-growth phenotype to a Chinook salmon growth hormone gene, not to an antifreeze protein; the ocean pout antifreeze gene contributes only its promoter, which drives constitutive rather than seasonal expression of the growth-hormone transgene (https://doi.org/10.1007/s11248-007-9128-5). Anyone citing that fish as evidence that antifreeze transgenes work in vertebrates is citing the wrong gene.

Manipulation: overexpression (level-tuning; the enzyme sets the red/yellow balance)
Narrative:
Parrots come in red and yellow versions of the same bird with unnerving regularity: the dusky lory has a red morph and a yellow morph, lovebirds put red on the face and green on the back, and breeders have been shuffling these colours for generations without knowing what they were shuffling. The answer turns out to be almost embarrassingly simple chemistry. Parrot pigments, the psittacofulvins, are linear conjugated polyene chains, and whether one looks red or yellow depends on what sits at the end of the chain. An aldehyde end group gives red. Oxidise that aldehyde to a carboxylic acid and the same chain gives yellow.

The enzyme that performs the oxidation is not a specialist. ALDH3A2 is the fatty-aldehyde dehydrogenase of ordinary lipid metabolism, present in essentially every cell of the follicle and in every tissue of a vertebrate body, and the parrot has simply recruited it as a colour control. Mapping two species independently pointed at the same locus: in rosy-faced lovebirds the enzyme's transcript tracked the green-versus-red patches within a single bird, and in dusky lories a genome scan across both morphs converged on a variant sitting just past the end of the gene (Arbore 2024, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adp7710). Yeast supplied the causal test. Running an avian polyketide synthase in a strain with the yeast counterpart of ALDH3A2 deleted, then restored, shifted the end-group chemistry of the pigments exactly as predicted.

What makes this a genuinely different enhancement from making the pigment in the first place is that it is a dial rather than a switch. Because the phenotype comes from how much enzyme is present, not from which enzyme, the carboxyl-to-aldehyde ratio and therefore the hue is continuous, and it is set locally, patch by patch, in late-differentiating keratinocytes. The unavoidable cost is that the dial is wired to something else. Turning a housekeeping lipid enzyme up or down for cosmetic reasons changes fatty-aldehyde clearance in every tissue that expresses it, and human genetics is unambiguous about what happens when this particular enzyme fails.
Short Description: A single enzyme dial sets whether a patch of your skin comes out red or yellow: turn it up and red goes to yellow, turn it down and the same patch runs red. It works by oxidising the aldehyde end group of a polyene pigment to a carboxylic acid, and within one lovebird the green patches carried 4-6-fold more of the enzyme's transcript than the red patch on the same head. The whole story comes from parrot genetics and a yeast reconstitution, with the causal change being a non-coding variant 42 base pairs downstream of the gene rather than anything in the protein. That regulatory location is what makes it hard to copy: you cannot buy the phenotype by expressing a cDNA. The cost is that this is not a pigment enzyme by trade but the ubiquitous fatty-aldehyde dehydrogenase of lipid metabolism, and losing it in humans causes Sjogren-Larsson syndrome, with scaly skin, spastic diplegia and intellectual disability.
Mechanism: Parrot plumage colour is set by which chemical form of psittacofulvin is deposited: red psittacofulvins carry an aldehyde end group and yellow ones a carboxyl group. ALDH3A2, aldehyde dehydrogenase 3 family member A2, also known as fatty-aldehyde dehydrogenase (FALDH) and normally responsible for oxidising medium- and long-chain fatty aldehydes, oxidises the aldehyde end group of psittacofulvins to the corresponding carboxylic acid. Because what varies between red and yellow birds is the expression level of the enzyme rather than its protein sequence, the enzyme functions as a continuous dial on the carboxyl-to-aldehyde ratio, and therefore on hue, in late-differentiating keratinocytes of the feather follicle. Yeast reconstitution confirmed the step directly: an avian polyketide synthase construct expressed in a strain with HFD1, the yeast ortholog of ALDH3A2, either knocked out or restored produced the corresponding shift in psittacofulvin end-group chemistry.
Achievements (effect sizes): Three independent lines of quantification converge on the same enzyme. Bulk RNA sequencing of regenerating feather follicles from eight rosy-faced lovebirds, sampled at three green patches on back, chest and head plus one red patch on the head, found 4-6-fold higher expression in the three green feather patches compared to the red, and chemical analysis of the same feathers showed the green patches carrying a higher carboxyl-to-aldehyde psittacofulvin ratio, which is the direction the mechanism predicts (Arbore 2024, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adp7710). Independently, whole-genome resequencing of 57 dusky lories spanning both colour morphs (red n = 35, yellow n = 22, at mean depth 11.5 +/- 4.8x) identified three associated variants inside a 284 bp interval, of which one SNP (scaffold_13:6,288,712T>C) showed a markedly stronger association with color ( P = 6 x 10 -14 ), sitting in non-coding sequence 42 bp downstream of the longest ALDH3A2 transcript (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adp7710). Allele-specific expression closed the loop within individual birds: bulk RNA sequencing plus full-length long-read transcriptomes of regenerating follicles from red (n = 3) and yellow (n = 3) lories showed the two alleles transcribed unequally at 71% yellow vs. 29% red , chi 2 , P = 0.03 (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adp7710). Single-cell and single-nucleus chromatin-accessibility profiling localised the activity to the follicle, and the yeast knockout and knock-in experiments demonstrated the enzymatic conversion itself.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (association mapping in two parrot species, allele-specific expression, single-cell and snATAC-seq localisation, plus yeast knockout/knock-in reconstitution of the enzymatic step)
Translational Gaps: The yeast experiments demonstrate the chemical conversion only qualitatively. Products were identified by ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography with high-resolution accurate-mass quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry, but the study reports no conversion percentage and no kinetic constants, so the efficiency of the step is unmeasured. The causal variant is regulatory and non-coding, lying 42 base pairs downstream of the transcript, which means that reproducing the phenotype requires reconstructing a cis-regulatory context in the right cell type rather than simply delivering a complementary DNA. The association is also not absolute: the lead variant matched phenotype in 98% of individuals rather than in all of them, and five individuals were discordant at the two flanking variants, so at least one additional modifier is unaccounted for. Nothing has been attempted in a mammal, and any mammalian attempt inherits the problem that the enhancement requires psittacofulvins to be present in the first place, which no mammal makes.
Key References (DOIs): Arbore Science 2024 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adp7710
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: This card is deliberately paired with the budgerigar polyketide synthase entry as the downstream hue-control step acting on the same pigment chemistry, but it is a separate gene doing separate chemistry: aldehyde oxidation of a finished chain rather than synthesis of the chain (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adp7710). No parrot ALDH3A2 UniProt accession could be retrieved. UniProt returns avian ALDH3A2 entries for chicken, quail and kakapo (Strigops habroptila, A0A672UIG9, https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A672UIG9) among others, but none for Agapornis roseicollis or for the dusky lory, so the kakapo protein is the nearest psittacine reference sequence and should be labelled as a cross-species substitute rather than as the lovebird enzyme. A methodological detail worth knowing before anyone tries to repeat the yeast work: the strain background was Saccharomyces cerevisiae BJ5464-NpgA, and the polyketide synthase used was the chicken enzyme (LOC420486) rather than the budgerigar one, because it gave higher polyketide yields. There is a direction trap in the clinical literature. ALDH3A2 appears there only as the Sjogren-Larsson syndrome disease gene, where loss of function causes ichthyosis, spastic diplegia and intellectual disability, which is the opposite framing from this card's gain-of-expression enhancement; no trial administers or upregulates the enzyme, and none tests the colour phenotype.

Manipulation: base editing knockout (adenine base editor delivered by GalNAc-lipid nanoparticle to hepatocytes); also natural loss-of-function
Narrative: ANGPTL3 was found the way several of the best lipid targets were found: by noticing people who were unusually healthy. Sequencing across the DiscovEHR cohort turned up 246 heterozygotes among European-ancestry participants, roughly 1 in 237, whose blood carried about half the normal amount of the protein and correspondingly less fat - and who reached the clinic with coronary artery disease considerably less often than everyone else (Dewey 2017, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1612790). The protein is a hepatokine, made by the liver and released into blood, where it does nothing more complicated than sit on two enzymes and stop them working: lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase, the machines that strip triglycerides out of circulating lipoproteins. Remove the brake and both lipases run faster. What lifted this from an interesting genotype to a clinical program is a property that sounds technical and is actually decisive: the LDL-lowering half of the effect does not need the LDL receptor. For a patient with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, whose LDL receptors do not work at all, statins and PCSK9 inhibitors have little to push against - the entire mechanism they rely on is missing. ANGPTL3 loss bypasses it. Getting an editor into such a liver posed its own version of the same problem, because the standard lipid nanoparticle also arrives via the LDL receptor. The fix was to decorate the particle with GalNAc sugar so it docks instead on the asialoglycoprotein receptor, and it worked spectacularly in LDL-receptor-deficient monkeys (Kasiewicz 2023, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-37465-1). Two companies are now doing this in living patients. Both trials are single-ascending-dose, both are primarily asking whether it is safe, and both write a change into the genome that no one yet knows how to undo.
Short Description: Switching off a liver-secreted brake on fat clearance releases two lipases at once, so triglycerides and LDL cholesterol fall together after a single infusion instead of a daily pill. In monkeys bred without a working LDL receptor, one dose of a GalNAc-targeted base editor raised liver editing from 5% to 61% and held circulating ANGPTL3 protein down by up to 89% at six months. Two Phase 1 trials are recruiting patients right now - VERVE-201 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06451770) and CTX310 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07491172) - and the same pathway is already drugged by the approved antibody evinacumab. Humans born with one inactive copy carry 27% lower triglycerides and 41% lower odds of coronary artery disease, though the heart-attack arm never reached significance. The edit is a permanent letter change in hepatocyte DNA: monkeys showed transient rises in the liver enzymes ALT and AST, and there is no way to dial it back if a carrier later needs their lipids.
Mechanism: ANGPTL3, angiopoietin-like protein 3, is a 460-amino-acid hepatokine: the liver makes it and secretes it into the bloodstream, where it inhibits two enzymes that hydrolyse circulating fat, lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase. Losing the protein de-represses both, so triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are broken down faster and their remnants cleared sooner. The LDL-cholesterol-lowering arm of the effect does not require the LDL receptor, and that independence is the whole clinical rationale, because it makes the mechanism usable in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia where the LDL-receptor route is simply absent. The therapeutic version installs the loss permanently instead of inhibiting the protein repeatedly. An adenine base editor - a Cas9 protein fused to a deaminase, supplied as messenger RNA together with a guide RNA - is packaged inside a lipid nanoparticle whose surface carries an N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) ligand. That ligand binds the asialoglycoprotein receptor on hepatocytes, giving the particle a way into liver cells that does not depend on the LDL receptor. Once inside, the editor converts a single adenine to guanine at a splice or coding position, disrupting the gene without cutting both DNA strands, so one infusion produces a knockout that persists as the cell divides rather than a drug level that has to be maintained.
Achievements (effect sizes): Humans born with one inactive copy of the gene have "27% lower triglyceride levels than noncarriers (P = 2.5x10-21), 9% lower LDL cholesterol levels (P = 2.8x10-5), and 4% lower HDL cholesterol levels (P = 0.02)", and "a 41% lower odds of coronary artery disease (adjusted odds ratio for any loss-of-function variant, 0.59; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.41 to 0.85; P = 0.004)" across up to 45,226 DiscovEHR participants (Dewey 2017, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1612790). The same study puts carrier frequency at 1 in 237 participants of European ancestry and confirms haploinsufficiency biochemically, with median protein of 50 ng/mL in 125 carriers against 99 ng/mL in 53 matched noncarriers (P = 9.4x10-16); the myocardial-infarction arm, however, was only numerically lower (odds ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.06, P = 0.09) and should not be cited as a significant benefit. On the therapeutic side, adding a GalNAc ligand to the lipid nanoparticle "increased liver editing from 5% to 61% with minimal editing in nontargeted tissues" in LDL-receptor-deficient monkeys, produced "durable blood ANGPTL3 protein reduction up to 89% six months post dosing" against 13% for a standard particle, and drove blood LDL cholesterol down by 35% - roughly a 100 mg/dL absolute fall - stable for three months (Kasiewicz 2023, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-37465-1). Specificity and dose-sensitivity were both quantified in the same work: across 17 additional sites and tissues, editing outside the liver stayed under 2%, while in Ldlr-knockout mice "as little as 0.01 mol % GalNAc-Lipid substantially rescued editing to a mean of 26.3%" from 1.3% with none at all, and 0.05 mol % gave the best result of 31.4%, with higher ligand densities performing worse.
Highest Evidence Tier: T9 (human clinical - two independent Phase 1 in vivo gene-editing trials actively recruiting, backed by human loss-of-function genetics n>58,000 and single-dose nonhuman-primate durability to 6 months)
Translational Gaps: Neither editing trial has released human efficacy data. VERVE-201's Phase 1b primary endpoint is safety - treatment-emergent and serious adverse events through Day 365 - and the numbers a visitor would care about, percent change in serum ANGPTL3, LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, are secondary endpoints only (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06451770). Durability in monkeys has been shown to six months and no further, so anyone claiming a lifelong knockout is extrapolating from half a year of primate data. The permanence works in both directions: because the editor rewrites hepatocyte DNA rather than occupying a protein, there is no dose to reduce and no way to restore the gene if a recipient later needs their lipid transport intact, for instance during a wasting illness or a pregnancy. Most importantly, no outcome trial exists for any ANGPTL3 editor, so the claim that editing prevents heart attacks rests entirely on carrier genetics - an odds ratio of 0.59 for coronary artery disease in people who were born this way (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1612790) - rather than on any edited human having avoided an event.
Key References (DOIs): Dewey New England Journal of Medicine 2017 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1612790 | Kasiewicz Nature Communications 2023 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-37465-1 | Pinzon Grimaldos Journal of Translational Medicine 2025 https://doi.org/10.1186/s12967-025-07448-5
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: A direction audit matters here, because the registry is crowded with the opposite modality. Of 46 ClinicalTrials.gov records returned for ANGPTL3, only two are gene-editing interventions in which the gene itself is the treatment: VERVE-201 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06451770), base editing, and CTX310 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07491172), a Cas9 nuclease. The remainder are antisense and small interfering RNA agents (vupanorsen, zodasiran/ARO-ANG3, olezarsen-class, ALN-ANG3, solbinsiran), the approved antibody evinacumab (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03452228), observational carrier studies such as the University of Pennsylvania physiology protocol (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04234724), and a long tail of records where the protein was merely measured as a biomarker, including pecan- and cottonseed-oil feeding studies and a ketogenic-diet trial. Two Novartis cartilage-regeneration trials of LNA043 also surface in these searches and have nothing to do with this gene. Verve's earlier VERVE-101 and VERVE-102 programs target PCSK9, not ANGPTL3, and should not be conflated with the separate pcsk9_edit entry in this library. On the biology of the low-lipid state itself, a 2025 study of familial combined hypolipidemia type 2 reports that lipid deprivation amplifies type I interferon responses in monocytes through altered protein prenylation, meaning the immune cells of a lipid-poor body behave measurably differently (Pinzon Grimaldos 2025, https://doi.org/10.1186/s12967-025-07448-5). Pharmacological inhibition of the same pathway is already approved: evinacumab (Evkeeza, Regeneron) is licensed for homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, a different modality reaching the same axis. Reference structures are UniProt Q9Y5C1 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q9Y5C1) and the single solved structure PDB 6EUA (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/6EUA). One cross-entry collision belongs in this record as much as in the other one. The GalNAc ligand that carries this editor into hepatocytes docks on the asialoglycoprotein receptor, whose major subunit is the product of ASGR1 (Kasiewicz 2023, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-37465-1). The separate asgr1_lof entry in this library sells loss of that subunit as a cardiovascular benefit, so a visitor who buys both has removed the docking site this delivery route depends on, and has built a contradiction rather than a stack.

Manipulation: Loss-of-function knockout (human null variants R19X / IVS2+1G>A / IVS3+1G>T)
Narrative:
Most cardiovascular genetics is about cholesterol. This one is about the other half of the lipid problem: the fat-laden particles that leave the gut and liver after a meal, and how fast the body takes them apart. Apolipoprotein C-III is a small protein that rides on those particles and acts as a brake, blocking the enzyme that hydrolyses their triglyceride in the capillary bed and slowing their removal by the liver. Some people are born without a working copy of it, and the brake is never installed.

In 2014 two research groups arrived at the same answer from opposite directions in the same issue of the same journal. One sequenced the exomes of thousands of Americans, found four rare loss-of-function variants in the gene, and tested them against coronary disease in 110,970 people. The other went through 75,725 participants of two Danish population studies with 10,797 incident vascular events on the books. Carriers had triglycerides 39% and 44% lower respectively, and their risk of coronary heart disease was 40% lower in the American cohort and 41% lower for ischemic vascular disease in the Danish one. That kind of agreement between an exome-sequencing study and a population cohort is unusually strong replication for a rare-variant result.

What makes this card different from most of the library is that the enhancement is already for sale, and the FDA has read the file. Ionis Pharmaceuticals built an antisense oligonucleotide that finds the messenger RNA for this protein inside hepatocytes and destroys it — a pharmacological imitation of being born a carrier — and sells it as TRYNGOLZA for familial chylomicronemia syndrome and severe hypertriglyceridemia. Arrowhead reached the same target by RNA interference with plozasiran. A visitor buying this gene is buying a phenotype that roughly one person in 150 already has, that two independent cohorts of a hundred thousand people agree about, and that two companies have independently turned into a product.
Short Description: Deletes the brake on fat clearance, so triglyceride-rich particles are stripped out of the bloodstream within hours instead of lingering — the inhibitor that normally shuts down lipoprotein lipase in the capillary bed is simply absent. Roughly one person in 150 already carries such a broken copy, and they run 39% lower triglycerides for life with 40% less coronary heart disease (odds ratio 0.60). The pharmacological version is on sale: olezarsen, marketed as TRYNGOLZA, is an FDA-approved antisense drug that silences the same protein in the liver and cut triglycerides by 53.1 percentage points against placebo at its higher dose. The catch is that this is not the LDL axis — in the same trial olezarsen lowered apolipoprotein B and non-HDL cholesterol but produced no significant change in LDL cholesterol, so LDL-driven atherosclerosis is left untouched. The germline allele is free and permanent; the drug is a monthly injection for life.
Mechanism: Apolipoprotein C-III (apoC-III) is a 99-amino-acid protein secreted by liver and intestine that coats chylomicrons and very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL). It works as a double brake on the clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins: it inhibits lipoprotein lipase (LPL), the enzyme that hydrolyses triglyceride as those particles pass through the capillary bed, and it inhibits hepatic uptake of the leftover remnant particles through the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) and LDL receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1). Nonsense and splice-site null alleles remove the inhibitor altogether, so LPL runs unopposed and remnants are cleared faster. Because that clearance route is driven by LPL and remnant receptors rather than by the LDL receptor pathway, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol is essentially unchanged — the cardiovascular protection arrives entirely through the triglyceride-rich lipoprotein axis. The antisense and RNA-interference drugs reproduce the same state by destroying the messenger RNA in hepatocytes rather than by altering the gene.
Achievements (effect sizes): Exome sequencing of 18,666 genes in 3,734 participants identified rare loss-of-function variants in APOC3, and follow-up association testing in 110,970 people compared 498 carriers against 110,472 noncarriers. Triglyceride levels in carriers were 39% lower than in noncarriers (P<1×10^-20), circulating apoC-III was 46% lower (P=8×10^-10), and coronary heart disease risk was 40% lower, with an odds ratio of 0.60 (95% CI 0.47–0.75; P=4×10^-6); about one person in 150 carried one of the four variants (Crosby / TG-HDL Working Group 2014, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1307095). Independently, 75,725 participants of the Copenhagen City Heart Study and Copenhagen General Population Study, contributing 10,797 incident ischemic vascular disease events, showed a mean reduction in nonfasting triglycerides of 44% (P<0.001) in heterozygotes, a 41% lower risk of ischemic vascular disease (hazard ratio 0.59; 95% CI 0.41–0.86; P=0.007) and a 36% lower risk of ischemic heart disease (HR 0.64; 95% CI 0.41–0.99; P=0.04) (Jørgensen 2014, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1308027). The pharmacological phenocopy has since been tested head-to-head against placebo: in Bridge-TIMI 73a, a phase 2b randomized trial in 154 patients at 24 North American sites with a median baseline triglyceride of 241.5 mg/dL, olezarsen reduced triglycerides by 49.3 percentage points at 50 mg and 53.1 percentage points at 80 mg relative to placebo over six months (P<0.001 for both) (Bergmark 2024, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2402309).
Highest Evidence Tier: T8 (human loss-of-function genetics in more than 180,000 people, replicated across two independent cohorts, plus an FDA-approved drug that phenocopies the allele)
Translational Gaps: The 40% reduction in coronary heart disease is a property of the germline allele, measured in people who were born without the protein and lived their whole lives that way. The drugs deliver a comparable triglyceride reduction over months rather than decades, and cardiovascular outcome trials for apoC-III lowering have not yet reported, so nobody has yet shown that starting the knockdown in middle age buys the same protection from heart attacks. Full biallelic APOC3 deficiency in humans is very rare and its long-term phenotype is essentially uncharacterised, which means the exhibit's version of this gene — both copies gone — is less well described in humans than the single-copy version the epidemiology rests on. The approved indications are also narrower than the enhancement framing: the label covers familial chylomicronemia syndrome and severe hypertriglyceridemia, not primary prevention in healthy people.
Key References (DOIs): The TG and HDL Working Group of the Exom New England Journal of Medicine 2014 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1307095 | Jørgensen New England Journal of Medicine 2014 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1308027 | Bergmark New England Journal of Medicine 2024 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2402309
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The two 2014 papers reached the same conclusion by different routes — United States exome sequencing (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1307095) versus Danish population cohorts (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1308027) — which is unusually strong replication for a rare-variant association. Two companies now sell an apoC-III-lowering agent by different modalities: olezarsen is a GalNAc-conjugated antisense oligonucleotide approved as TRYNGOLZA under NDA 218614 (Ionis), given as a monthly subcutaneous injection at 80 mg for familial chylomicronemia syndrome and 50 mg for severe hypertriglyceridemia, and plozasiran is a quarterly small interfering RNA marketed by Arrowhead as REDEMPLO. The pivotal records are the Balance phase 3 study (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04568434) and PALISADE (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05089084), with further phase 3 recruitment ongoing (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07727538). Where the literature disagrees is on which agent is better: matching-adjusted indirect comparisons find no statistically significant efficacy difference between olezarsen and either volanesorsen or plozasiran in familial chylomicronemia syndrome (https://doi.org/10.57264/cer-2026-0069 and https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacl.2026.05.001), so claims of superiority between these drugs are not currently supported.

Narrative: One woman in Colombia should have lost her memory in her forties. She carried PSEN1-E280A, the mutation that runs through the world's largest known autosomal dominant Alzheimer's kindred, about 1,200 identified carriers within an extended family that this record gives as over 6000 members around Medellin, and which in that family reliably produces mild cognitive impairment in the mid-forties. She reached her seventies intact, roughly 30 years late. When Arboleda-Velasquez and colleagues worked out why, they found two copies of an extraordinarily rare APOE3 variant, Christchurch, in which arginine 136 is replaced by serine; her brain carried an unusually heavy amyloid burden but strikingly limited tau tangles and little neurodegeneration (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-019-0611-3). That single case reframed the field, because it separated amyloid from the downstream damage and pointed at APOE as the switch between them. The cell-biology groundwork was already in place. In 2018 Wang and colleagues in Yadong Huang's group showed that human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons homozygous for APOE4 carried elevated phosphorylated tau independent of their increased amyloid-beta production and lost GABAergic neurons, and that converting APOE4 to APOE3 by gene editing rescued all of those phenotypes (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-018-0004-z). In 2023 Nelson and colleagues closed the loop by engineering the R136S change into APOE4 itself, in both human stem-cell neurons and mice, and found that the homozygous edit protected against APOE4-driven tau pathology, neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-023-01480-8). Editing a patient's APOE4 alleles toward a protective form is now arguably the sharpest genetic target in Alzheimer's prevention. Two things stand in the way. Nobody has achieved a brain-wide APOE edit in a living animal, and the obvious protective allele carries a metabolic penalty of its own: APOE2 homozygosity raises the risk of a lipid disorder that clogs arteries.
Short Description: This secreted lipid-carrier shuttles cholesterol between brain cells and helps clear amyloid-beta out of the space between neurons; the high-risk version does the clearing badly, so plaque accumulates and tau pathology follows. A Colombian woman carrying a mutation that guarantees early-onset Alzheimer's disease stayed cognitively intact into her seventies, roughly 30 years past her family's expected onset, because she had two copies of a rare variant called Christchurch. Editing the risky allele reverses tau phosphorylation and neuron loss in human stem-cell-derived neurons and in mice, but no one has edited the gene across a living brain; the best delivery result so far knocked expression down by only 12.6% in one hippocampus. The protective E2 allele carries its own price, since roughly 5 to 10% of E2 homozygotes develop type III hyperlipoproteinaemia.
Mechanism: Apolipoprotein E is a 299-amino-acid secreted glycoprotein that carries cholesterol and phospholipid between cells; in the brain, astrocytes are the main source and neurons the main customer. The three common human alleles differ at just two positions: E4 has arginine at both 112 and 158, E3 has cysteine at 112 and arginine at 158, and E2 has cysteine at both. Those substitutions change the protein's conformation. In E4, arginine 112 permits a salt bridge that draws the N-terminal and C-terminal domains together, and this domain interaction is the structural basis proposed for E4's toxicity, which is why small molecules that break it are called structure correctors (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-018-0004-z). Functionally, E4 promotes amyloid-beta aggregation and impairs its clearance through the LRP1 receptor and heparan sulfate proteoglycan (HSPG) routes, and it independently raises tau phosphorylation, an effect that persists in stem-cell neurons even when amyloid-beta production is pharmacologically suppressed. The Christchurch variant is a different kind of change: R136S sits in the receptor-binding region and weakens the protein's interaction with heparan sulfate proteoglycans, which reduces HSPG-dependent uptake of extracellular tau into neurons, preserves lipid handling by microglia and dampens neuroinflammation. In stem-cell neurons the effect on tau uptake is direct: homozygous R136S neurons already showed reduced uptake of labelled tau, and treating APOE4 neurons with heparin, which blocks the same interaction, lowered uptake by about 40% to levels indistinguishable from the edited or APOE-knockout cells (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-023-01480-8). E2 achieves partly overlapping protection through the same receptor-binding weakness.
Achievements (effect sizes): Wang and colleagues generated human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons homozygous for APOE4 and found higher levels of phosphorylated tau that were unrelated to their increased amyloid-beta production, together with degeneration and loss of GABAergic neurons confirmed by immunofluorescent staining against isogenic APOE3 lines; converting APOE4 to APOE3 by gene editing rescued each of these phenotypes, and neurons lacking APOE entirely behaved like APOE3 neurons while reintroducing APOE4 recapitulated the pathology, establishing the effect as a gain of toxic function rather than a loss of protection. Treating APOE4 neurons with beta-secretase or gamma-secretase inhibitors cut amyloid-beta levels by more than 95%, yet phosphorylated tau was unaffected, which is the direct evidence that the tau effect is amyloid-independent; a small-molecule structure corrector ameliorated the detrimental effects (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-018-0004-z). Nelson and colleagues engineered the R136S mutation into APOE4 in human stem-cell neurons and in mice. Homozygous APOE4-R136S neurons showed roughly a 40% reduction in phosphorylated tau relative to APOE4 neurons, while heterozygous R136S neurons showed no such reduction; in PS19 tauopathy mice carrying human APOE, the APOE4 animals had significantly reduced hippocampal volume at 10 months against wild-type and APOE3 controls, and hippocampal atrophy in the homozygous R136S animals was reduced to levels comparable with wild-type and APOE3, alongside reduced neuroinflammation (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-023-01480-8). Arboleda-Velasquez and colleagues reported the clinical case: a PSEN1-E280A carrier from a kindred of roughly 1,200 identified Colombian mutation carriers, drawn from an extended family the record gives as over 6000 members, who did not develop mild cognitive impairment until her seventies, roughly 30 years after the expected age of clinical onset, homozygous for APOE3-Christchurch (R136S), with unusually high brain amyloid but limited tau, tangle and neurodegeneration measures (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-019-0611-3). Two papers published in 2025 extended the approach into living animals. Golden and colleagues built an inducible knock-in mouse that synthesises E4 at baseline and E2 after tamoxifen; a whole-body allelic switch produced a metabolic profile resembling human E2/E2 and, on the 5xFAD background, an astrocyte-specific E4-to-E2 switch improved cognition, decreased amyloid pathology, lowered gliosis and reduced plaque-associated apolipoprotein E (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-025-02094-y). Zheng and colleagues used focused ultrasound to transiently open the blood-brain barrier and deliver an all-in-one CRISPR-based AAV vector intravenously at 1.5 x 10^12 viral genomes per mouse, achieving 12.6% knockdown of humanised APOE4 expression in the targeted hippocampus with more than a 20% fall in apoE4 protein and significant reductions in astrocyte and microglia levels (https://doi.org/10.1002/alz.70464).
Highest Evidence Tier: T6
Translational Gaps: No brain-wide APOE edit has been achieved in any animal. The two in-vivo 2025 results define the current ceiling and both fall short of it in instructive ways: the allelic-switch mouse works because the switch is built into the genome and triggered pharmacologically rather than delivered, which is not an option in a patient (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-025-02094-y), and the focused-ultrasound delivery that is translatable in principle reached only 12.6% knockdown of APOE4 expression in a single targeted hippocampus (https://doi.org/10.1002/alz.70464). Getting an editor across the blood-brain barrier at therapeutic coverage, by adeno-associated virus or lipid nanoparticle, is therefore the central unsolved problem. Off-target base editing is the second: APOE3 and APOE4 differ by a single base, so the edit demands precision at a site where the wrong outcome is permanent. Mosaicism is the third, since partial editing leaves a mixed population of astrocytes whose net effect on amyloid and tau handling is unmeasured. And the destination allele carries its own risk: roughly 5 to 10% of APOE2 homozygotes develop type III hyperlipoproteinaemia, so switching a patient from E4 to E2 trades a neurodegenerative risk for a cardiovascular one. The only registered trial in this record is not a gene-editing study at all: a completed 380-participant phase 2 dose-ranging study of the 5-HT6 antagonist SB-742457 in Alzheimer's disease, which began enrolling in the autumn of 2005, in which APOE appears among the measures rather than as the intervention (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00224497).

Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Several caveats bear directly on whether this edit would work in a human. APOE2 homozygosity carries its own risk, with roughly 5 to 10% of E2 homozygotes developing type III hyperlipoproteinaemia, so the protective allele is not free. The Christchurch evidence is a single case, which is the sharpest limitation in the record: the variant is extraordinarily rare, and one patient, however thoroughly characterised, cannot establish an effect size (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-019-0611-3). That case also sits on a different genetic background from the intended therapeutic target. The Colombian woman was APOE3-Christchurch, not APOE4-Christchurch, so the proposition that R136S rescues an E4 background rests on the engineered mouse and stem-cell work rather than on any human observation (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-023-01480-8). Species specificity is a further complication and cuts against relying on mouse models: APOE4 increased amyloid-beta production in human neurons but not in mouse neurons (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-018-0004-z), so a mouse cannot report on the amyloid arm of the mechanism. Finally, the protection is dose-dependent in a way that matters for any editing strategy that achieves partial conversion: heterozygous R136S neurons did not show the reduction in phosphorylated tau that homozygous neurons did, so a one-allele edit may deliver little or nothing (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-023-01480-8). One bookkeeping note: this gene's record also carries https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2018.05.007, which resolves in Crossref to a 2018 Neuron paper by Chen and colleagues titled 'It's About Time: Temporal Dynamics of Dentate Gyrus Pattern Separation', a paper unrelated to APOE (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2018.05.007). It is retained in key_references because the house rules require keeping every DOI already present, but no claim in this entry rests on it.

Narrative: Aquaporins are membrane pores so narrow that water crosses them in single file, which is how a cell moves water about ten times faster than plain diffusion would allow while still excluding ions and protons. Peter Agre shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for identifying them, and the experiment that settled the matter was elegantly simple: inject frog eggs with RNA encoding the red-cell protein CHIP28, and the eggs swell as water rushes in, an effect reversibly blocked by mercuric chloride (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.256.5055.385). Deleting the gene in mice produces a real and measurable phenotype. The animals cannot concentrate their urine and become severely dehydrated and lethargic when water is withheld (https://doi.org/10.1074/jbc.273.8.4296). The same defect in humans is a curiosity rather than a disease: people of the Colton-null blood group lack aquaporin-1 and are grossly normal. The Australian water-holding frog Cyclorana platycephala survives months of drought sealed in a cocoon, and is frequently invoked as carrying a supercharged aquaporin-1 worth transplanting into a human. Here the chain of evidence breaks at its first link: the frog's own aquaporin-1 has never been cloned, sequenced or functionally characterised. What has actually been measured in the frog is whole-animal water balance, and the animal's survival strategy turns out to rest on the cocoon, on metabolic depression and on bladder water storage rather than on any single channel (https://doi.org/10.1086/523856). Worse for the premise, the one aestivating vertebrate in which branchial aquaporin-1 expression has been measured through dormancy shows it going down, not up (https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2016.00532). This entry is therefore best read as a case study in how a plausible enhancement story can be assembled entirely from sources that do not support it.
Short Description: Four copies of this protein assemble into a pore so narrow that water molecules cross single-file, moving water through a membrane roughly ten times faster than diffusion alone allows. Mice engineered to lack it lose 35% of body weight after 36 hours without water and cannot concentrate their urine, yet humans born without it, the Colton-null blood group, notice nothing in ordinary life. The drought-surviving Australian water-holding frog is routinely credited with a supercharged version, but its aquaporin-1 has never been cloned or functionally tested in any laboratory. The closest real data point runs the wrong way: in African lungfish entering dry-season dormancy, aquaporin-1 transcript and protein levels fall rather than rise.
Mechanism: Aquaporin-1 is a constitutively active, water-selective channel. Four identical subunits assemble into a tetramer in the membrane, and each subunit forms its own pore, so one tetramer carries four independent conduction pathways. The pore's selectivity comes from two features in series: a constriction, the aromatic/arginine region, whose diameter admits a single water molecule at a time and whose fixed positive charge repels protons, and a pair of asparagine-proline-alanine motifs whose carbonyl groups hand each water molecule along by hydrogen bonding while forcing a reorientation that breaks the proton-hopping chain. The result is a channel that conducts water at near diffusion-limited rates while excluding ions, including the hydronium ion that would otherwise short-circuit the membrane potential. Unlike aquaporin-2, whose surface abundance is controlled by vasopressin, aquaporin-1 is not gated or trafficked on demand; it is always open, and physiological control is exerted through where and how much of it a tissue makes. In mammals it is expressed almost everywhere, with the highest densities in the renal proximal tubule and descending limb of Henle, in vasa recta endothelium and in erythrocytes, which is why deleting it specifically breaks the countercurrent multiplication that concentrates urine (https://doi.org/10.1074/jbc.273.8.4296).
Achievements (effect sizes): The founding experiment on aquaporin-1 generally is the 1992 demonstration by Preston and colleagues that Xenopus laevis oocytes microinjected with in-vitro-transcribed CHIP28 RNA acquired increased osmotic water permeability, a rise conventionally quoted as 10 to 20-fold, reversibly inhibited by mercuric chloride, establishing CHIP28 as a functional water channel (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.256.5055.385). The knockout phenotype was established by Ma, Verkman and colleagues, who disrupted the gene in mice and found osmotic water permeability in proximal tubule membrane vesicles reduced eight-fold relative to wild type; after 36 hours of water deprivation the knockout animals became severely dehydrated and lethargic, body weight fell by 35 ± 2% against 20 to 22% in wild-type and heterozygous littermates, serum osmolality rose above 500 mOsm while wild-type stayed at 310 to 330 mOsm, and urine osmolality of 657 ± 59 mOsm failed to rise at all and could not be raised by the V2 agonist DDAVP (https://doi.org/10.1074/jbc.273.8.4296). Follow-up micropuncture work in the same knockout line found unanaesthetised animals drinking 2.8 times more fluid than wild type with baseline urine osmolality of 505 ± 40 mOsm against 1081 ± 68 mOsm in wild type, and transepithelial osmotic water permeability in isolated microperfused S2 proximal tubule segments of 0.033 ± 0.005 cm/s against 0.15 ± 0.03 cm/s, a reduction of roughly five-fold, alongside the 5 to 8-fold proximal-tubule permeability deficits reported for this line (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.95.16.9660). Humans of the Colton-null blood group, who lack the protein, are subclinical. Against that mammalian background, the source-organism side of this entry is empty: the Cyclorana-specific aquaporin-1 has not been cloned and has not been functionally characterised, and all published work on the frog is whole-animal physiology. Cartledge, Withers and Bradshaw followed cocooned Cyclorana platycephala through a 15-month aestivation and found the frogs losing up to 36 ± 6.5% of initial standard mass, plasma osmolality climbing to 487 mOsm/kg by the ninth month and then holding stable to the fifteenth, and urine osmolality continuing to rise until plasma and urine were isosmotic, with the pattern of slow plasma concentration indicating that bladder water was being drawn on to defend circulating volume (https://doi.org/10.1086/523856). Bladder water storage in cocooning frogs of this kind has been reported at up to 50 to 60% of body mass, a figure carried in this record from the earlier text that I could not trace to the Cartledge paper or to another source. Desiccation tolerance in this animal is therefore a composite of the cocoon, metabolic depression, bladder storage, urea accumulation and skin-type water channels, not aquaporin-1 acting alone.
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 for mammalian endogenous AQP1 (Colton-null); T0–T1 for Cyclorana-specific AQP1
Translational Gaps: The entire frog-to-human enhancement chain is missing its first link. No Cyclorana aquaporin cDNA has been published, so there is no sequence to synthesise; with no sequence there has been no heterologous expression in any mammalian system, and with no expression there is no functional measurement showing the frog protein outperforms the human one. Even if that work were done, the mammalian baseline sets a low ceiling on what a gain-of-function could deliver: humans who lack aquaporin-1 entirely are essentially asymptomatic, which argues that this channel is not the rate-limiting step in human water retention (https://doi.org/10.1074/jbc.273.8.4296). The registered trials that mention aquaporins measure them rather than treat with them, and none tests water retention: an international paediatric peritoneal biobank collecting biopsy samples from 500 participants (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01893710), a 407-participant renal cell carcinoma biomarker study (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02923284) and a 200-participant study of renal progenitors and polyploid tubular cells in glomerular and tubular disease (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06325059). The one trial in which the gene is genuinely the treatment points in an unrelated therapeutic direction: a phase 1 study delivering AAV2hAQP1, an adeno-associated viral vector encoding human aquaporin-1, to a single parotid salivary gland in 17 people with irradiation-induced salivary hypofunction after head and neck cancer, to restore saliva production rather than whole-body hydration (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02446249).
Key References (DOIs): Preston Science 1992 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.256.5055.385 | Ma Journal of Biological Chemistry 1998 https://doi.org/10.1074/jbc.273.8.4296 | Schnermann Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 1998 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.95.16.9660 | Cartledge Physiological and Biochemical Zoology 2008 https://doi.org/10.1086/523856 | Chng Frontiers in Physiology 2016 https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2016.00532 | Noren Physiological and Biochemical Zoology 2008 https://doi.org/10.1086/588489
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The central contradiction in this record runs directly against the model that more aquaporin-1 means more water retention. In the African lungfish Protopterus annectens, which aestivates on land through drought, branchial aquaporin-1 transcript levels fell significantly during the induction phase of aestivation while protein abundance initially held steady, and both transcript and protein were then significantly down-regulated during the maintenance phase, alongside aquaporin-3 (https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2016.00532). An animal actually solving the problem of surviving desiccation reduced its water channels rather than adding them, which is the opposite of what this enhancement proposes; the likely reason is that once branchial function shuts down, an open water channel is a leak rather than an asset. The second caveat is the human genetics. Colton-null individuals lack aquaporin-1 and are asymptomatic under ordinary conditions, so the protein's dose-response curve in humans is flat across the range that matters, making a dramatic gain-of-function unlikely (https://doi.org/10.1074/jbc.273.8.4296). Third, even the mouse phenotype is mild at baseline: knockout animals are normal in survival, appearance and organ morphology, and only decompensate when water is withheld (https://doi.org/10.1074/jbc.273.8.4296). Finally, a bookkeeping problem worth recording: the DOI https://doi.org/10.1086/588489, which the previous version of this entry attached to Cartledge, resolves in Crossref to a 2008 paper by Noren and colleagues on thermoregulation in Weddell seals (https://doi.org/10.1086/588489), which is unrelated to frog water balance. The correct Cartledge, Withers and Bradshaw paper on Cyclorana water balance is https://doi.org/10.1086/523856.

Narrative:
Bats carry viruses that devastate other mammals — Ebola, SARS-CoV-2, Nipah — and do not get sick from them. A large part of that tolerance comes from their inflammasomes, the intracellular sensor complexes that convert danger signals into interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18 release. Bats have altered inflammasome signalling, and ASC2 is one of the pieces that alters it. It is a PYD-only protein, meaning it consists essentially of the interaction domain and nothing else, and it acts as a competitive brake on inflammasome assembly rather than on any single cytokine downstream.

Wang and colleagues found that bat ASC2 is highly expressed at both the messenger RNA and protein levels and is highly potent at inhibiting both human and mouse inflammasomes, with four key residues responsible for the gain of function relative to the human protein (Ahn 2023, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2023.03.036). The evolutionary logic is a tradeoff resolved in an unusual direction: powered flight imposes an oxidative and thermal load that would trigger chronic inflammation in a comparably sized mammal, and bats appear to have bought tolerance of that load, and of the viruses they carry, by raising the threshold at which inflammation fires at all. Bats also live exceptionally long for their body size, and inflammation is one of the processes that ties infection biology to ageing biology.
Short Description: Bats hold their inflammatory alarm below the level at which it damages their own tissue, which is how they survive both the oxidative load of powered flight and a lifetime of viral infection. Four bat-specific amino acid residues make their version of this inflammasome brake far stronger than the human one, and mice engineered to carry it shrugged off gout-crystal peritonitis, showed dampened inflammation from several viruses, survived influenza A at higher rates and suppressed SARS-CoV-2 immune-complex-driven inflammasome activation. Paratus Sciences launched on a $100 million Series A built around this biology and is aiming its lead antibody-fusion candidate at a first-in-human trial in 2027. Capping the inflammasome is also, precisely, how you produce an immunosuppressed patient.
Mechanism: ASC2 is a pyrin-domain-only protein. It competitively binds the pyrin domains of the NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasome sensors, which blocks nucleation of the ASC speck — the large filamentous platform that inflammasome assembly depends on — and thereby prevents caspase-1 activation and the maturation and release of interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18. Because the block sits at the shared assembly node rather than at any one sensor or cytokine, it caps the whole inflammatory output below the threshold at which it damages the animal's own tissue. Four bat-specific residues, identified as responsible for the gain of function relative to the human protein, make the bat version substantially more potent; the record gives that difference as roughly tenfold (Ahn 2023, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2023.03.036).
Achievements (effect sizes):
Transgenic expression of bat ASC2 in mice reduced the severity of peritonitis induced by gout crystals and by ASC particles. The same mice showed dampened inflammation induced by multiple viruses and reduced mortality from influenza A virus infection, and bat ASC2 also suppressed inflammasome activation driven by SARS-CoV-2 immune complexes. The four residues responsible for the gain of function were identified directly (Ahn 2023, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2023.03.036).

On the commercial side, Paratus Sciences launched in the spring of 2023 with a $100 million Series A financing co-led by Polaris Partners, ARCH Venture Partners, ClavystBio, EcoR1 Capital and Leaps by Bayer, built on bat comparative genomics (https://paratussciences.com/press-release/paratus-sciences-launches-with-100m-series-a-financing-to-develop-novel-therapeutics-based-on-the-unique-biology-of-bats/). Its lead candidate PS-1001, a VHH-Fc fusion protein developed under a collaboration with Duke-NUS Medical School, targets ASC itself rather than the bat protein, and is described as both preventing the assembly of new inflammasome complexes and disassembling existing ones (https://paratussciences.com/pipeline/).
Highest Evidence Tier: T5
Translational Gaps: Humans already have an ASC2 orthologue and it is far weaker, so this is not a case of activating something dormant: a gene therapy would have to deliver the bat-specific variant, with its four substituted residues, rather than upregulating the human gene. The obvious risk is the mechanism working as designed. An inflammasome brake potent enough to blunt influenza A mortality is potent enough to blunt inflammatory responses a patient needs, and the immunosuppression question has not been answered in any long-term model.
