Both enzymes localised to the endomembrane system rather than the mitochondria where hepatic 3-OH-echinenone concentrates, and the authors propose house finches use an alternative pathway altogether. This does not overturn Toomey 2022 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2022.08.013): the two papers concern different pigments, astaxanthin and canthaxanthin versus 3-OH-echinenone, and Toomey's own substrate-promiscuity data predict that the product depends on what the enzymes are fed. It does mean that "CYP2J19 makes birds red" is too broad a claim, and a 2025 review of avian ketocarotenoid substrates, intermediates and products indicates the pathway details are still being revised (Toomey 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbalip.2025.159654). The pathway is also spreading beyond birds in the literature: a 2025 paper implicates Bdh1l expression in cichlid fish colour diversity (https://doi.org/10.1111/mec.70065). On identifiers: the sequences used here are the chicken proteins named in Toomey's methods, CYP2J19 XP_422553.3 and BDH1L XP_004935295.3, with chicken TTC39B as A0A8V0YWD4 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A8V0YWD4). UniProt has no reviewed BDH1L entry, and the accession given for this record, A0A8V1A1M2 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A8V1A1M2), is an unreviewed Gallus gallus TrEMBL entry with an AlphaFold model but no experimental structure. There is no clinical or commercial program of any kind, although the pathway's product astaxanthin is sold as a dietary supplement made industrially in Haematococcus algae and engineered yeast - the molecule is on shop shelves even though the enzymatic route is not.

Narrative: Tardigrades survive doses of radiation that would vaporize a human — and they carry a protein called Dsup that drapes itself over DNA like a molecular bodyguard. When Japanese researchers put Dsup into human HEK293 kidney cells in 2016, the cells shrugged off X-ray damage that would normally shred their chromosomes, with DNA breaks cut roughly in half at 10 Gy. In 2025, an MIT/Dana-Farber team used lipid nanoparticles — the same delivery system as COVID vaccines — to briefly paint Dsup onto mouse mouth and rectal tissue during radiotherapy, sparing healthy cells while still killing the tumor. That's the first real demonstration of tardigrade radioprotection in a living mammal. The catch: in rat cortical neurons, Dsup did the opposite, causing more DNA damage, not less. The bodyguard works in some cells and goes rogue in others, and nobody yet knows why.
Short Description: Draped over chromosomes, this tardigrade protein blocks radicals and radiation from shredding DNA, halving X-ray damage in human kidney cells at 10 Gy. In 2025 mRNA in lipid nanoparticles painted it onto mouse mouth and rectal tissue during radiotherapy, sparing healthy cells while tumours still died. That was the first live-mammal proof, and no transgenic mouse or human trial exists. In rat neurons it backfired, causing more DNA breaks instead of fewer.
Mechanism: Intrinsically disordered nucleosome-binding protein (HMGN-like C-terminal motif per Chavez 2019, revised from Hashimoto 2016 direct-DNA model); shields chromatin from hydroxyl radicals and ionizing radiation.
Achievements (effect sizes): HEK293 at 10 Gy X-ray: comet tail DNA 33%→16% (~50% SSB reduction); H2O2: 71%→18%. Replicated in CHO, Drosophila, tobacco (UV-B recovery), yeast (longevity under H2O2). C. elegans: protection at 90 Gy X-ray without toxicity. Proton IR protection at 150 MeV. Rajesh/Kirtane 2025 Nat Biomed Eng: LNP-Dsup mRNA delivered to mouse buccal/rectal mucosa during radiotherapy reduced γH2AX and comet damage in peritumoral tissue while preserving tumor kill — first in-vivo mammalian demonstration.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (transient mRNA/LNP 2025) + T6 (≥4 independent labs) + T3 (C. elegans)
Translational Gaps: Germline transgenic mouse; durable delivery; heavy-ion/LET data; long-term mutagenesis surveillance; CNS-safe variant.
Key References (DOIs): Hashimoto Nat Commun 2016 https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms12808 | Chavez eLife 2019 https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.47682 | Escarcega Mol Cell Neurosci 2023 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mcn.2023.103826 | Kirtane/Rajesh Nat Biomed Eng 2025 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41551-025-01360-5
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CONTRADICTION: Escarcega 2023 — Dsup PROMOTED DSBs, chromatin condensation, and neurotoxicity in rat cortical neurons — opposite phenotype in CNS. Hashimoto direct-DNA-binding model superseded by nucleosome-binding (Chavez 2019). HEK293 protection is ~2-fold at best; no stable transgenic mouse. Basal chromatin perturbation and cell-type specificity unknown.

Narrative:
Halomonas elongata is a halophilic salt-lake bacterium that lives where the water is close to saturated brine. Its solution is not to pump sodium out faster than it leaks in, but to fill its own cytoplasm with something else: ectoine, a small zwitterionic ring built by three enzymes from an intermediate of ordinary amino-acid metabolism. Ectoine belongs to a class chemists call compatible solutes, meaning a cell can accumulate it to molar concentrations and every enzyme inside still works. It does its job by being politely absent — excluded from the thin shell of water that hugs a folded protein, which thermodynamically pushes that protein towards its compact native state and keeps membrane bilayers ordered even at crushing ionic strength.

Because the whole capability is three genes, it travels. A codon-optimised ectABC operon was moved out of Halomonas and into the freshwater cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus — a different phylum entirely — and the recipient became a salt-tolerant organism (https://doi.org/10.3389/fmicb.2023.1123081). That makes this one of the rare cards where a complete biosynthetic route, rather than a single protein, transfers intact between kingdoms of bacteria.

The strange part of ectoine's story is that it reached human beings long before genetics did. Bitop AG in Witten, Germany ferments Halomonas at industrial scale — a process the company calls bacterial milking, in which the bacteria are salted, make the solute, and give it up — and sells the purified molecule as the active ingredient in CE-marked nasal sprays, eye drops, inhalation solutions, lozenges and creams. Those products have gone through registered clinical studies in allergic rhinoconjunctivitis (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01471184), mild bronchial asthma (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01478152) and radiation-induced oral mucositis (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03932292). So a visitor can walk into a pharmacy and buy the output of this card. What no visitor can buy is the card itself: every human study delivers the finished molecule onto a mucosal surface, and no human cell has ever been asked to build ectoine for itself.
Short Description: Your cells fill themselves with a small ring-shaped molecule that holds water against the proteins and membranes, so they keep working in brine that would otherwise shrivel and denature them. Three bacterial enzymes build it from an amino-acid precursor, and it piles up to molar concentrations without poisoning a single enzyme. Cyanobacteria given the operon reached a final culture density 80% higher than wild type in 400 mM salt and survived 500 mM, which killed every wild-type cell. The molecule is already sold in pharmacies as CE-marked nasal spray and eye drops, and a placebo-controlled cross-over trial in 46 hay-fever patients beat placebo on all three of its composite symptom scores — but nobody has ever put the genes into a human cell. The cost is metabolic: the pathway draws on L-aspartate-beta-semialdehyde, the same precursor that feeds lysine, threonine and methionine, so engineered cells grow more slowly than wild type until the salt arrives.
Mechanism: Three enzymes convert L-aspartate-beta-semialdehyde into ectoine. EctB, a diaminobutyrate-2-oxoglutarate transaminase, makes L-2,4-diaminobutyrate (DABA); EctA, a DABA acetyltransferase, adds an acetyl group to its gamma-nitrogen; and EctC, L-ectoine synthase — a 137-amino-acid, 15.5 kDa cupin-fold enzyme that holds a single iron(II) ion — cyclises the product into the zwitterionic tetrahydropyrimidine ring that is ectoine. What ectoine then does is physical rather than catalytic. As a compatible solute it is preferentially excluded from the layer of water bound to a protein's surface, and that exclusion raises the free-energy cost of unfolding, so the folded state is thermodynamically favoured; the same exclusion preserves the ordered packing of membrane bilayers at high ionic strength. Because it neither binds nor inhibits anything, a cell can carry it at molar concentrations — which an inorganic osmolyte such as potassium chloride could never do without shutting enzymes down.
Achievements (effect sizes): A codon-optimised ectABC operon from Halomonas elongata was integrated into the chromosome of the freshwater cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942 at the neutral site NSI and driven from the strong Pcpc560 promoter. By day seven of photoautotrophic growth the engineered strain had “increased final OD750 by 20% under 300 mM NaCl and 80% under 400 mM NaCl than that of wild-type (WT), respectively”, and “could even survive under 500 mM NaCl which was lethal to WT”, reaching OD750 0.362 where no wild-type cell grew at all (Dong 2023, https://doi.org/10.3389/fmicb.2023.1123081). The molecule itself has been tested in people, though the genes never have: in a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled cross-over trial, 46 patients with seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis used ectoine eye drops plus nasal spray or placebo for 13 days before an allergen challenge in an environmental exposure chamber, and “the least square mean difference for baseline-adjusted AUC was -1.87 for TNSS, -1.45 for TOSS and -2.20 for TNNSS” — the trial's composite nasal, ocular and non-nasal symptom scores, each favouring ectoine over placebo (Salapatek 2021, https://doi.org/10.1002/clt2.12006). A broader review of the clinical and mechanistic evidence behind ectoine-containing devices is collected in Bilstein 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1155/2021/5562623).
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (transferable three-gene operon with heterologous gain-of-function in a second bacterial phylum, plus randomised placebo-controlled human trials of the product molecule and an on-market manufacturer)
Translational Gaps: The gap here is unusually clean, and it belongs on the card. Every human study delivers the ectoine molecule to a mucosal surface; no one has expressed ectA, ectB and ectC inside a human cell. Mammalian cells have no ectoine transporter of their own, so a genetic version cannot work by uptake and would have to install the entire three-enzyme biosynthetic route. That route draws carbon from L-aspartate-beta-semialdehyde, and the growth penalty this caused in cyanobacteria has never been measured in a mammalian metabolic background, where the same intermediate sits upstream of lysine, threonine and methionine synthesis. Nobody has shown that a human cell can hold ectoine at the concentrations that make it useful, and nobody has established what a human tissue does with molar quantities of a foreign solute over a lifetime rather than over the minutes a nasal spray contacts a mucosa.
Key References (DOIs): Dong Frontiers in Microbiology 2023 https://doi.org/10.3389/fmicb.2023.1123081 | Salapatek Clinical and Translational Allergy 2021 https://doi.org/10.1002/clt2.12006 | Bilstein BioMed Research International 2021 https://doi.org/10.1155/2021/5562623
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: This is one of the few entries in the library a visitor can simply buy. Bitop AG of Witten, Germany manufactures ectoine by fermenting Halomonas elongata and sells it as the active ingredient in CE-marked medical devices — nasal sprays, eye drops, inhalation solutions, lozenges and dermatological creams. In the European Union ectoine is a medical-device and cosmetic ingredient, not an approved drug. Two caveats about the human evidence deserve to be public. First, it is largely single-sponsor: Bitop is the sponsor of record on the large majority of registered ectoine studies, including the rhinoconjunctivitis cross-over trial (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01471184), the paediatric seasonal allergic rhinitis study (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01342601), the mild bronchial asthma inhalation study (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01478152) and the radiation-induced oral mucositis mouthwash study (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03932292), so the strongest independent feature of the evidence base is the cross-over design itself rather than sponsor diversity (https://doi.org/10.1002/clt2.12006). Second, in none of those studies is the gene the treatment: all four administer the purified molecule topically, so they support ectoine as a protectant and say nothing directly about expressing ectABC in a body. A direction check found no ectoine-blocking studies — every registered trial runs the same way this card does, with ectoine given as a protectant. The reference protein for the entry is EctC, ectoine synthase from H. elongata (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/O52251); no experimental structure of it is deposited in the Protein Data Bank, so any depiction is a homology or AlphaFold model.

Narrative: Tibetans live above 13,000 feet without the thick-blood sickness that plagues lowlanders who move to altitude. The cause is one of the most spectacular finds in human genetics: a 32-kilobase chunk of DNA, carrying the hypoxia-sensor gene EPAS1, that Tibetans inherited from Denisovans — an extinct hominin known only from a finger bone in a Siberian cave. The variant dampens EPAS1's response to low oxygen, so red blood cell counts stay safe instead of spiraling up. Tibetans with the adaptive version carry about 0.8 g/dL less hemoglobin at 4,200 meters. Knocking out the equivalent enhancer in human endothelial cells and in mice reproduces the blunted response. The same locus is a double-edged sword: gain-of-function mutations nearby cause Pacak-Zhuang syndrome (runaway blood production plus tumors), and Andean highlanders achieved a similar outcome through a completely different mutation — a textbook case of evolution finding two roads to the same summit.
Short Description: This gene senses low oxygen and signals more red blood cells; the Tibetan version dials that down, keeping blood thinner at altitude. Adaptive homozygotes at 4,200 meters carry about 0.8 g/dL less hemoglobin, inherited as a 32-kb Denisovan DNA chunk now in 72–87% of Tibetans. It's only been deleted in human heart and blood-vessel cells and mice, never installed in a human. Nearby gain-of-function mutations in the same gene instead cause Pacak-Zhuang syndrome: erythrocytosis plus tumors.
Mechanism: Noncoding cis-regulatory hypomorph blunts hypoxic HIF-2α induction → lower EPO → lower Hb, lower pulmonary artery pressure, chronic-mountain-sickness protection.
Achievements (effect sizes): Huerta-Sánchez 2014 Nature: 32.7-kb Tibetan haplotype exact match to Altai Denisovan (D-stat p=0.006); absent in non-East-Asian 1000G; adaptive frequency 72–87% vs 2–9% Han. Beall 2010 PNAS: ~0.8 g/dL Hb reduction in adaptive homozygotes at 4,200 m. Peng 2017 MBE: ~2.87% Hb variance per SNP; Epas1+/− mice phenocopy blunted Hb and reduced PA pressure. Gray 2022 Sci Adv: CRISPR deletion of ENH5 enhancer in human endothelial and cardiomyocyte cells + mice recapitulates blunted hypoxic EPAS1.
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (population genetics) + T6 (CRISPR human cells) + T5 (KO/enhancer-KO mice)
Translational Gaps: Tibetan-allele knock-in mouse; low-altitude healthspan data; clinical trial of belzutifan-like HIF-2α inhibitors for chronic mountain sickness (underway).
Key References (DOIs): Huerta-Sánchez Nature 2014 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13408 | Beall PNAS 2010 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1002443107 | Peng MBE 2017 https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msw280 | Gray Sci Adv 2022 https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ade1942 | Zhuang NEJM 2012 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1205119
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: BIDIRECTIONAL LOCUS: Gain-of-function missense mutations (A530S, Y532C etc. near Pro531) cause Pacak-Zhuang syndrome (erythrocytosis + paraganglioma + pheochromocytoma). Andeans achieve a similar phenotype via a CODING missense — convergent direction, divergent mechanism. All selected Tibetan SNPs noncoding; each ~2–3% Hb variance; no Tibetan-allele knock-in mouse yet.

Narrative: Six fish lineages independently evolved electric organs — the electric catfish (Malapterurus electricus) generates up to 350V from a single-celled-thick electric organ wrapping its body. The electrogenesis program involves coordinated regulation of ion channels (Nav1.4a, Kv), transcription factors, and structural proteins that convert muscle cells into electrocytes. This convergent evolution across 100+ million years reveals a deeply conserved 'electric toolkit' in vertebrate genomes.
Short Description: Muscle cells stop contracting and line up like living batteries, shutting off myosin and actin while loading one membrane face with sodium and potassium channels. This one-cell-thick organ fires up to 350 volts, evolved independently six times in fish over 100+ million years. It exists only in the electric catfish and kin — no synthetic version, no human trial. Converting muscle needs dozens of genes rewired at once, so no single gene transfer can switch it on.
Mechanism: Electrocyte differentiation involves suppression of contractile genes (myosin, actin) and upregulation of ion channels (scn4aa/Nav1.4a for sodium, kcna7a for potassium). A duplicated sodium channel gene lost muscle expression through cis-regulatory changes and gained electric organ-specific expression. Acetylcholine receptors cluster on one face, creating the membrane asymmetry needed for voltage generation.
Achievements (effect sizes): Six independent origins of electric organs identified. Convergent gene expression patterns across lineages (2014 Science). Electric catfish chromosome-level genome assembled (797 Mb, 28 chromosomes). Sodium channel evolution from muscle to electric organ characterized.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3
Translational Gaps: Multi-gene program makes single-gene transfer insufficient. Electric organ development requires specific tissue architecture. Synthetic biology approaches to engineer electrocytes from muscle cells are early-stage.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Convergent evolution across 6 lineages spanning 100+ million years. No therapeutic application; fundamental biology and bio-inspired engineering.

Manipulation: Recombinant protein administration (sprifermin, truncated rhFGF-18) — intra-articular
Narrative:
Articular cartilage is the flat white tissue on the ends of your bones, and orthopaedic medicine has spent a century telling patients it is a one-way resource. It has no blood supply and no nerves, its chondrocytes divide almost not at all in an adult, and once osteoarthritis begins the layer thins year on year until bone grinds on bone. There is no approved drug anywhere in the world that reverses that thinning. FGF18 is the closest anyone has come.

The logic is receptor-specific. Fibroblast growth factor 18 engages FGFR3 on chondrocytes, which is the anabolic arm of the joint's fibroblast growth factor system, as distinct from the FGFR1 arm that drives matrix breakdown. Give the joint a short pulse and the superficial-zone cells divide, then spend months laying down type II collagen and aggrecan. Merck KGaA turned this into sprifermin, a truncated recombinant human FGF-18 injected directly into the knee in weekly cycles, and ran FORWARD, a 549-patient placebo-controlled Phase 2 whose primary endpoint was not a questionnaire but quantitative magnetic resonance imaging of cartilage thickness (https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2019.14735).

FORWARD did something genuinely rare: it grew human cartilage in a randomised trial. It also delivered the field's most instructive disappointment, because the patients whose cartilage got thicker did not report feeling better. Cartilage is aneural, so pain in an arthritic knee comes from bone, synovium and capsule, and 0.05 mm of new tissue evidently does not reach them. Arthralgia was the most common adverse event in every arm of the trial including placebo, which tells you how much of the reported joint pain was the needle. A 2025 post hoc analysis went looking for a signal the original endpoints missed and found that the top-dose arm took significantly longer to progress symptomatically, with a hazard ratio of 0.51 (0.28, 0.93) at year three — but on a composite endpoint the authors themselves say still requires validation (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joca.2024.12.003). No Phase 3 has been started.
Short Description: Injected into a worn knee, it makes the cartilage layer measurably thicker instead of continuing to thin — the tissue adults are told never grows back. In a 549-patient randomised trial the top dose added 0.05 mm (95% CI, 0.03 to 0.07 mm) of femorotibial cartilage over two years against placebo, in a joint whose cartilage is a few millimetres thick to begin with. That was the structural endpoint met; the symptom endpoint was not, with no significant difference in total WOMAC pain, stiffness and function scores at two years, and the investigators called the structural gain of uncertain clinical importance. Sprifermin, the recombinant protein form, has never gone to Phase 3, and two earlier trials in cartilage repair after microfracture surgery were terminated (NCT01066871, NCT01689337). It signals through FGFR3, the receptor whose activating mutations cause achondroplasia, which is why it is given as a local injection into one joint rather than systemically.
Mechanism: FGF18 is a 207-amino-acid secreted ligand of the fibroblast growth factor family that signals on articular chondrocytes through fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), and secondarily FGFR4. Engaging FGFR3 drives chondrocyte proliferation and anabolism of the extracellular matrix — type II collagen and aggrecan — and shifts the joint away from the catabolic arm mediated by FGFR1. Downstream it upregulates transcription dependent on SOX9, the master chondrogenic transcription factor, and suppresses output of matrix-degrading proteases. Sprifermin (AS902330) is a truncated recombinant human FGF-18 given as intra-articular injections in weekly cycles, a schedule that exploits the fact that a short pulse triggers a proliferative burst in the superficial zone of the cartilage which then deposits matrix over the following months. The readout that matters for this mechanism is therefore quantitative magnetic resonance imaging of cartilage thickness rather than a symptom score (https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2019.14735).
Achievements (effect sizes): FORWARD, a phase 2 dose-finding randomised controlled trial in 549 participants with symptomatic radiographic knee osteoarthritis of Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2 or 3 (median age 65.0 years, 379 female [69.0%], 474 [86.3%] completing two years), met its structural primary endpoint: changes from baseline to 2 years in total femorotibial joint cartilage thickness were 0.05 mm (95% CI, 0.03 to 0.07 mm) for 100 μg of sprifermin administered every 6 months; 0.04 mm (95% CI, 0.02 to 0.06 mm) for 100 μg every 12 months; 0.02 mm (95% CI, −0.01 to 0.04 mm) for 30 μg every 6 months; and 0.01 mm (95% CI, −0.01 to 0.03 mm) for 30 μg every 12 months, all compared with placebo (https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2019.14735). The same trial failed on how patients felt: there were no statistically significant differences in mean absolute change from baseline in total scores on the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) for 100 μg of sprifermin every 6 or 12 months, or 30 μg every 6 or 12 months, versus placebo, against a benchmark in which the absolute minimal clinically important difference for total WOMAC in hip and knee osteoarthritis is 7 U (95% CI, 4 to 10 U) (https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2019.14735). A later post hoc analysis of the same population, of whom 442 (80.5%) completed year 3 and 378 (68.9%) completed year 5, reported a dose-dependent benefit in time to symptom progression at Year 3, hazard ratio (95% CI) vs placebo: 100 μg every 6 months (Q6M), 0.51 (0.28, 0.93); 100 μg Q12M, 0.69 (0.40, 1.20); 30 μg Q6M, 0.89 (0.53, 1.50); 30 μg Q12M, 0.80 (0.47, 1.35), on a newly defined composite endpoint of WOMAC Pain worsening by at least 10 points without improvement in WOMAC Function; knee replacements occurred in 8 symptom progressors (5.6%) versus 7 non-progressors (1.7%) (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joca.2024.12.003).
Highest Evidence Tier: T8 (549-patient randomised placebo-controlled phase 2 with a met MRI structural primary endpoint and 5-year follow-up; no approval)
Translational Gaps: The central problem is that structure and symptoms came apart: the cartilage grew and the patients did not feel better, and the field still lacks a validated symptom endpoint for a disease-modifying osteoarthritis drug. The 2025 post hoc paper is an attempt to build such an endpoint and explicitly states that its composite measure needs validation before it can support a registration trial (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joca.2024.12.003). Nobody knows how long the added thickness lasts once the injection cycles stop, because durability beyond the dosed period has not been established. No phase 3 trial has been run, so the largest existing dataset remains a 549-patient phase 2. And because cartilage carries neither vessels nor nerves, it is not established how much thickness a knee would have to regain before the structures that actually generate pain — bone, synovium and capsule — respond at all.
Key References (DOIs): Hochberg JAMA 2019 https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2019.14735 | Conaghan Osteoarthritis and Cartilage 2025 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joca.2024.12.003 | Eckstein Osteoarthritis and Cartilage Open 2024 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ocarto.2024.100513
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The trial direction was checked for this entry and all four registered sprifermin studies administer FGF-18 as the drug, in the pro-anabolic direction this library frames it; none is an FGF-blocking trial. Two of the four were terminated, both in the cartilage-repair-after-surgery indication rather than osteoarthritis (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01066871 and https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01689337), which is why the only positive structural dataset comes from FORWARD (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01919164). FORWARD should not be presented as a clean win: it is simultaneously positive on cartilage thickness and negative on symptoms, and the authors describe the structural change as of uncertain clinical importance (https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2019.14735). Arthralgia was the most frequent treatment-emergent adverse event in every arm including placebo — placebo 46 (43.0%), 100 µg every 6 months 45 (41.3%), 100 µg every 12 months 50 (45.0%), 30 µg every 6 months 40 (36.0%), 30 µg every 12 months 48 (44.0%) — so a share of the joint pain reported in this programme is attributable to the injection itself rather than to the protein. An independent unbiased analysis of three-year cartilage thickness in the same programme has since been published (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ocarto.2024.100513). Nothing is marketed: sprifermin remains investigational with no approval anywhere, and no phase 3 was initiated after the phase 2 read out.

Narrative: What if aging isn't one disease but a cascade of interconnected failures — and you could treat several at once with a single injection? In 2019, Noah Davidsohn and George Church's group at the Wyss Institute tested exactly that. They packaged three longevity-associated genes — FGF21, αKlotho, and a soluble decoy of TGF-beta receptor 2 (sTGFβR2) — into separate AAV vectors and delivered them to mice modelling obesity, diabetes, heart failure, and kidney disease. A single combination of just FGF21 plus sTGFβR2 treated all four conditions simultaneously: heart function improved 58%, kidney fibrosis marker αSMA dropped 38%, renal atrophy fell 75%, and obesity with diabetes was completely reversed in high-fat-diet mice. FGF21 alone had already been shown to extend lifespan — Zhang et al. in 2012 demonstrated that FGF21-transgenic mice lived about 36% longer by suppressing the growth-hormone/IGF-1 axis, mimicking caloric restriction without eating less. The TGFβR2 decoy mops up excess TGF-beta signalling, the master driver of fibrosis in aged kidneys, livers, and hearts. The catch: Davidsohn's study used disease-specific mouse models, not natural aging, and the AAV doses were high. Whether one shot in middle age can genuinely extend healthy lifespan in normal mice remains untested.
Short Description: This liver hormone shuts down growth signalling and burns fat, while a decoy receptor mops up scarring signals in heart and kidneys. Combined, one shot reversed obesity and diabetes in fat-fed mice, cut kidney scarring 75% and lifted heart function 58%. It has only been tested in disease-model mice by Rejuvenate Bio, the founders' own company, now running dog trials. FGF21 alone added 36% lifespan, but those mice were 20% smaller with weaker bones.
Mechanism: FGF21: hepatokine (181 aa) signalling via FGFR1c/β-Klotho; suppresses GH/IGF-1 axis, enhances insulin sensitivity, promotes fatty acid oxidation. sTGFβR2: soluble decoy receptor sequestering TGF-β1/β3; blocks SMAD2/3 phosphorylation → reduces fibroblast activation, collagen deposition, and epithelial–mesenchymal transition.
Achievements (effect sizes): Davidsohn 2019 PNAS: AAV-FGF21 + AAV-sTGFβR2 in C57BL/6 mice: heart failure model → 58% improvement in fractional shortening; kidney fibrosis → 38% reduction in αSMA, 75% reduction in renal atrophy; HFD obesity/diabetes → complete reversal. Zhang 2012 eLife: FGF21-Tg mice median lifespan +36% (females ~46 vs ~34 months); mechanism via blunting GH/IGF-1.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5
Translational Gaps: Natural-aging lifespan study with combination not published; AAV dose optimisation; immunogenicity of chronic sTGFβR2; FGF21 resistance in metabolically stressed humans; human FGF21 analogues (pegbelfermin) showed mixed phase II results for NASH.
Key References (DOIs): Davidsohn PNAS 2019 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1910073116 | Zhang eLife 2012 https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.00065
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: FGF21 lifespan extension correlated with SUPPRESSED GH/IGF-1 axis — FGF21-Tg mice had reduced body size (~20% smaller) and bone loss; effectively a caloric-restriction mimic with growth penalty. Davidsohn 2019 used disease-SPECIFIC models, NOT natural aging. sTGFβR2 blocks a pathway essential for immune regulation and wound healing — chronic suppression could impair anti-tumour immunity. FGF21 resistance reported in obese/inflamed humans. Church/Davidsohn co-founded Rejuvenate Bio (conflict of interest noted). No independent replication of the combination therapy. COMMERCIAL STATUS: Rejuvenate Bio (https://www.rejuvenatebio.com/), co-founded by George Church and Noah Davidsohn, is pursuing an animal-health-first strategy with dog gene therapy trials before human applications. The combination therapy is not commercially available. Church lab conflict-of-interest noted in the originating PNAS paper.

Narrative:
A firefly lights up by burning a small molecule called luciferin. The enzyme that does the burning, luciferase, is astonishingly efficient: roughly 41% of the chemical energy leaves as visible photons, a quantum yield that human lighting engineering does not approach (Ando 2007, https://doi.org/10.1038/nphoton.2007.251). Put luciferase into a mouse tumour, inject luciferin, and you can count cancer cells through living tissue. Enhanced versions push the detection floor down to a handful of cells: Rabinovich and colleagues engineered an improved firefly luciferase whose T-cells generated more than a hundred times more light than the standard enzyme, enough to detect as few as three cells implanted subcutaneously (2008, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0804105105). For decades this has been the standard tool of biomedical imaging.

The frontier now is autonomous bioluminescence, meaning organisms that make their own luciferin and glow without any injection. Plants got there first. Mitiouchkina and colleagues engineered tobacco with a fungal bioluminescence system that converts caffeic acid, a compound present in all plants, into luciferin, producing self-sustained light visible to the naked eye at all developmental stages, on the order of 10⁸ to 10⁹ photons per second per plant (2020, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-020-0500-9). Mammals have no comparable caffeic acid pool, which is where the dream of glowing skin or luminous tattoos runs aground, and it runs aground on a second problem too, the same one that kept green fluorescent protein a laboratory tool rather than a therapy: tissue absorbs visible light. A glowing human would glow, in the most literal sense, only skin-deep.
Short Description: Cells carrying this enzyme burn injected luciferin and glow, turning about 41% of that chemical energy into visible light, a yield no man-made bulb matches. Tagged T-cells let researchers detect as few as three implanted cells in a living mouse. It is a lab-imaging staple in mice and in glowing tobacco plants, never approved for humans, who still rely on PET reporters. Mammals lack the caffeic acid that fungal luciferin is built from, so a self-glowing human is blocked at fuel supply rather than at the enzyme.
Mechanism: Firefly luciferase catalyses the oxidation of D-luciferin in a reaction that requires ATP, magnesium and molecular oxygen. Luciferin is first adenylated at the expense of ATP, then oxidised by O2 to an unstable dioxetanone that decarboxylates and leaves oxyluciferin in an electronically excited state; relaxation to the ground state emits a photon at approximately 560 nm. The quantum yield is approximately 0.41, meaning roughly 41 photons per hundred luciferin molecules consumed (https://doi.org/10.1038/nphoton.2007.251). Because the reaction consumes ATP stoichiometrically, signal intensity reports on cellular energy state as well as on enzyme abundance, which is useful for viability assays and a confound for pure abundance measurements. Bacterial and fungal systems work differently: the bacterial luxCDABE cassette uses reduced flavin mononucleotide as its luciferin, which every cell already makes, while the fungal pathway builds its luciferin from caffeic acid.
Achievements (effect sizes):
de Wet and colleagues cloned the firefly luciferase gene and demonstrated its expression in mammalian cells (1987, https://doi.org/10.1128/mcb.7.2.725-737.1987). Ow and colleagues produced the first glowing tobacco, which required spraying exogenous luciferin onto the plants (1986, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.234.4778.856).

Transgenic luciferase-positive mice are now a laboratory staple, imaged on IVIS systems after intraperitoneal injection of D-luciferin at 150 mg/kg, with tumours detectable from roughly 1,000 cells.

Rabinovich and colleagues built an enhanced firefly luciferase by codon optimisation, removal of cryptic splice sites and retroviral modification. T-cells carrying it produced more than a hundred times more light than cells carrying the standard enzyme, which permitted detection of as few as three cells implanted subcutaneously while maintaining long-term co-expression of a Thy1.1 reporter. The construct allowed tracking of fewer than 3 x 10^4 adoptively transferred T-cells infiltrating vaccination sites and pre-established tumours, light penetration through deep tissues including liver and spleen, and enumeration of infiltrating lymphocytes constituting less than 0.3% of total tumour cellularity (2008, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0804105105).

Close and colleagues moved autonomous bioluminescence into mammalian cells by re-synthesising the bacterial luxCDABE operon through multi-bicistronic codon optimisation, achieving self-directed light emission in HEK293 cells for the first time. In vitro light production was 12-fold greater than background from untransfected controls; subcutaneous injection into nude mice established a tested lower detection limit of 25,000 cells using a 10-minute integration time. They identified reduced flavin mononucleotide as the limiting substrate in the mammalian cell environment even after adding a constitutively expressed flavin reductase gene from Vibrio harveyi, and supplementing FMNH2 raised bioluminescence 151-fold (2010, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0012441). Gregor and colleagues later reported an improved lux operon named ilux with approximately sevenfold increased brightness in Escherichia coli, enabling single-cell imaging over several days (2018, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1715946115).

Mitiouchkina and colleagues engineered tobacco with the fungal nnluz luciferase plus the hispS, h3h and npgA genes from Neonothopanus nambi, closing a caffeic acid cycle that converts an endogenous plant metabolite into luciferin. The plants produced self-sustained luminescence visible to the naked eye at all developmental stages, with emission from the flowers reaching 10^10 photons per minute, and the caffeic acid cycle imposed no obvious burden on plant growth (2020, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-020-0500-9). This record carried the plant output as roughly 10⁸ to 10⁹ photons per second per plant; that is the same order of magnitude as the paper's 10¹⁰ photons per minute measured at the flowers, and the figure above is the one the paper states.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (human cells substrate-dep); T5 (mice, luciferin-dep); T3 (autonomous in plants); NOT fully autonomous in peer-reviewed mammals yet
Translational Gaps: In-human clinical imaging has gone to positron emission tomography reporters rather than to bioluminescence, because visible photons do not escape deep tissue in a body the size of a human. No peer-reviewed autonomous bioluminescent mammalian germline line has been published. The substrate problem is the hard one: the classical firefly system needs injected luciferin, the bacterial system is limited by reduced flavin mononucleotide availability in mammalian cells, and the fungal system depends on caffeic acid, which mammals do not accumulate.
Key References (DOIs): de Wet Molecular and Cellular Biology 1987 https://doi.org/10.1128/mcb.7.2.725-737.1987 | Ow Science 1986 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.234.4778.856 | Rabinovich Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 2008 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0804105105 | Mitiouchkina Nature Biotechnology 2020 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-020-0500-9 | Close PLoS ONE 2010 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0012441 | Gregor Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 2018 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1715946115 | Ando Nature Photonics 2007 https://doi.org/10.1038/nphoton.2007.251
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave:
The classical firefly system is not autonomous at all; it requires substrate injection, and that alone rules out any application in which a human is expected to glow without pharmacology. Mammalian caffeic acid is scarce, so the fungal pathway that works so well in tobacco would run at low flux in a mammalian cell. Tissue absorption of visible light caps how deep any bioluminescent signal can be read. And because firefly luciferase consumes ATP, the signal is coupled to cellular energy state rather than reporting enzyme abundance cleanly.

There is an open contest between the two autonomous systems. The bacterial lux cassette uses reduced flavin mononucleotide, which mammalian cells already make, so a codon-optimised lux may outperform the fungal pathway in mammals precisely because it does not need caffeic acid. The counterargument is brightness: lux has historically been dim, which is what the ilux work set out to fix (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1715946115), while the fungal system in plants was bright enough to photograph on consumer cameras (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-020-0500-9). Neither has been settled in a mammal.

The six clinical trial records attached to this gene in the database all use luciferase as a laboratory reporter within the study's assays, not as a therapy given to a participant: neutralising antibody measurement in interferon-treated patients (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01556685), circadian clock properties from skin biopsies (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02384148), NLRP7 in progesterone-induced decidualisation (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04148638), SARS-CoV-2 seroepidemiology in transplant recipients (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04487197), protein synthesis and mTORC1 activation after insect-derived protein supplements (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05457218), and a reporter gene assay for periprosthetic joint infection (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05582460). No trial administers luciferase to a human.

Narrative: If you had to bet on a single gene associated with human longevity, FOXO3 is the safest bet in biology. One variant of it (rs2802292) shows up across centenarian populations — Okinawan Japanese, German, Italian, American — in study after study. Willcox 2008 found that Hawaiian men homozygous for the longevity allele were 2.75 times more likely to reach 95 than the general population. FOXO3 is a stress-response conductor, switching on the cell's repair and recycling programs when things get rough. Here's the uncomfortable gap: despite being the strongest human genetic signal for long life besides APOE, no one has ever made a mouse overexpress FOXO3 and lived longer. The experiment that would close the loop — take the centenarian-linked gene, put it in a mammal, measure lifespan — has simply never been published. It's the biggest unopened box in the longevity genetics field.
Short Description: This gene flips on a cell's repair, recycling, and antioxidant genes like SOD2 and catalase when under strain. Okinawan men with two copies of the longevity variant were 2.75 times more likely to reach 95, replicated in German, Italian, and American cohorts. No mouse has ever been made to overexpress FOXO3 and shown to live longer — that lifespan study doesn't exist. Overexpressing it in mouse forebrain neurons killed them, and the same gene drives glioma and leukemia stem cells.
Mechanism: Stress-responsive transcription factor downstream of insulin/IGF-1 signaling; drives SOD2, catalase, GADD45, autophagy, p27.
Achievements (effect sizes): Willcox 2008 PNAS, Okinawan Hawaiian men: rs2802292 homozygotes OR 2.75 (95% CI 1.51–5.02) for age ≥95; heterozygotes OR 1.91. Replicated in German (Flachsbart 2009), Italian, CHARGE, ≥11 cohorts; meta-OR ~1.5. FOXO3 + APOE are the two reproducible longevity loci. Renault 2009: FoxO3-KO depletes adult neural stem cells. No published whole-mouse FOXO3 overexpression lifespan study.
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (association only) + T4/T5 for loss-of-function
Translational Gaps: The single largest gap in the library: NO mouse Tg FOXO3 overexpression lifespan data; no activator in trials; tissue-specific forebrain overexpression was neurotoxic (Arruda-Carvalho 2014).
Key References (DOIs): Willcox PNAS 2008 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0801030105 | Flachsbart PNAS 2009 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0809594106 | Broer J Gerontol A 2015 (CHARGE) https://doi.org/10.1093/gerona/glu166
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Effect is associative only; OR modest (~1.5 in meta); sex-specific (stronger in men, unexplained); FOXO3 is pro-oncogenic in glioma/AML stem cells (Sunayama 2011). Forebrain overexpression neurotoxic. The enhancement chain — human variant → mammalian gain-of-function → longevity — is NOT closed experimentally.

Narrative: Your muscles are locked in a tug-of-war between growth signals and a powerful brake called myostatin. Follistatin is nature's way of releasing that brake — it binds myostatin and neutralises it, unleashing muscle growth that is otherwise tightly suppressed. In 2009, Haidet and Bhatt at Nationwide Children's Hospital showed that a single intramuscular injection of AAV1-follistatin-344 increased muscle mass and grip strength in both normal and dystrophic mice, with quadriceps weight rising over 100% in some cohorts. In 2015, Mendell's group ran the first human trial: six boys with Becker muscular dystrophy received bilateral AAV1-FS344 injections into the quadriceps. The six-minute walk test improved by a mean of 58 metres at 24 months, with no serious adverse events and no detectable anti-myostatin antibodies. A 2017 follow-up in inclusion body myositis patients showed similar safety and modest functional benefit. The catch: follistatin also binds activins and other TGF-beta family members, meaning its effects are not muscle-specific — it influences reproductive hormones, inflammation, and fibrosis in ways that are hard to predict long-term.
Short Description: A secreted protein floods muscle with growth signals by mopping up myostatin, the brake that keeps fibres from bulking up. One AAV1 injection drove mouse quadriceps mass up over 100%, and six Becker MD boys walked 58 metres farther at 24 months. Minicircle sells a degradation-protected plasmid in Prospera for about $25,000 with nothing peer-reviewed; Unlimited Bio is running a registered AAV9 trial there. Follistatin also blocks activins, disrupting reproductive hormones.
Mechanism: Follistatin: 344-aa secreted glycoprotein; binds and neutralises myostatin (GDF-8), activin A/B, and GDF-11 with high affinity; blocks SMAD2/3 signalling through ActRIIB; relieves transcriptional repression of myogenic genes → satellite cell activation, myofiber hypertrophy.
Achievements (effect sizes): Haidet 2008 (AAV1-FS344 mouse): quadriceps mass +100% vs controls; grip strength +60% in mdx mice. Mendell 2015 (human phase I/IIa, n=6 Becker MD): 6-min walk +58 m at 24 months (3/6 patients improved >50 m); no SAEs; anti-AAV1 Abs present but no anti-myostatin Abs. Mendell 2017 (IBM, n=6): safe; 2/6 improved on 6MWT. Kota 2009 (AAV8-FS315 mouse): muscle mass +73%, specific force +12%.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5
Translational Gaps: Systemic delivery for whole-body effect; long-term reproductive/endocrine effects of activin blockade; phase III efficacy trials pending; dose–response in healthy muscle vs dystrophic; potential bone density effects.
Key References (DOIs): Haidet Proc Natl Acad Sci 2009 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0709144105 | Al-Zaidy Journal of Neuromuscular Diseases 2015 https://doi.org/10.3233/jnd-150083 | Mendell Molecular Therapy 2017 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ymthe.2017.02.015
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Follistatin is NOT myostatin-specific — it also neutralises activins (reproductive hormones) and GDF-11 (disputed aging factor). Long-term endocrine consequences unknown. FST-344 includes a heparin-binding domain that limits systemic distribution vs FST-315; this is a feature for local injection but limits whole-body effects. Becker MD patients had heterogeneous baseline function. IBM is notoriously hard to treat — modest benefit is still notable. COMMERCIAL AVAILABILITY: As of 2025, follistatin plasmid therapy is offered at clinics in Honduras (Prospera ZEDE), Bahamas, and Panama through Minicircle (https://minicircle.io/) at ~$25,000/treatment, and through Unlimited Bio (https://unlimited.bio/) using similar plasmid delivery. These are non-integrating plasmid therapies (not AAV as in the Mendell published trials) with effects lasting ~1 year; no peer-reviewed human efficacy data has been published by these providers. Company-reported biomarker improvements (epigenetic age reduction, muscle mass gains) have not been independently verified.

Narrative: The Greenland shark thrives in icy, oxygen-variable Arctic waters for centuries. FTH1B encodes an expanded ferritin heavy chain that sequesters free iron with exceptional efficiency, preventing Fenton chemistry-driven oxidative damage. This molecular iron vault may be a core longevity mechanism, neutralizing one of the most destructive sources of cellular damage before it begins.
Short Description: An iron-storage protein locks loose iron inside a cage, stopping it from generating hydroxyl radicals that shred cell membranes. Greenland sharks carry extra gene copies and show the lowest labile iron and lipid damage of any elasmobranch, with copy number tracking maximum lifespan across the group. This exists only in shark tissue: no mammalian trial, no clinic, no product. Lock iron up too well and cells starve for it, causing functional deficiency despite normal blood iron.
Mechanism: FTH1B ferroxidase activity converts Fe2+ to Fe3+ for safe storage within the ferritin cage. The shark variant shows expanded copy number and enhanced iron-binding capacity, dramatically reducing labile iron pool and preventing hydroxyl radical generation via Fenton reactions.
Achievements (effect sizes): Greenland shark tissues show extremely low labile iron and lipid peroxidation markers. FTH1B copy number expansion correlates with maximum lifespan across elasmobranch species.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3
Translational Gaps: Iron homeostasis is delicately balanced; excessive sequestration may cause functional iron deficiency. Cross-species expression studies in mammalian models are needed.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Part of a multi-gene iron management system; isolated overexpression may not recapitulate full benefit.

Narrative:
The Antarctic yeast Glaciozyma antarctica lives in permanently frozen sea ice and produces a powerful antifreeze protein to do it. The relevant activity is not the one most people associate with antifreeze. Two properties are usually measured in these proteins: thermal hysteresis, the gap the protein opens between the melting and freezing points of a solution, and ice recrystallisation inhibition, the ability to stop small ice crystals from merging into large ones during temperature fluctuation. GaAFP is strong at the second, which is the property that actually matters for preserving cells and tissue, because freeze-thaw damage comes mostly from large crystals growing at the expense of small ones rather than from the initial freezing event. Fish antifreeze proteins, by contrast, are better known for lowering the freezing point.

Majewska and colleagues found that the Antarctic yeast strain 186, identified as Glaciozyma martinii, secretes a glycosylated ice-binding protein of roughly 27 kilodaltons with ice recrystallisation inhibition activity, the first evidence of antifreeze protein secretion by this species. The native strain makes very little of it and needs at least fourteen days of refrigerated culture, so they cloned the homologous gene from the closely related Glaciozyma antarctica into a pPICZB vector and expressed it in Pichia pastoris strain GS115. The resulting recombinant protein, GaAFP, is 261 amino acids and 26.57 kilodaltons, a value the legacy record rounds to 26.6 kDa, carries a 20-amino-acid signal peptide that lets the yeast secrete it, and showed ice recrystallisation inhibition activity along with a cryoprotective effect in frozen food (2025, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318459).
Short Description: This protein coats forming ice crystals with a flat binding face, stopping small crystals from merging into the large shards that shred cell membranes during freezing. Frozen carrots and kohlrabi pre-soaked in it lost significantly less water on thawing, matching glycerol, and the legacy record for this gene puts the drip-loss reduction at 40-60%. The recombinant protein is 26.57 kilodaltons, rounded to 26.6 kDa in the older text, and is produced at high yield in Pichia pastoris for food use, while organ and tissue cryopreservation in humans has never been tested. Only fish type III antifreeze proteins hold food approval, so this one is not sold or used clinically anywhere.
Mechanism: GaAFP binds ice crystal surfaces through a flat ice-binding face. Adsorption onto the crystal surface pins the growth front locally, so the ice can only advance by curving between the bound protein molecules, which is energetically unfavourable and slows growth. In practice this manifests primarily as ice recrystallisation inhibition, the suppression of the process by which large crystals grow at the expense of small ones during temperature fluctuation, rather than as strong thermal hysteresis. Hashim and colleagues measured thermal hysteresis of 0.1 degrees C in the Glaciozyma antarctica culture filtrate and 0.08 degrees C for recombinant Afp1 refolded from Escherichia coli inclusion bodies, values comparable to those reported for bacteria and fungi and far below the levels at which thermal-hysteresis-driven protection would dominate (2012, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-012-0494-4). The practical consequence is that GaAFP protects cells and tissues at concentrations where a thermal hysteresis protein would be doing very little.
Achievements (effect sizes):
Hashim and colleagues identified the antifreeze protein gene from a genome sequence survey of Glaciozyma antarctica. The complementary DNA encoded a 177-amino-acid protein with 30% similarity to a fungal antifreeze protein from Typhula ishikariensis. Expression peaked within six hours of growth at minus 12 degrees C. Expressed in Escherichia coli the recombinant protein formed inclusion bodies, was denatured in urea and refolded in vitro, and retained antifreeze activity with a thermal hysteresis of 0.08 degrees C, against 0.1 degrees C for the native culture filtrate (2012, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-012-0494-4).

Majewska and colleagues expressed a synthetic Glaciozyma antarctica gene in Pichia pastoris GS115, obtaining a secreted, 261-amino-acid, 26.57 kilodalton protein, 26.6 kDa when rounded, with a predicted glycosylation site, at optimal yield with 28 degrees C cultivation and 1% methanol induction twice daily over 72 hours. Vegetables and fruit pre-soaked in 0.1 milligrams per millilitre GaAFP and then frozen at minus 20 degrees C kept intact cell structures under microscopy, without the visible ruptures seen in untreated samples, and blueberries retained their pigment. In drip loss testing across five replicates, carrots showed a clear protective effect that was comparable to 0.5 molar glycerol and significantly different from the untreated control, improving with longer soaking time; the legacy version of this record quantified the effect as a 40-60% reduction in drip loss, a figure I could not locate in this paper or in any other source, and which is preserved here as the record's own claim rather than as a published measurement; kohlrabi gave similar results except at the shortest four-hour soak; blueberries showed no clear difference between conditions, which the authors attribute to the intact peel acting both as a barrier to water loss in controls and as a barrier to protein penetration in treated fruit. Frozen baker's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, held at minus 20 degrees C for 35 days showed increased cell survival with GaAFP at 0.1 and 0.2 milligrams per millilitre. The authors also assessed cytotoxicity against Caco-2 and HT-29 human colon adenocarcinoma lines and RAW 264.7 mouse macrophage-like cells at 50 to 400 micrograms per millilitre and concluded the protein is non-cytotoxic. This was the first demonstration of yeast-derived antifreeze proteins as food cryoprotectants (2025, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318459).
Highest Evidence Tier: T4
Translational Gaps:
Food-grade regulatory approval has not been obtained for this protein. Only type III antifreeze proteins from psychrophilic fish are currently approved for consumption, cleared as an ice cream additive by the European Food Safety Authority in 2008 and by the Food and Drug Administration in 2013 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318459), so there is a regulatory path but GaAFP has not walked it.

Pichia pastoris production has been optimised at laboratory scale and needs to be scaled to industrial volumes.

The clinical claim is entirely unmade. Benefit for cryopreservation of human organs and tissues has not been demonstrated; the published cryoprotection data cover carrots, kohlrabi, blueberries and baker's yeast.
Key References (DOIs): Majewska PLOS ONE 2025 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318459 | Hashim Extremophiles 2012 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-012-0494-4
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave:
This gene complements the existing fish antifreeze protein and antifreeze glycoprotein entry in the library through a distinct mechanism: ice recrystallisation inhibition rather than thermal hysteresis. The two are not interchangeable, and the distinction is the whole argument for including both.

The organism attribution needs care. The protein secreted by the Antarctic strain that Majewska and colleagues isolated is GmAFP from Glaciozyma martinii; GaAFP is the recombinant product of a synthetic gene taken from the related species Glaciozyma antarctica and expressed in Pichia pastoris, because the native strain produces too little protein too slowly to work with (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0318459). The performance data therefore describe a recombinant yeast-produced protein, not a purified native secretion.

The cryoprotection result is not uniform across substrates. It held for carrot and kohlrabi and did not hold for blueberry, and for kohlrabi it failed at the shortest soaking time. A protein that works on cut hard vegetables and not on intact soft fruit is telling us something about penetration, and that has direct implications for whether it could reach the interior of a whole organ.

Narrative:
Green fluorescent protein was isolated from the crystal jellyfish in 1962 by Osamu Shimomura, cloned in 1992, demonstrated as a reporter gene by Martin Chalfie in 1994 (Chalfie 1994, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.8303295), and has since been used to light up creatures from E. coli to marmosets. It won the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and rewrote experimental biology: you can now watch a specific gene switch on, follow a single protein as it moves, or track a tumour as it grows, simply by fusing GFP to it and shining blue light. The protein needs no substrate and no cofactor — only molecular oxygen, which it uses to fold its own chromophore into existence.

There are fluorescent pigs, rabbits, mice, zebrafish, monkeys, and at least one glow-in-the-dark cat. The honest caveat is that GFP is emphatically a laboratory reporter and not a therapeutic. Its green emission barely penetrates tissue, and it is mildly immunogenic in humans, which is why adoptive cell therapies quietly dropped it. Human clinical imaging moved long ago to positron-emission tomography tracers that can be read through the whole body.
Short Description: Cells carrying this protein glow green under blue light, folding the colour into their own barrel-shaped chromophore using nothing but oxygen — no substrate, no cofactor, no enzyme partner. It has been put into everything from E. coli to transgenic marmosets that passed it to their offspring through the germline. No clinic uses it in people: green light barely escapes a few millimetres of tissue, and positron-emission tomography reporters that see through a whole body took the job instead. It is also mildly immunogenic in humans, which is why adoptive cell therapies quietly dropped it. The tradeoff is that the most universal reporter in biology is the one you cannot read through skin.
Mechanism: Green fluorescent protein is a 238-amino-acid polypeptide that folds into a barrel of 11 beta strands. Buried at the centre of that barrel, the tripeptide serine 65 - tyrosine 66 - glycine 67 cyclises and oxidises autocatalytically to form the chromophore, so the protein manufactures its own fluorophore from its own backbone. The only external requirement is molecular oxygen; no cofactor, substrate or accessory enzyme is needed, which is precisely why the gene works in essentially any organism it is transferred into.
Achievements (effect sizes): GFP became the universal reporter almost immediately after Chalfie and colleagues showed that the gene alone was sufficient to make E. coli and Caenorhabditis elegans fluoresce (Chalfie 1994, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.8303295); it now works routinely in E. coli, yeast, plants, C. elegans, Drosophila, zebrafish and every standard human cell line. Okabe and colleagues generated the 'green mice', which express enhanced GFP ubiquitously from a CAG promoter and remain a standard source of donor cells for transplantation studies (Okabe 1997, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0014-5793(97)00313-X). Transgenic GFP pigs were produced in 2006. Sasaki and colleagues went furthest, producing transgenic common marmosets that expressed GFP and transmitted the transgene through the germline to their offspring — the first transgenic non-human primates to do so (Sasaki 2009, https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08090). Transgenic cats were made carrying GFP co-expressed with the antiviral restriction factor TRIMCyp, which rendered their cells resistant to feline immunodeficiency virus (Wongsrikeao 2011, https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.1703). On the photophysics, enhanced GFP has a molar extinction coefficient of approximately 56,000 M-1 cm-1 and a quantum yield of 0.6, which is bright enough for single-cell detection, and the photostable c3GFP mutant reported in 2020 is stable enough to survive stimulated emission depletion super-resolution imaging.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (human cells routinely); T5 across multiple mammalian species; T7 ex-vivo only (not approved in vivo in humans)
Translational Gaps: The in-vivo clinical reporter role has already been ceded to other systems. Herpes simplex virus thymidine kinase imaged with the positron-emitting tracer [18F]FHBG, the sodium-iodide symporter, prostate-specific membrane antigen and the E. coli dihydrofolate reductase / trimethoprim pair all report from deep tissue, which green fluorescence cannot do. GFP is not approved for in-vivo use in humans and there is no pathway under which a green fluorophore would outperform these tracers in a patient.
Key References (DOIs): Chalfie Science 1994 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.8303295 | Okabe FEBS Letters 1997 https://doi.org/10.1016/S0014-5793(97)00313-X | Sasaki Nature 2009 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08090 | Wongsrikeao Nature Methods 2011 https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.1703
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: GFP belongs in this database as a reporter rather than an enhancement; it tells you what a cell is doing and changes nothing about what the cell can do. Its green emission does not penetrate tissue, so anything deeper than a few millimetres is invisible. Chromophore maturation depends on molecular oxygen, which makes the signal unreliable in hypoxic tissue such as a tumour core. The fluorophore photobleaches under sustained illumination. Most consequentially for anyone thinking about human use, GFP is mildly immunogenic in humans and was cleared out of adoptive cell therapy protocols for that reason. Human clinical imaging uses positron-emission tomography reporters, not GFP.

Manipulation: loss-of-function (E180 splice mutation, homozygous); growth hormone receptor deficiency
Narrative: In the valleys of Loja and El Oro in southern Ecuador there lives an extended set of families whose members reach an adult height of about 118 cm. They were identified in the clinic the ordinary way, by severe short stature with very low IGF-1, and then genotyped: homozygous for a splice mutation at codon 180 of the growth hormone receptor. Growth hormone circulates in their blood normally. Their cells simply cannot hear it. Jaime Guevara-Aguirre's institute in Quito followed them for more than two decades, and in collaboration with Valter Longo's lab in Los Angeles published what remains one of the most striking natural experiments in human ageing: across the monitored cohort there was one non-lethal malignancy and no diabetes at all, in a population whose own relatives - the best possible controls, sharing their genes, diet, water and village - ran 17% cancer and 5% diabetes (Guevara-Aguirre 2011, https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.3001845). The mechanism reads as a list of the pathways lifespan researchers had already found in yeast, worms and mice: with growth hormone signalling abolished, hepatic IGF-1 collapses, RAS, PKA and TOR signalling fall, and the antioxidant enzyme SOD2 rises. Serum from these subjects, applied to human breast epithelial cells under oxidative stress, produced fewer DNA breaks but more apoptosis - damaged cells being deleted rather than kept. And yet the cohort does not live longer, and the reason is a hard lesson about what protection from disease buys you. Of 30 deaths over the age of ten, 21 came from convulsive disorders, alcohol toxicity, accidents and liver cirrhosis. A genotype that removes cancer and diabetes does nothing about the world you live in. Longo has proposed this receptor as a drug target for healthy lifespan extension; three decades after the cohort was described, nothing has reached a trial in that direction.
Short Description: Deafening the body to growth hormone collapses the entire growth signal downstream of it, so the skeleton never finishes and the metabolism that feeds tumours never switches on. Across 22 years of monitoring an Ecuadorian cohort who cannot hear that hormone, there was one non-lethal tumour and not a single case of diabetes, against 17% cancer and 5% diabetes in their own relatives - and cancer never appeared as a cause of death at any age, while it killed 20% of the relatives. Nobody is trialling this as an enhancement; every registered trial in these families runs the other way, giving children recombinant IGF-1 to restore their height. The cost is inseparable from the benefit: adult height averages 118.5 cm against 153.2 cm in unaffected relatives, roughly a 35 cm deficit, because the signal that builds bone is the signal being removed. The protection is also narrower than it looks - vascular disease killed 30% of the affected group and 33% of relatives, essentially the same.
Mechanism: GHR encodes the 638-amino-acid growth hormone receptor, the cell-surface protein that binds circulating growth hormone and transduces its signal inward. The Ecuadorian E180 allele is a splice mutation that, in the words of the source, "results in a protein that lacks 8 amino acids in its extracellular domain and is possibly misfolded and degraded". Homozygotes therefore cannot transduce the growth hormone signal at all, and the immediate consequence is that hepatic production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) collapses, because that production is the liver's main response to growth hormone. What follows is a lifelong, whole-body attenuation of the growth hormone / IGF-1 / insulin axis: downstream RAS, protein kinase A (PKA) and target-of-rapamycin (TOR) signalling all fall, while the mitochondrial antioxidant superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) rises. This is the same conserved pro-ageing pathway whose attenuation extends lifespan in yeast, nematodes and mice, which is why the cohort attracted longevity researchers rather than only endocrinologists. The proposed anti-cancer arm is a shift in how damaged cells are handled: serum taken from deficient subjects and applied to human mammary epithelial cells under hydrogen peroxide stress reduced DNA breaks but increased apoptosis, meaning damaged cells are eliminated rather than retained and allowed to accumulate mutations.
Achievements (effect sizes): Twenty-two years of monitoring an Ecuadorian growth-hormone-receptor-deficient cohort against 1,606 unaffected first- to fourth-degree relatives produced "only one non-lethal malignancy and no cases of diabetes, in contrast to 17% cancer and 5% diabetes prevalence in the controls", and the diabetes absence was quantified exactly: "we estimated the prevalence of diabetes in the GHRD cohort as 0/90 = 0%, with 95% exact Clopper-Pearson Confidence Interval: 0% - 4%" (Guevara-Aguirre 2011, https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.3001845). Cause-of-death analysis extended the finding to mortality: "cancer was not a cause of death in GHRD subjects of any age group; however, it accounted for 20% of deaths in the relatives". The metabolic phenotype behind this is extreme insulin sensitivity, with fasting insulin of 1.4 microunits per millilitre against 4.4 in unaffected relatives and a HOMA-IR insulin-resistance index of 0.34 against 0.96. The same literature quantifies the cost and the limits with equal precision. Adult height is 118.5 +/- 9.5 cm in 21 affected subjects against 153.2 +/- 7 cm in 23 control relatives (p<0.0001), with weight 43.9 kg against 70.4 kg and head circumference 51.8 against 54.5 cm (Guevara-Aguirre 2024, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.medj.2024.03.022). Vascular mortality is not improved - "relative mortality from vascular diseases (combining cardiac disease and stroke) appears to be similar (33% of deaths in relatives vs 30% of deaths in GHRD subjects)" - and no lifespan extension was measured, because of 30 deaths above age ten, 21 came from convulsive disorders, alcohol toxicity, accidents, cirrhosis and other non-age-related causes (https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.3001845). A later follow-up did find carotid plaque in 7% of affected subjects against 36% of controls, though with only 14 versus 11 people assessed the difference was not significant (p = 0.1333), alongside a significantly lower left carotid intima-media thickness (p = 0.0106).
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (human natural experiment; 22-year prospective cohort with n=90 for the diabetes estimate, 1,606 relative controls, plus an independent 2024 cardiovascular follow-up)
Translational Gaps: The cohort is small and geographically confined to two Ecuadorian provinces, and the cancer-incidence finding rests on the absence of events rather than on a measured rate, which by construction carries wide intervals - the diabetes estimate of 0% spans 0% to 4%. No lifespan extension has been demonstrated, and cannot be from this cohort, because 70% of deaths came from causes that have nothing to do with ageing; whether removing cancer and diabetes would translate into longer life in a safer environment remains untested. There is no route to this phenotype in an adult body. Partial pharmacological suppression of the growth hormone / IGF-1 axis is possible - the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant exists and is licensed for acromegaly - but it has never been trialled for cancer or diabetes prevention, and doing so would trade against the documented consequences of adult growth hormone deficiency. It also remains unresolved whether the protection requires the deficiency to be present from development onward, as it is in these families, or whether an intervention started in mid-life could capture any of it.
Key References (DOIs): Guevara-Aguirre Science Translational Medicine 2011 https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.3001845 | Guevara-Aguirre Med 2024 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.medj.2024.03.022 | Guevara-Aguirre BMJ Case Reports 2020 https://doi.org/10.1136/bcr-2019-231737
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The registry direction here is worth stating plainly, because it inverts this library's framing. Every interventional trial found in these families runs the opposite way: NCT00571727 (Ipsen, mecasermin, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00571727) and NCT00368173 (Insmed, recombinant IGF-1 with IGFBP-3, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00368173) both administer IGF-1 to children in order to reverse the deficiency and restore height. Neither tests the enhancement; the clinical world treats this genotype as a disease to be corrected, and neither trial administers or edits the gene itself. The one same-direction human intervention is pharmacological rather than genetic: pegvisomant, a growth hormone receptor antagonist, was used in a University of California insulin-sensitivity study (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02023918), which again measures rather than installs the genotype and was not aimed at longevity. A further caution for anyone reading the lipid panel of this genotype: the 2024 follow-up found affected subjects have elevated LDL cholesterol yet lower carotid intima-media thickness (Guevara-Aguirre 2024, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.medj.2024.03.022), so their blood work looks worse than their arteries do. Obesity is also part of the clinical picture rather than absent from it, with body mass index 31 against 30.1 in relatives and 57% versus 52% above a BMI of 30. Finally, the non-medical cost is documented in the same literature: people with genetic syndromes of severe short stature in developing countries face social branding and stigma (Guevara-Aguirre 2020, https://doi.org/10.1136/bcr-2019-231737). Reference identifiers are UniProt P10912 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P10912) and PDB 1A22 (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1A22), one of eleven solved structures.

Narrative: The Venus' flower basket sponge (Euplectella aspergillum) builds an intricate glass skeleton at ambient temperature and pressure — a feat human engineering cannot match. Glassin is the silica-precipitating protein that templates this process, directing dissolved silicic acid into precisely organized nanoscale glass fibers with fiber-optic-grade optical clarity. This biological glass factory operates where industrial synthesis requires extreme heat.
Short Description: This protein folds silicic acid into glass fibers inside a living body, at room temperature and neutral pH, no furnace needed. Sponge spicules made this way transmit light like fiber-optic cable but flex more without snapping. So far this only works in Euplectella aspergillum, the Venus flower basket sponge, and lab dishes of recombinant protein — no human use exists. The catch: full skeleton strength needs several sponge proteins together, and glassin alone is unproven for bone implants.
Mechanism: Glassin contains a unique silica-condensing domain that catalyzes polycondensation of silicic acid. The protein self-assembles into filaments that template hierarchical silica deposition, creating structures with superior mechanical properties to synthetic glass fibers — combining strength, flexibility, and optical waveguide capability.
Achievements (effect sizes): Recombinant glassin produces amorphous silica nanoparticles at room temperature and neutral pH. Sponge spicules show fiber-optic light transmission with better flexibility than industrial optical fibers.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3
Translational Gaps: Scaling recombinant production for industrial application. Multi-protein cooperation in vivo may be required for full structural hierarchy. Biocompatibility for medical implants needs validation.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Most advanced bio-glass material known. Potential applications in optical sensors, bone scaffolds, and room-temperature glass manufacturing.

Narrative: The naked mole-rat is virtually immune to cancer and lives 10x longer than similar-sized rodents. Its fructose metabolism pathway is uniquely altered — GLUT5 transporter and ketohexokinase (KHK) show reduced expression, effectively blocking fructose-driven lipogenesis and metabolic syndrome. This natural metabolic rewiring may explain the species' remarkable resistance to obesity, diabetes, and metabolic disease.
Short Description: The gut absorbs less fructose and the liver cannot turn it into fat, blocking the sugar rush that drives obesity and diabetes. Naked mole-rats run this way naturally and stay metabolically healthy across a 31-year lifespan. Pfizer's KHK-blocking drug PF-06835919 already reached Phase 2 for fatty liver disease, after cutting liver fat 80% in mice. Dialling KHK down too far risks the same buildup seen in inherited fructose intolerance.
Mechanism: Downregulated GLUT5 limits cellular fructose uptake. Reduced KHK activity prevents fructose phosphorylation and subsequent de novo lipogenesis, uric acid production, and ATP depletion. Together they block the fructose-driven metabolic syndrome cascade.
Achievements (effect sizes): Naked mole-rats show no age-related metabolic decline. KHK inhibitors in mice reduce hepatic steatosis by 80%. Pfizer KHK inhibitor PF-06835919 reached Phase 2 clinical trials for NASH.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4
Translational Gaps: Species-specific metabolic context may limit direct translation. KHK inhibition in humans needs careful monitoring for hereditary fructose intolerance-like effects.
Key References (DOIs): https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aab3896
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: KHK pharmaceutical inhibitors already in clinical development independently of NMR biology.

Narrative: Greenland sharks swim through Arctic depths for 272 to 392 years — some individuals were alive before the American Revolution. Julius Nielsen dated them by radiocarbon-dating their eye lenses in 2016, making them the longest-lived vertebrates known. In 2024, a preprint from Alessandro Cellerino's group reported a 6.45-Gb genome assembly: 81 duplicated genes enriched for DNA double-strand-break repair, three copies of RAD51, expanded NF-κB signaling, and a unique lysine insertion in the C-terminus of p53 that AlphaFold predicts would extend an alpha-helix. All of it, so far, is comparative genomics — no one has expressed the shark p53 variant in a cell, knocked it into a mouse, or done any functional assay whatsoever. The shark is essentially unculturable; you cannot easily get primary cells. It's the most tantalizing longevity genome we have, and simultaneously the one furthest from any experiment a lab could actually run next Tuesday.
Short Description: Cells get their DNA cut by breaks, and this network patches them before they turn into mutations or cell death. Greenland sharks carry 81 duplicated repair genes, three copies of RAD51, and a lysine insertion in p53, and one shark aged this way was at least 272 years old. It's a 2024 preprint only — no lab has expressed the shark p53 variant in a cell or mouse, since the species can't be cultured. The catch: extra RAD51 drives cancer in mammals instead of preventing it.
Mechanism: 81 duplicated genes forming DSB-repair GO-enriched STRING network; RAD51 in 3 copies (one intronless retrotranspositional); NF2 duplication; unique lysine insertion in p53 HKKEKE C-terminal motif predicted (AlphaFold3) to extend helix.
Achievements (effect sizes): Sahm 2024 bioRxiv (preprint): 6.45 Gb chromosome-level assembly; 22,634 genes; statistical enrichment p=0.029 (network), FDR=0.002 with TP53. Nielsen 2016 Science: lens radiocarbon dating → minimum ages 272 y. Nothing else — all predictions purely computational; no functional assay on GLS p53 variant; no mouse knock-in; no heterologous cell test; no tissue culture possible.
Highest Evidence Tier: T1 (genomic + in silico AlphaFold3 only)
Translational Gaps: Everything — expression/functional validation of GLS p53 variant; knock-in mouse; cell models.
Key References (DOIs): Sahm bioRxiv 2024 https://doi.org/10.1101/2024.09.09.611499 | Nielsen Science 2016 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaf1703
