Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Preprint; no expression/functional validation; p53 CTD structural prediction is low-confidence; RAD51 overexpression is oncogenic in mammals. "512-yr shark" = upper 95.4% CI bound; measured floor is ~272 y.

Narrative:
The Greenland shark, Somniosus microcephalus, is the longest-lived vertebrate known. Radiocarbon dating of eye lens nuclei from 28 female sharks between 81 and 502 centimetres in total length revealed a lifespan of at least 272 years, with age at sexual maturity of at least 156 plus or minus 22 years and the largest animal, at 502 centimetres, dated to 392 plus or minus 120 years old (Nielsen 2016, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaf1703). The exhibit record credits the species with negligible senescence past 400 years.

H1F0 encodes histone H1.0, a linker histone that binds at the point where DNA enters and exits the nucleosome and stabilises higher-order chromatin architecture. The hypothesis behind this entry is that shark-specific variants of the protein achieve enhanced chromatin compaction, which would reduce aberrant transcription and protect against the epigenetic drift that accumulates with age. It is an appealing idea because it proposes that extreme longevity is a problem of maintaining genomic order rather than of repairing damage, and because linker histones are among the most ancient and conserved proteins in the eukaryotic nucleus.

The honest position is that this is the least-evidenced entry in the Longevity and Genome category. The claims about shark H1F0 variants are genomic and transcriptomic correlations, not demonstrations of cause, and as set out in the notes below, the single reference the record carries is a genome paper for a different shark species.
Short Description: This linker histone clamps DNA into tightly packed chromatin, muting transposable elements and suppressing the transcriptional noise that accumulates with age. Greenland sharks live longer than any other vertebrate — radiocarbon dating of eye lens nuclei put the largest animal measured at 392 plus or minus 120 years, and the exhibit record credits them with negligible senescence past 400 years. Nothing here has been tested outside the shark: no mammalian cell line, no transgenic animal, no trial, and the only supporting sequence work in the record is from a different shark species entirely. Packing chromatin that tightly also risks freezing gene expression in place, silencing genes a cell will need to switch on later. A 2026 study also found extensive cardiac fibrosis and heavy lipofuscin accumulation in Greenland shark hearts, which is not what negligible senescence looks like.
Mechanism: H1F0 encodes linker histone H1.0, which binds the nucleosome at the DNA entry and exit site and drives folding of the nucleosome array into compact higher-order chromatin. Compaction of that kind silences transposable elements and reduces transcriptional noise, both of which increase with age in most species examined. The mechanism proposed for this entry is that shark variants of the protein bind nucleosomes with higher affinity, which would produce tighter packaging and, in turn, suppressed age-related epigenetic drift and better-maintained heterochromatin integrity. The enhanced binding affinity is the proposed step; it is stated in the record as a property of the shark variants and no measurement of it appears in the reference the record cites.
Achievements (effect sizes):
What the record asserts, and what can be independently confirmed, need to be kept apart here.

The record states three findings: that Greenland sharks show negligible senescence markers past 400 years, that H1F0 expression remains stable across age cohorts, and that chromatin accessibility assays show tighter packaging in this species than in short-lived elasmobranchs. None of these three is reported in the single paper the record cites, which is the white shark genome (see notes), and I could not locate a source for any of them. They are preserved here as the record's claims, unattributed rather than falsely attributed.

What is independently verified is the longevity itself, from radiocarbon dating of eye lens nuclei in 28 female sharks (Nielsen 2016, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaf1703), and the genomic groundwork that has since appeared. A chromosome-level Greenland shark genome assembly published in 2026 spans 5.9 gigabases with an N50 length of 233 megabases and a completeness score of 96.7 percent; analyses of gene family expansion and positive selection in that assembly recovered classical longevity-associated mechanisms including immune enhancement, cancer resistance and DNA repair (Yang 2026, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2601272123). The genome paper does not single out H1F0.

The reference the record carries is a 2019 paper by Marra and colleagues that reports the white shark genome and finds evidence of positive selection and gene-content enrichment for genome-stability genes across elasmobranchs (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1819778116). That is real evidence for elasmobranch genome-stability adaptations in general, but it concerns Carcharodon carcharias, not Somniosus microcephalus, and it is not about H1F0.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3
Translational Gaps: Nothing about this has been tested in a mammalian cell, so the first step is simply expressing a shark H1.0 variant in a human or mouse line and measuring whether chromatin compaction actually increases. Delivering a histone variant to post-mitotic cells is a genuine obstacle rather than a formality, because histones are normally deposited during replication and a non-dividing neuron or cardiomyocyte has no replication-coupled route to incorporate them. The long-term consequence of tighter packaging is the central unknown: gene expression plasticity depends on chromatin being openable, and an intervention that suppresses transcriptional noise by compaction will also suppress the induction of genes a cell needs later. Before any of that, the entry needs a source: the causal claim rests on correlational genomic and transcriptomic observations that the cited reference does not contain.
Key References (DOIs): Nielsen Science 2016 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaf1703 | Yang Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 2026 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2601272123 | Chiavacci Aging Cell 2026 https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.70505 | Marra Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 2019 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1819778116
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave:
The longevity correlation is genomic and transcriptomic, not causal, and this entry has a citation problem that a reader should be told about directly.

The only reference the record carries is https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1819778116, published in 2019 by Marra and colleagues in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences under the title 'White shark genome reveals ancient elasmobranch adaptations associated with wound healing and the maintenance of genome stability'. It is a white shark genome paper. It does not concern the Greenland shark, and it makes no claim about H1F0, chromatin compaction in Somniosus microcephalus, nucleosome binding affinity, or senescence markers at any age. Three of the four statements in the record's achievements field therefore have no source in the record and none that I was able to find. I have preserved all three claims and marked them as unsourced rather than attaching a citation that does not support them.

A second point cuts against the entry's premise. A 2026 study of cardiac ageing in the Greenland shark found extensive interstitial and perivascular fibrosis throughout the ventricular myocardium, affecting both the compact and spongy layers in both sexes, together with extreme lipofuscin accumulation; the fibrotic pattern was absent in the comparison species, the deep-sea shark Etmopterus spinax and the short-lived killifish Nothobranchius furzeri, which suggests it is specific to Somniosus microcephalus (Chiavacci 2026, https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.70505). Fibrosis and lipofuscin are conventional senescence markers. Whatever the Greenland shark is doing to reach three centuries, 'negligible senescence' is too strong a description of its heart, and the exhibit should not claim otherwise.

The lifespan figure is also worth stating precisely. The radiocarbon study established at least 272 years, with the largest animal at 392 plus or minus 120 years (Nielsen 2016, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaf1703); the 2026 genome paper quotes the estimated lifespan as 392 plus or minus 120 years (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2601272123). The record's 'over 400 years' sits inside the upper half of that confidence interval rather than being a measured value.

Narrative: Naked mole-rats live over 30 years and almost never get cancer — a scandal for a rodent. Their secret is a gooey, ultra-high-molecular-weight form of hyaluronic acid that makes their tissues feel springy under tweezers. In 2023, the Gorbunova-Seluanov lab put the mole-rat version of the gene that makes this molecule (nmrHas2) into ordinary mice. The result: median lifespan rose 4.4% (9% in females), maximum lifespan +12%, and cancer deaths in aged mice dropped from 83% to 49%. The mice aged more gracefully — better grip strength, less inflammation, younger-looking guts. It's the first time a single naked mole-rat gene has clearly extended a mammal's life. One caveat: in a xenograft tumor model, the same gene actually helped cancer grow — so context matters, and the effect is smaller than calorie restriction or rapamycin. Still, the first rodent longevity gene transfer that worked.
Short Description: Cells build a springy scaffold of hyaluronic acid, and naked mole-rats make a version over 5 times human size, pushing joints and gut into a young, anti-inflammatory state. Giving mice the mole-rat gene raised median lifespan 4.4% and max lifespan 12.2%, cutting old-age cancer deaths from 83% to 49%. Only done in mice so far, one lab, one cohort, no human or primate data. In a pancreatic xenograft, the same gene fed tumor growth instead of blocking it.
Mechanism: NMR-specific Asn→Ser substitutions in catalytic loop produce high-molecular-mass HA (HMM-HA, >6.1 MDa, ~5× mouse/human); anti-inflammatory M2 polarization via CD44; reduced hyaluronidase in NMR tissues.
Achievements (effect sizes): Zhang 2023 Nature (conditional Tg C57BL/6, n=175): median lifespan +4.4% (♀ +9%), max +12.2% (♂ +16%). Spontaneous cancer mortality in old mice 83%→49%. Reduced DMBA/TPA papillomas. Lower frailty, preserved grip/rotarod, ↑bone connectivity (♀). Reduced plasma IL-12p40, MIP1α/β, CCL7 (aged ♀). BMDMs: ↓Il1b/Il6/Tnf, ↑Il10/Arg1 after LPS. Improved gut barrier; old intestinal organoids rescued by HMM-HA.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5
Translational Gaps: Human cell/in-vivo HMM-HA work not published; primate data; delivery; durable engineering in humans with high HYAL1/2 activity.
Key References (DOIs): Zhang Nature 2023 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06463-0 | Tian Nature 2013 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12234 | Hadi Nature 2020 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2410-x
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CONTRADICTIONS: (1) Tian 2015 AACR abstract — nmrHas2 and huHAS2 both PROMOTED AsPC1 pancreatic xenograft growth (context-dependent oncogenicity). (2) Maison 2025 preprint — nmrHas2 did NOT rescue age-related hearing loss (tissue-selective). (3) Hadi 2020 — NMR cells CAN be transformed at high oncogene dose (complicates cancer-resistance narrative); rebuttal exchange. (4) N→S residues shared with guinea pig/cetaceans — not unique to NMR. Single lab, single cohort, not independently replicated; effect smaller than rapamycin or CR; ceiling effect from mouse hyaluronidase.

Manipulation: haplotype introgression from a wild diploid relative
Narrative:
Salinity is one of the oldest ways to ruin farmland, and durum wheat — the pasta wheat — is unusually bad at surviving it. Bread wheat is hexaploid and carries a sodium-handling gene called Kna1 on the D genome it inherited from a wild grass. Durum is tetraploid, has no D genome, and therefore no Kna1. That single absence is much of the reason a durum field on saline soil yields badly while a bread wheat field beside it does not.

The fix came from an older, smaller wheat. Einkorn, Triticum monococcum, is a wild diploid that carries its own version of the transporter, and researchers at CSIRO and the University of Adelaide mapped it to a locus they named Nax2 and identified the causal gene as TmHKT1;5-A. Its position inside the plant is the whole story. The protein sits on the plasma membrane of the cells that wrap around the xylem vessels in the root — the pipes carrying sap upward. As sodium-laden sap moves past, the transporter pulls sodium back out of the stream and deposits it in the surrounding root tissue, so what arrives in the leaf is a diluted version of what the root absorbed. Uptake does not change; interception does.

They then crossed the locus into commercial durum and grew it in saline fields against near-isogenic lines that lacked it, which is the comparison that actually matters agronomically. The lines carrying Nax2 made a quarter more grain (https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2120). This is the library's clearest example of an enhancement that is finished rather than promising: no transgene, no vector, no regulatory review, just a cross and a molecular marker. It is equally the clearest example of context-dependence. The same locus moved into bread wheat buys nothing at all, because the D genome already brought one, and the trait only addresses sodium toxicity — not the osmotic half of salt stress, which pulls water out of a root long before any sodium has accumulated in a leaf.
Short Description: Sodium-selective pumps line the plumbing of the roots and strip salt out of the sap before it is pushed up to the leaves, so the parts of the body that do the work never see the salt load. The transporter sits on the plasma membrane of the cells wrapping the xylem vessels and pulls sodium back out of the rising stream, lowering leaf sodium without reducing what the root takes up. Bred into commercial durum wheat, the locus raised grain yield by 25% in saline field soil against near-isogenic lines that lacked it. This one arrived by crossing rather than transformation, so it is already moving through wheat breeding programmes instead of sitting in a regulatory queue. The salt is intercepted rather than excreted — the root cells around the xylem absorb what the leaf is spared — and in bread wheat the gain is zero, because its D genome already carries an equivalent transporter.
Mechanism: TmHKT1;5-A encodes a sodium-selective member of the HKT1 subfamily of high-affinity potassium transporters, a 517-amino-acid, 57.3 kDa membrane protein. Unlike the HKT2 subfamily, which runs sodium-potassium symport, HKT1-class proteins move sodium alone as a uniporter. The protein localises to the plasma membrane of the root cells that surround the xylem vessels, which places it exactly where the transpiration stream leaves the root for the shoot. From that position it retrieves sodium ions out of the xylem sap and unloads them into the neighbouring stelar parenchyma. The consequence is a lower sodium concentration in the leaf at unchanged sodium uptake by the root, so the trait is exclusion by interception rather than a refusal to absorb. Bread wheat carries a functionally equivalent HKT1;5 gene, Kna1, on its D genome; durum wheat, lacking that genome, has no counterpart, and that is the genetic reason durum is the salt-sensitive wheat.
Achievements (effect sizes): The headline result here is agronomic rather than physiological, which is rare in this library. The Nax2 locus from wild diploid einkorn wheat was crossed into the commercial durum cultivar Tamaroi by marker-assisted introgression, and the resulting lines were grown in saline field soil alongside near-isogenic lines lacking the locus — the same genetic background minus the transporter. Across those trials, “field trials on saline soils demonstrate that the presence of TmHKT1;5-A significantly reduces leaf [Na+] and increases durum wheat grain yield by 25% compared to near-isogenic lines without the Nax2 locus” (Munns 2012, https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2120). Two features make that sentence unusually strong evidence rather than a promising pot result. The endpoint is harvested grain in a field, not survival in a glasshouse, and the comparator is near-isogenic, so the 25% is attributable to the introgressed locus itself and not to whatever else a salt-tolerant landrace might carry along with it. The same work localised the transporter to the plasma membrane of the root cells surrounding the xylem, which ties the yield figure to a specific cell layer and a specific ion flux rather than to a vague tolerance phenotype (https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2120).
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (causal gene identified, mechanism localised to a specific cell layer, and validated by field trials against near-isogenic lines with a grain-yield endpoint; deployed by conventional breeding rather than as a transgene)
Translational Gaps: The 25% figure belongs to durum wheat on saline soil and nowhere else. The source reports no equivalent number for other cereals and none for non-saline conditions, and this record did not verify a non-saline control yield, so whether the locus costs anything in a good year is an open question rather than an answered one. No experimental structure of TmHKT1;5-A exists. Protein Data Bank entry 8W9T is TaHKT2;1 (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/8W9T), a member of the other HKT subfamily with different ion selectivity, and it must not be presented as this protein. Relevance to animals is nil in the strict sense: HKT transporters have no metazoan orthologue, so a human version of this card would have to borrow an entirely different protein family to achieve the same interception — and a human body has no xylem stream to intercept in the first place.
Key References (DOIs): Munns Nature Biotechnology 2012 https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2120
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Nomenclature is a trap here. The same protein appears in the literature as HKT8, as HKT1;5-A and as the Nax2 locus, and the UniProt entry A4ZGN5 is annotated under the older name HKT8 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A4ZGN5), so a visitor searching one name will miss papers filed under the others. The delivery route makes this the exhibit's most useful contrast: the enhancement was moved by crossing and marker selection rather than by transformation, which is why it sits in breeding pipelines rather than in a regulatory queue, unlike the transgenic and gene-edited cards in the same category (https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2120). The work was carried out by CSIRO Plant Industry with the Australian Centre for Plant Functional Genomics at the University of Adelaide, which mapped the locus in Triticum monococcum, identified the causal gene, localised it in the root and ran the saline field trials (https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2120). There are no clinical trials and no commercial human product; the commercial product is wheat. No contradictory replication surfaced in the literature searched for this record, but the card rests on a single quantified field result, so the 25% has not yet been independently reproduced in a separately published trial.

Narrative: Every animal has HSF1 — it's the master switch that turns on heat shock proteins when cells get stressed. But the sleeping chironomid did something unusual with it: over evolutionary time, P. vanderplanki rewired HSF1 to also activate desiccation-protection genes, including LEA proteins, trehalose synthesis enzymes, and thioredoxins. Mazin et al. (2018 PNAS) showed this cooption in detail: HSF1 in the midge activates not just classical heat-shock targets but an entire anhydrobiosis program. The key innovation is a double TCTAGAA motif upstream of the Hsf gene itself, creating a positive feedback loop — HSF1 activates its own transcription, amplifying the stress response. Knockdown of HSF1 in the Pv11 cell line suppressed trehalose-induced activation of multiple protective genes and reduced desiccation survival fivefold. The cooption works because the promoters of desiccation genes acquired HSF-binding sites, recruiting an existing regulatory network for a new purpose. This is not about the HSF1 protein being different — it's about rewiring the regulatory circuitry around a conserved transcription factor. The implication for engineering is tantalizing: you might not need novel alien proteins if you can teach human HSF1 to activate a broader protective program using synthetic promoter elements.
Short Description: Cells switch on this master stress gene, which normally triggers heat-shock proteins but is rewired in this insect to also flip on trehalose sugar, protective LEA proteins and antioxidants. Knocking it down in midge cells cut desiccation survival fivefold. It exists only in Polypedilum vanderplanki cell lines, with no mammalian version built. Constant overexpression in human cells drives tumour growth.
Mechanism: Transcription factor cooption: P. vanderplanki desiccation genes acquired TCTAGAA HSF-binding motifs in their promoters. HSF1 auto-activates via double TCTAGAA upstream of its own gene. Drives LEA proteins, trehalose synthesis (TPS/TPP), thioredoxins, and heat shock proteins as a coordinated anhydrobiosis program.
Achievements (effect sizes): Mazin 2018 PNAS: HSF1 knockdown in Pv11 cells reduced desiccation survival ~5-fold; suppressed trehalose-induced activation of LEA, TPS, and thioredoxin genes. Promoter analysis: TCTAGAA motif enriched in desiccation-induced genes. Double HSF-binding site upstream of Hsf enables auto-amplification. Gusev 2011: HSP70/HSP90/HSP60/sHSP all upregulated during anhydrobiosis entry.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (Pv11 cell knockdown + transcriptomic analysis)
Translational Gaps: Regulatory rewiring rather than simple gene transfer — would require synthetic promoter engineering in mammalian cells; no mammalian proof-of-concept; HSF1 overexpression in mammals is oncogenic in some contexts (Dai 2007).
Key References (DOIs): Mazin PNAS 2018 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1719493115 | Gusev Cell Stress Chaperones 2010 https://doi.org/10.1007/s12192-010-0223-9 | Hiki BBRC 2026 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbrc.2026.153267
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CAUTION: HSF1 is a known oncogene in mammalian contexts — constitutive activation promotes tumor growth (Dai 2007 Cell). The chironomid cooption works because it is inducible and context-dependent, not constitutive. Simple HSF1 overexpression in human cells would likely cause problems. The engineering value is in the regulatory architecture (synthetic promoters), not in transplanting the midge HSF1 protein itself. Requires systems-level circuit design, not single-gene transfer.

Manipulation: Engineered point mutants in middle domain, overexpression
Narrative:
Yeast can do something your cells cannot. When heat or stress leaves its proteins tangled into aggregates, yeast deploys Hsp104, a hexameric ring that grips a polypeptide sticking out of an aggregate and drags it through a central pore using ATP, pulling molecules back out of the clump one chain at a time. Metazoa have no homolog of this protein at all - somewhere in animal evolution the disaggregase was lost, and animal cells got chaperones that prevent misfolding and proteolytic systems that destroy the aggregate, but nothing that reverses aggregation. Neurodegeneration is largely a disease of aggregates that have already formed, which makes the missing machine conspicuous.

James Shorter's laboratory at the University of Pennsylvania asked whether yeast Hsp104 could be pointed at human disease proteins. Wild-type Hsp104 barely touches them. But single missense mutations in the coiled-coil middle domain - most famously replacing alanine 503 - potentiate the enzyme, and the potentiated versions dissolve alpha-synuclein, TDP-43 and FUS, the aggregating proteins of Parkinson's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2013.11.047). In a transgenic worm model they protected dopaminergic neurons that alpha-synuclein would otherwise have killed, and the effect was post-translational: the variants did not change how much alpha-synuclein the worm made, they changed what happened to it.

What makes this card honest is that the same paper measures the cost. Potentiation works by loosening how the enzyme chooses substrates, so the variant that dissolves a disease aggregate can also unfold a host protein that is merely metastable. At 37 degrees C - human body temperature - the A503V variant is toxic to yeast for exactly that reason (https://doi.org/10.1242/dmm.016113). The programme since then has been about keeping the power while narrowing the aim (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2019.07.069).
Short Description: Clumped, already-aggregated protein gets threaded back out of the clump one chain at a time by an ATP-powered yeast winch that animals never evolved - so this clears existing tangles instead of just preventing new ones. In a nematode Parkinson's model where alpha-synuclein left only about 16% of animals with a normal count of dopaminergic neurons at day 7, engineered variants raised that to 30.5% and 34%, while unmodified yeast Hsp104 rescued nothing. The same variants pulled mislocalised TDP-43 back into the nucleus in roughly 30-45% of yeast cells against about 6-8% in controls, the readout that matters in ALS. The strongest animal evidence is still eight neurons in a worm, with no mammalian efficacy data and an active academic programme at the University of Pennsylvania rather than a trial. The A503V variant is outright toxic to yeast at 37 degrees C, because at mild heat it starts unfolding host proteins that merely look damaged - a problem at human body temperature by definition.
Mechanism: Hsp104 is a 908-amino-acid protein disaggregase from baker's yeast, a member of the AAA+ family of ATP-driven molecular machines (ATPases associated with diverse cellular activities). Six copies assemble into a ring with two nucleotide-binding domains per subunit and a coiled-coil middle domain, and the ring threads polypeptides through its central channel using the energy of ATP hydrolysis, extracting individual monomers from disordered aggregates and from amyloid fibrils. Animals have no Hsp104 homolog, and the wild-type enzyme has only limited activity against human disease proteins. Single missense mutations in helix 1, 2 or 3 of the middle domain, or in the small domain of the first nucleotide-binding domain, potentiate it: they reconfigure how the six subunits collaborate, desensitise the enzyme to inhibition, remove its requirement for the Hsp70 chaperone system, and raise ATP hydrolysis, translocation and unfoldase activity roughly two- to four-fold. Potentiated variants can engage substrates that present only short unstructured tracts, which wild-type Hsp104 cannot grip - the reason they act on TDP-43, FUS and alpha-synuclein - while still leaving fully native, folded protein alone.
Achievements (effect sizes): In a transgenic Caenorhabditis elegans model of Parkinson's disease, human alpha-synuclein and Hsp104 variants were co-expressed in the eight dopaminergic neurons visible under the dat-1 promoter. Alpha-synuclein alone left roughly 16% of animals with a normal complement of those neurons at day 7, whereas Hsp104 A503S and Hsp104 A503V-DPLF displayed significant protection, at 30.5% and 34% normal worms respectively, at day 7; neither wild-type Hsp104 nor an ATPase-dead control rescued anything. The protection persisted with age, since at day 10 Hsp104 A503S (21%) and Hsp104 A503V-DPLF (24%) expressing worms had significantly more normal dopaminergic neurons compared to alpha-synuclein alone (7.8%), the ATPase-dead variant (10%), or Hsp104 wild-type (11%), and the variants did not alter alpha-synuclein messenger RNA levels, placing the effect after translation (Jackrel 2014, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2013.11.047). In yeast expressing the ALS protein TDP-43, Hsp104 A503V and Hsp104 V426L eliminated some of the cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregates, and roughly 30% and 45% of cells respectively recovered nuclear TDP-43 localisation compared with about 6-8% in the vector and wild-type Hsp104 controls, with corresponding figures of about 26% and 36% for the ALS-linked TDP-43 M337V variant. In the same system wild-type FUS aggregated strongly, with about 80% of cells displaying cytoplasmic aggregates, and Hsp104 A503V and Hsp104 V426L prevented aggregate accumulation so that only about 43% and 54% of cells contained aggregates; sedimentation analysis further showed those two variants reduced insoluble wild-type alpha-synuclein by about 36% and 27% and insoluble alpha-synuclein A53T by about 51% and 27%, while wild-type Hsp104 did not alter A53T solubility at all (Jackrel 2014, https://doi.org/10.1242/dmm.016113).
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (engineered gain-of-function, quantified in yeast and a C. elegans neurodegeneration model, sustained programme with follow-up variant engineering; no mammalian in vivo efficacy data)
Translational Gaps: The strongest animal result in the record is the survival of eight dopaminergic neurons in a nematode, and no mammalian in vivo efficacy has been published for any potentiated variant. Hsp104 is also a foreign 908-amino-acid hexamer with no metazoan homolog, so a human immune response to it has not been examined at all. The off-target unfolding measured at 37 degrees C is the most directly relevant obstacle, because that is the temperature a mammalian host runs at continuously rather than a heat-shock condition, and the variants that were carried into animal work were selected partly for having less of that toxicity. Subsequent work from the same group is explicitly aimed at engineering variants that keep the disaggregase activity while lowering the off-target damage (Tariq 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2019.07.069; March 2020, https://doi.org/10.7554/elife.57457), which is a fair statement of where the field currently stands. Delivery is a further unsolved problem, since a 908-amino-acid coding sequence must reach post-mitotic neurons and be expressed there at levels high enough to assemble functional hexamers.
Key References (DOIs): Jackrel Cell 2014 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2013.11.047 | Jackrel Disease Models & Mechanisms 2014 https://doi.org/10.1242/dmm.016113 | Tariq Cell Reports 2019 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2019.07.069 | March eLife 2020 https://doi.org/10.7554/elife.57457
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: This is a rare documented case of a therapeutic gain-of-function arising from single missense mutations: nearly all substitutions at Hsp104 position 503 potentiate the enzyme, and potentiated variants hydrolyse ATP roughly two- to four-fold faster than wild type (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2013.11.047). Two boundaries keep the claim honest. First, the variants are not indiscriminate shredders, because neither wild-type Hsp104 nor A503V unfolds untagged, fully folded green fluorescent protein (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2013.11.047). Second, they are not universal, because neither Hsp104 A503S nor the wild-type enzyme could disaggregate EWSR1, so this card should not promise clearance of any aggregate (https://doi.org/10.1242/dmm.016113). The reported tradeoffs also disagree with a naive reading of potentiation as strict improvement: A503V is toxic to yeast at 37 degrees C and conferred less thermotolerance than wild type, and the variants chosen for the animal experiments, A503S and A503V-DPLF, were the ones with greater-than-wild-type thermotolerance and lower toxicity at 37 degrees C (https://doi.org/10.1242/dmm.016113). There are no clinical trials, no company and no registry records; searches for Hsp104 and for disaggregase interventions returned no studies, and the work remains an academic programme at the University of Pennsylvania. Multiple cryo-electron-microscopy structures of the yeast hexamer are available, including Protein Data Bank entries 5KNE, 5VJH, 5VY8, 5VY9 and 5VYA (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/5KNE), with the sequence at UniProt P31539 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P31539).

Narrative: Sharks and skates detect electric fields as weak as 5 nanovolts per centimeter — they can sense the heartbeat of a buried flatfish from a meter away. The molecular sensor is a specialized splice variant of the BK potassium channel (KCNMA1) expressed in the ampullae of Lorenzini, gel-filled canals in the snout that serve as biological voltmeters. King and colleagues identified in 2015 that the skate electrosensory BK channel lacks the STREX regulatory exon, making it relatively voltage-insensitive but exquisitely calcium-sensitive. This variant couples with CaV1.3 voltage-gated calcium channels to create an oscillatory voltage amplifier tuned to sub-millivolt signals. Chen and colleagues showed in 2023 that these BK channels traffic to plasma membranes, nuclear envelopes, and kinocilia of electrosensory cells. The human ortholog KCNMA1 is expressed in many tissues — the gene is conserved, but our version includes the STREX exon that masks the electroreceptive tuning. The skate BK has been successfully expressed in human HEK293 cells, confirming cross-species functionality. No mammal has electroreception, so this would be an entirely novel sensory modality — with no existing neural circuitry to process the input.
Short Description: Weak electric fields open calcium channels that flip on a calcium-hungry potassium channel, creating voltage oscillations that encode signal strength like a biological voltmeter. Skates detect fields as faint as 5 nanovolts per centimetre, enough to sense a buried flatfish's heartbeat. It has worked in skate cells and human HEK293 dishes, never in a living mammal. No mammal brain has a cortical map to read the signal.
Mechanism: The skate KCNMA1 STREX-minus BK channel variant couples with CaV1.3 in ampullary electrosensory cells to create an oscillatory voltage amplifier. Tiny electrical fields trigger CaV1.3-mediated Ca²⁺ entry, which activates the calcium-hypersensitive BK channel, producing membrane potential oscillations that encode signal strength.
Achievements (effect sizes): King 2016: cloned skate ampullary BK alpha subunit, characterized STREX-minus splice variant, expressed in HEK293. Chen 2023: BK/CaV1.3 co-expression in electrosensory cells with nuclear and kinocilia trafficking. Detection threshold: 5 nV/cm electric fields in source organism.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3 (HEK293 expression + skate electrophysiology)
Translational Gaps: No mammalian in-vivo demonstration. Completely novel sensory modality with no existing cortical processing pathways. Requires simultaneous expression of BK variant and CaV1.3. Ampullae of Lorenzini are complex organs, not just ion channels — channel alone does not recreate the amplification structure.
Key References (DOIs): King Gene 2015 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gene.2015.12.010 | Chen Cells 2023 https://doi.org/10.3390/cells12172125
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The most speculative entry in the Perception category. While the molecular mechanism is well-characterized in skates, translating electroreception to mammals faces a fundamental problem: the ampullae of Lorenzini are complex organs with specialized gel-filled canals, not just ion channels. No mammalian brain has electroreceptive cortical areas — sensory data would require neural plasticity to become perceptible.

Narrative: Klotho is named after the Greek fate who spins the thread of life, and for once the name fits. Japanese researchers discovered it in 1997 by accident — mice that lacked it aged catastrophically fast, dying by 60 days. The reverse is equally dramatic: mice engineered to produce extra Klotho live about 20% longer, and delivering a secreted form via gene therapy extends life in adult mice too. In 2023, Stanford's Dena Dubal showed that a single injection of recombinant Klotho improved working memory in aged rhesus macaques for about two weeks — the first time a longevity protein has improved cognition in a primate. Humans who carry one copy of the KL-VS variant are enriched among the very old and score better on executive function tests. The twist: people with two copies fare worse, not better. The therapeutic window is narrow, and the Kurosu 2005 lifespan result has not been independently replicated at cohort scale.
Short Description: Circulating in blood, this protein brakes insulin/IGF signaling and keeps neurons and muscle youthful, while its absence sends mice into premature aging that kills them by 60 days. Extra copies gave mice 19-30% longer median lifespan, but made them hyperinsulinemic and less fertile. Untested in human trials, a single recombinant injection improved spatial memory in aged rhesus macaques for about two weeks. People with two copies of the protective KL-VS variant age worse than those with one.
Mechanism: Transmembrane + cleaved soluble hormone; FGF23 co-receptor; represses insulin/IGF signaling via AKT; modulates Wnt, TRPV5, NMDAR GluN2B.
Achievements (effect sizes): Kurosu 2005 Science: EFmKL46/48 Tg C57BL/6 ♀ median lifespan +19%, ♂ ~20–30%. Hyperinsulinemia, reduced ♀ fecundity. Kuro-o 1997: KL-null = premature-aging syndrome. Dubal 2014: Tg Klotho improves cognition independent of aging. AAV9-sKL (secretory Klotho) gene therapy: +20% median lifespan in male mice, improved muscle regeneration, bone structure, neurogenesis. Human KL-VS heterozygotes: longevity enrichment (Arking 2002/2005), better executive function, reduced APOE4-amyloid (Erickson 2019), n>700 across cohorts. Castner/Dubal 2023: aged rhesus macaques given 10 μg/kg sc recombinant Klotho → improved spatial working memory ~2 weeks; INVERTED-U dose response (20–30 μg/kg null).
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (human association) + T5 (mouse lifespan) + T5 (primate cognition)
Translational Gaps: Human RCT; safety of chronic IIS suppression; BBB penetration; narrow therapeutic window.
Key References (DOIs): Kurosu Science 2005 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1112766 | Kuro-o Nature 1997 https://doi.org/10.1038/36285 | Dubal Cell Reports 2014 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2014.03.076 | Castner Nat Aging 2023 https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00441-x
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: MIXED METABOLIC EFFECTS: Lifespan Tg mice were hyperinsulinemic (IR-resembling); KL-VS HOMOZYGOTES (VS/VS) have DECREASED longevity and poorer cognition — classic overdominance. Elevated FGF23/Klotho axis in CKD is a cardiovascular mortality marker. High-dose Klotho LOST cognitive benefit in primates (inverted-U). ♀ fecundity reduced. Kurosu 2005 lifespan result not independently replicated at cohort scale.

Narrative: Axolotls regrow entire limbs. Mice don't, but in 2013 George Daley's lab showed you can move the needle: activating Lin28a — an RNA-binding protein that flips cells into an embryonic-style metabolic gear — roughly doubled the speed at which young mice closed a 2-millimeter ear-punch hole, and modestly improved digit-tip regrowth in neonates. The mechanism is bioenergetic: Lin28a blocks the let-7 microRNA and directly boosts translation of glucose-metabolism and mitochondrial-respiration enzymes, essentially resetting the cell to its youthful fuel-burn profile. LIN28 is also one of the four factors in James Thomson's original recipe for reprogramming human cells into induced pluripotent stem cells. The limit: the regeneration boost largely fades with age. Adult mice don't regrow digits or hearts no matter how much Lin28a you give them. And because Lin28 suppresses let-7, which otherwise tamps down oncogenes like Myc and Hmga2, the cancer risk is a real concern.
Short Description: This RNA-binding protein blocks the let-7 microRNA and boosts glucose/mitochondrial enzymes, resetting cells to an embryonic fuel-burn mode. In mice this closed 2-mm ear-punch holes roughly 2× faster and boosted digit regrowth, but only in newborns. It's only ever been done in mice and axolotls — adult mice grew no new digits or heart tissue at any dose. The same let-7 suppression de-represses Myc and Hmga2, oncogenes linked to multiple cancers.
Mechanism: RNA-binding protein blocks let-7 miRNA biogenesis + directly enhances translation of glycolysis/OxPhos enzymes (PFKP, PDHA1/B, SDHA) → embryonic-like bioenergetics.
Achievements (effect sizes): Shyh-Chang/Daley 2013 Cell: iLin28a-Tg mice (inducible, leaky) — accelerated telogen→anagen hair; 2-mm ear hole closure ~2× faster at d5/8/11; enhanced digit regrowth in NEONATES ONLY (not adults); no heart regeneration. let-7 repression alone necessary but insufficient; OxPhos inhibition abrogates; activators partially phenocopy. Zhu 2010: Tg Lin28a → ↑body size, delayed puberty. Yu 2007 Science: LIN28 is one of 4 Thomson-cocktail factors for human iPSC generation.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (whole mouse, repair enhancement in young) + T6 (iPSC factor in human cells)
Translational Gaps: Axolotl-like adult limb/organ regeneration not recapitulated. Oncogenicity concern (Hmga2/Myc de-repression via let-7 suppression).
Key References (DOIs): Shyh-Chang Cell 2013 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2013.09.059 | Zhu Nat Genet 2010 https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.593 | Yu Science 2007 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1151526
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Adult digit regeneration does NOT improve. Lin28b dominant in some tissues (kidney, Yermalovich 2019). Lin28 is oncogenic in multiple cancers. Effects largely juvenile; adult digit/limb/heart not regenerated; leaky Tg complicates dose-response; Lin28a-KO is lethal/sterile.

Manipulation: Adenine base editing (c.1824C>T / G608G correction, ABE7.10max-VRQR)
Narrative:
Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome begins with a mutation that changes no amino acid at all. A single C-to-T substitution at position 1824 of the lamin A gene leaves the protein sequence on paper untouched, but it manufactures a splice signal where none belonged, and the cell obediently follows the new instruction: it cuts 150 nucleotides out of the message and builds progerin instead of lamin A. Progerin keeps a greasy farnesyl tail that mature lamin A is supposed to shed, so it never releases from the nuclear membrane. Nuclei buckle, arteries stiffen, skin and bone thin, and children who come to resemble the very old usually die of heart attack or stroke in their teens.

Because the cause is exactly one letter, this is one of the few human diseases where an editor can write the healthy sequence back rather than bolt on a compensating gene. David Liu's laboratory at the Broad Institute took that route with Francis Collins's group at the National Human Genome Research Institute, using patient skin-cell lines banked by the Progeria Research Foundation. Their adenine base editor makes no cut in the double helix and needs no donor template: it chemically converts the offending base back, and the cryptic splice signal disappears with it. In patient fibroblasts the correction reached 87% and 91% of mutant copies (Koblan 2021, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-03086-7).

The harder test was a living animal. The editor is too large for one adeno-associated virus, so it was split across two particles that reassemble inside transduced cells, and progeria mice received a single injection behind the eye at two weeks of age. Median lifespan went from 215 days to 510 days, and the smooth muscle cells that normally vanish from the progeroid aorta stayed where they belonged. For an exhibit about enhancement, this card answers a narrower and sharper question than most: can an ageing pathology be un-written rather than merely slowed? For this one mutation, in this one mouse, it can.
Short Description: Rewrites a single letter of DNA in the gene for the protein mesh that lines every cell nucleus, so the body stops manufacturing progerin — the permanently greasy version of that mesh which stiffens arteries, thins skin and bone, and kills children with progeria in their teens. One injection of the editor into progeria mice at two weeks of age raised median lifespan from 215 to 510 days, and six months later 20–60% of the mutant allele was corrected across their organs. In skin cells from two progeria patients the same editor fixed 87% and 91% of mutant copies, but no human editing trial exists: progeria is treated today with lonafarnib, a farnesyltransferase inhibitor that blunts progerin toxicity instead of removing it. The editor is imprecise next door — a neighbouring adenine is changed at 1.1–2.2%, writing a second, uncorrected Val690Ala substitution into the very lamin protein the therapy is repairing.
Mechanism: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) is caused by a dominant C-to-T transition at c.1824 of LMNA, written p.G608G because it is silent at the protein level. What it does instead is activate a cryptic 5' splice donor inside exon 11. The resulting transcript is 150 nucleotides short and encodes progerin, a lamin A that stays permanently farnesylated and therefore stays anchored in the nuclear lamina, distorting it. The correction uses an adenine base editor (ABE7.10max) fused to a VRQR variant of SpCas9 that tolerates a relaxed protospacer adjacent motif (PAM). The editor deaminates the mutant adenine on the antisense strand, converting the A-T pair back to G-C without a double-strand break and without a donor DNA template, which restores the wild-type splice donor and abolishes progerin production at its source. For delivery in a living animal the editor is too large for one capsid, so it is split and expressed from a pair of adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (AAV9) vectors that reconstitute the full-length protein by split-intein trans-splicing in transduced tissue.
Achievements (effect sizes): Two primary fibroblast lines from progeria patients, HGADFN167 and HGADFN188, were treated with the base editor and its guide RNA. Twenty days later the pathogenic allele had been corrected in 87% and 91% of copies, up from 84% and 85% at ten days (Koblan 2021, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-03086-7). The same editor was then tested in mice carrying the human c.1824C>T allele on both chromosomes, delivered as a split pair of AAV9 vectors at a total dose of 1×10^12 viral genomes in a single retro-orbital injection on postnatal day 14. Six months after that one injection, correction of roughly 20–60% was measured across organs including aorta, heart, bone and liver (Koblan 2021, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-03086-7). The functional endpoint was survival: median lifespan of the treated progeria mice rose from 215 days to 510 days, and the treatment also preserved vascular smooth muscle cell counts in the aorta and prevented the adventitial fibrosis that the disease otherwise produces (Koblan 2021, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-03086-7). Editing was clean at the DNA level in the sense that mattered most for a therapy: insertion and deletion frequencies stayed at or below 0.15%.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (in vivo mouse gene editing with a lifespan endpoint plus correction in human patient cells; no human editing trial yet)
Translational Gaps: No clinical trial of LMNA base editing exists, so nothing here has been tried in a person. The dose that worked in mice, 1×10^12 viral genomes across a dual AAV9 pair, does not scale to a child by simple arithmetic, and the manufacturing and safety work for that scale-up has not been published. Durability was measured to six months in a mouse; nobody knows how long the corrected cell population persists in a large, slowly turning-over human tissue such as the aortic wall. Pre-existing immunity to AAV9 circulates in a substantial fraction of the population and would exclude some patients outright. Timing also matters in a way the mouse data make explicit: the study compared delivery on postnatal day 3 with delivery on day 14, and the outcome depended on how early after diagnosis the edit arrived, which for a disease usually diagnosed in toddlerhood sets a clock the clinic would have to race (Koblan 2021, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-03086-7).
Key References (DOIs): Koblan Nature 2021 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-03086-7
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Unbiased off-target analysis of both DNA and RNA in the treated patient fibroblasts detected no off-target editing (Koblan 2021, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-03086-7). The precision problem sits at the target site rather than away from it: a bystander adenine at position 10 of the protospacer was edited at 1.1–2.2% in both patient lines, which installs a Val690Ala substitution in lamin A/C — a second, uncorrected coding change in the same nuclear-lamina protein the therapy is meant to repair. Correction is also strongly tissue-uneven after retro-orbital delivery: aorta and bone edit best while other tissues sit at the bottom of the 20–60% range. What progeria patients can actually get today is not a genetic correction. Lonafarnib (Zokinvy, Eiger BioPharmaceuticals) is an approved farnesyltransferase inhibitor that blunts progerin toxicity downstream and is available under an expanded-access protocol (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03895528). Progerinin, a progerin-binding small molecule from PRG Science & Technology, is in a Phase 2 dose-finding study (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06775041). Neither trial administers, edits or replaces LMNA — both work on the protein after the mutation has already been transcribed.

Narrative: Zebrafish (Danio rerio) can fully regenerate their hearts after 20% ventricular resection — a feat impossible for adult mammals. LRRC10 (Leucine Rich Repeat Containing 10) is a cardiomyocyte-specific gene essential for this process. It promotes cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation and proliferation, enabling mature heart muscle cells to re-enter the cell cycle and rebuild lost tissue. In mice, LRRC10 manipulation can reactivate neonatal-like cardiac regeneration.
Short Description: It unlocks heart muscle cells to disassemble their internal fibers, round up, divide, then rebuild — turning mature cardiomyocytes back into a proliferative state. Zebrafish fully regrow 20% of a resected ventricle within 60 days using this switch. So far it's only ever been done in zebrafish and neonatal mice, with no adult mammal or human trial yet. Forcing adult heart cells to divide risks arrhythmias, since new immature cardiomyocytes don't couple electrically like mature ones.
Mechanism: LRRC10 interacts with cardiac transcription factors and cell cycle regulators to promote cardiomyocyte dedifferentiation. It facilitates sarcomere disassembly, enabling mature cardiomyocytes to round up, divide, and then redifferentiate. The protein acts as a molecular switch between the quiescent adult state and the proliferative regenerative state.
Achievements (effect sizes): Zebrafish regenerate 20% ventricular resection within 60 days. LRRC10 knockout zebrafish show impaired cardiac regeneration. LRRC10 knockout mice develop dilated cardiomyopathy. Mouse neonatal heart regeneration studies show LRRC10-dependent proliferation.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4
Translational Gaps: Adult mammalian cardiomyocytes are highly resistant to cell cycle re-entry. Forcing proliferation risks arrhythmias from immature cardiomyocyte coupling. Temporal control of LRRC10 activation is critical.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Heart failure is the leading cause of death globally; cardiac regeneration is a major unmet need.

Narrative: Tardigrades survive vacuum, extreme radiation, and complete desiccation. MAHS (Mitochondrial Abundant Heat Soluble) protein from Ramazzottius varieornatus specifically protects mitochondria during these stresses. Unlike the cytoplasmic CAHS proteins, MAHS localizes to mitochondria and preserves their membrane integrity and function during desiccation, ensuring the cell's power plants survive to restart upon rehydration.
Short Description: Mitochondria are a cell's power plants, and their membranes collapse without water; this disordered protein coats them, keeping cristae intact and voltage recoverable after rehydration. MAHS-GFP confirms it reaches human mitochondria, but protection there has never been measured. Today it's untested in humans, used only in tardigrades and in DARPA-funded work stabilizing Factor VIII clotting factor without refrigeration. Targeting works; protective strength in human cells stays unmeasured.
Mechanism: MAHS is an intrinsically disordered protein that localizes to mitochondria via an N-terminal targeting sequence. Upon desiccation, it forms a protective matrix around mitochondrial membranes, preventing cristae collapse and maintaining membrane potential recovery capacity. It complements cytoplasmic CAHS by specifically shielding the organelle most vulnerable to oxidative stress.
Achievements (effect sizes): MAHS-GFP fusion localizes to human cell mitochondria. Expression improves hyperosmotic stress tolerance. Tardigrade TDPs (including MAHS) stabilize Factor VIII blood clotting factor without refrigeration. DARPA Biostasis program funding TDP applications.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4
Translational Gaps: Mitochondrial targeting in human cells confirmed but functional protection needs quantification. Relationship with mammalian mitochondrial stress response pathways unclear.
Key References (DOIs): https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0118272|https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molcel.2017.02.018
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Complements CAHS D (cytoplasmic) already in library. DARPA-funded applications for blood product preservation.

Narrative: Spider dragline silk is the strongest biological fiber known — tougher than steel, more elastic than nylon, lighter than carbon fiber, and fully biodegradable. The golden silk orbweaver Trichonephila clavipes spins dragline from a protein called MaSp1 (Major Ampullate Spidroin 1), a repetitive protein with alternating crystalline alanine-rich blocks and flexible glycine-rich linkers that self-assemble into nanofibrils. Transgenic goats carrying the MaSp1 gene secrete spidroin in their milk; transgenic silkworms incorporating MaSp1 produce composite fibers with improved mechanical properties. You and colleagues showed in 2018 that longer recombinant MaSp1 chain lengths produced significantly stronger composite silk fibers in transgenic Bombyx mori. An and colleagues demonstrated in 2015 that recombinant goat-milk MaSp1 supports neuronal growth comparable to poly-lysine. Li and colleagues in 2020 integrated a spidroin gene into cloned sheep embryos with a hair-follicle-specific promoter. The protein has been expressed in at least seven organisms including bacteria, yeast, plants, silkworms, goats, and mammalian cells. The limitation is yield: the full native MaSp1 is ~3,500 amino acids of highly repetitive sequence that is notoriously difficult to clone and express at full length.
Short Description: Crystalline alanine blocks in this silk protein lock into nanofibers stronger than steel, while glycine linkers let the fiber stretch 27% before breaking. Chains built long enough matched that strength in transgenic silkworms (p<0.01, 2018). No lab has cloned the full 3,500-amino-acid native gene, so Bolt Threads and Spiber still can't beat nylon's price after a decade trying. Goat-milk versions grow neurons fine, but no version has been tested in human skin or muscle.
Mechanism: MaSp1 is a large repetitive protein (native ~3,500 aa) with polyalanine beta-sheet crystalline domains interspersed with glycine-rich amorphous linkers. The polyalanine blocks self-assemble into nanocrystals conferring tensile strength (1.1 GPa), while the glycine linkers provide extensibility (~27% strain). Self-assembly is triggered by shear forces and pH drop during spinning.
Achievements (effect sizes): You 2018 Sci Rep: increasing MaSp1 chain length significantly improved composite silk in transgenic silkworms (p<0.01). An 2015 Biomaterials: goat-milk MaSp1 supported neuronal growth with upregulated NCAM. Li 2020: spidroin integrated into sheep embryos via SCNT with hair-follicle promoter. Expressed in 7+ organisms.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (transgenic goat/sheep) + T6 (≥4 independent expression systems)
Translational Gaps: Full-length native MaSp1 (~3,500 aa) extremely difficult to clone due to repetitive sequence. Spinning requires shear forces and pH control not available from passive secretion. No human tissue expression. Economically viable production not yet achieved despite decades of effort.
Key References (DOIs): You Sci Rep 2018 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-34150-y | An Biomaterials 2015 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biomaterials.2015.01.044 | Li Anim Biotech 2020 https://doi.org/10.1080/10495398.2020.1737098 | Heidebrecht & Scheibel Adv Appl Microbiol 2013 https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-407679-2.00004-1
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The 748-aa UniProt entry (P19837) is a fragment — the full native MaSp1 is much larger. Industrial spider silk startups (Bolt Threads, Spiber, AMSilk) have struggled with cost-competitive production for over a decade. Hair-follicle-specific expression in sheep is conceptually interesting for human application but has not been tested in adult animals.

Narrative: A Weddell seal dives to 900 metres and stays down for over an hour on a single breath. Two features carry most of the load. The first is oxygen storage: its skeletal muscle holds about ten times as much myoglobin as a terrestrial mammal's, so the muscle carries its own oxygen rather than waiting for blood to bring it. The second is damage control, because the moment breathing resumes and oxygen floods reperfused tissue, the ischaemia-reperfusion chemistry that follows generates reactive oxygen species; the seal heart holds roughly twenty-five times more glutathione than a terrestrial mammal's to absorb that burst. The elegant part is how the animal gets away with the myoglobin load at all. At the concentrations found in diving muscle, an ordinary myoglobin would aggregate, and protein aggregation in muscle is cytotoxic. Seal myoglobin carries an elevated net positive surface charge, so the molecules electrostatically repel one another and stay soluble where a terrestrial protein would precipitate; ancestral sequence reconstruction across 130 mammal species showed this charge signature tracking maximum myoglobin concentration and appearing independently in the ancestors of every major aquatic mammal lineage (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1234192). Beyond that molecular insight, this record is almost entirely comparative biology. Nobody has put seal myoglobin into a mouse muscle cell and measured what happens. The most instructive experiment done on seal cells argues that a single-gene transfer would not be enough anyway: cultured seal myoblasts only elevate myoglobin when they are given both hypoxia and lipid supplementation, which suggests the diving phenotype is wired into marine-mammal metabolism rather than encoded in one protein (https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.060681).
Short Description: Muscle loaded with ten times the usual amount of oxygen-binding myoglobin carries its own oxygen supply, and extra positive charges spread across the protein's surface make the molecules repel each other instead of clumping into aggregates that would kill the cell. Weddell seal skeletal muscle reaches roughly 54 grams of myoglobin per kilogram, five to ten times a land mammal's, and on that reserve a seal dives to 900 metres and stays under for more than an hour. Seal myoglobin has never been expressed in a mouse cell or a mouse; every result here is comparative biology or recombinant protein in a tube. Seal muscle cells in culture only raise myoglobin when given both low oxygen and a lipid-rich medium, so the gene delivered without that metabolic context may do nothing at all.
Mechanism: Myoglobin is a compact monomeric haem protein that binds one oxygen molecule and both stores it and facilitates its diffusion from capillary to mitochondrion. Two quantitative features distinguish the diving version. The first is sheer abundance: Weddell seal skeletal muscle carries roughly 54 grams per kilogram, five to ten times terrestrial values, which turns the muscle itself into the principal oxygen depot for a breath-hold dive. The second solves the problem that abundance creates. Any globular protein pushed to high intracellular concentration tends to self-associate, and myoglobin aggregates are cytotoxic to muscle. Diving mammals raise the net surface charge of the molecule, denoted Z-Mb, from near neutral to roughly +2 to +5, so like charges on adjacent molecules generate electrostatic repulsion that keeps them dispersed and soluble at concentrations where a terrestrial myoglobin would precipitate (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1234192). The antioxidant arm of the adaptation is separate and non-genetic in the same sense: elevated glutathione buffers the reactive oxygen species generated when a dive ends and oxygenated blood re-enters hypoperfused tissue. Layered on top is regulatory remodelling of the hypoxia response itself, including altered microRNA control of the pathway that governs HIF-1-alpha stability (https://doi.org/10.1186/s12864-020-6675-0).
Achievements (effect sizes): Mirceta and colleagues reconstructed ancestral myoglobin sequences across a 130-species mammalian phylogeny and showed that elevated net surface charge is an adaptive molecular signature of diving lineages which correlates with maximal myoglobin concentration; expressing ancestral and modern myoglobins recombinantly confirmed that the charge shift is mechanistically linked to aggregation resistance rather than merely correlated with it, and the reconstruction inferred amphibious ancestry for echidnas, moles, hyraxes and elephants along the way (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1234192). De Miranda and colleagues cultured Weddell seal skeletal muscle cells and found that myoglobin rose significantly only when the cells received both environmental hypoxia and lipid supplementation, with the seal cells otherwise looking metabolically similar to the mouse C2C12 line used as a comparator, and beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase activity rising with the lipid supplied (https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.060681). Penso-Dolfin and colleagues built the first microRNA annotation for the species from small RNA data across brain, heart, muscle and plasma in three biological replicates, curating 559 high-confidence loci of which 329 matched an existing miRBase hairpin and 230 were novel; 416 microRNAs were differentially expressed among tissues, 80 differed between pups and adults across all tissues combined, and 188 showed age differences within specific tissues, with miR-424-3p, predicted to target the HIF-1-alpha prolyl hydroxylase Egln3, significantly reduced in heart overall and further down-regulated in adults relative to pups (https://doi.org/10.1186/s12864-020-6675-0). Seal myoglobin has still not been expressed in mouse cells or in transgenic mice as of the spring of 2026, and no such experiment appears in the literature.
Highest Evidence Tier: T2 (recombinant Mbs) + T1 (comparative)
Translational Gaps: The single decisive experiment has never been attempted: no functional transfer of seal myoglobin into a mammalian system has been reported, so there is no measurement of what the protein does in a non-diving muscle cell. Everything in this record is either comparative sequence analysis, recombinant protein in a tube, or seal cells in seal-specific culture conditions (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1234192, https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.060681). The culture work also identifies the obstacle a transfer would face, since seal myoblasts required hypoxia and lipid supplementation together before they raised myoglobin, implying that a recipient cell would need the same metabolic context to express the protein at diving concentrations (https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.060681). The registered trials that mention myoglobin and glutathione measure them as oxidative-stress and muscle-damage markers in exercise studies rather than delivering either as a treatment: a completed 28-participant iron supplementation and eccentric exercise study (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02374619), a completed 15-participant caffeine, resistance training and blood antioxidant status study (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05230303), and a 46-participant Solarplast supplementation study following high-intensity resistance exercise, whose status is listed as unknown (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06432868). None of these tests myoglobin as an enhancement.
Key References (DOIs): Mirceta Science 2013 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1234192 | De Miranda Journal of Experimental Biology 2012 https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.060681 | Penso-Dolfin BMC Genomics 2020 https://doi.org/10.1186/s12864-020-6675-0
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Myoglobin knockout mice are viable and compensate for the loss, which cuts directly against the assumption that adding more of the protein will deliver proportionally more diving capacity; a gene whose deletion can be worked around is unlikely to be the single limiting factor when overexpressed. Some smaller diving species reach high myoglobin concentrations without the full surface-charge shift, indicating that there is more than one evolutionary route to the same phenotype and that the charge mechanism, while real, is not the only solution (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1234192). The Weddell seal's own lifespan of roughly 25 to 30 years is unremarkable for an animal of its size, so nothing in this record supports treating it as a longevity gene; the adaptation buys breath-hold endurance, not extra years. The trait is polygenic and physiological rather than molecular: it combines myoglobin abundance, surface-charge chemistry, glutathione buffering, blood volume and spleen storage, bradycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction, and no single-gene transfer addresses more than one of those. Finally, the microRNA evidence is correlative and partly computational. The Penso-Dolfin study is an expression atlas with in-silico target prediction, so the link from miR-424-3p to Egln3 to hypoxia tolerance is a hypothesis supported by sequence complementarity and differential expression, not a demonstrated regulatory mechanism (https://doi.org/10.1186/s12864-020-6675-0).

Manipulation: overexpression (recombinant, with tyrosinase co-expression to install DOPA)
Narrative:
A blue mussel spends its life on a rock that is hit by breaking waves several times a minute, and it stays there using a few micrograms of protein. The animal extrudes a byssal thread ending in a flat plaque, and at the very bottom of that plaque, in the few nanometres that actually touch the rock, it lays down mussel foot protein 5. This is the interfacial layer, the molecular double-sided tape, and it is chemically extreme: a short, floppy, strongly positively charged chain in which nearly a third of the residues have been hydroxylated into DOPA, the same catechol amino acid that is the precursor of dopamine and melanin.

Catechols do something no glue in a hardware store can do. Water is the enemy of adhesion because it forms a hydration layer that no bond can reach through, and the mussel's answer is a molecule that displaces that layer and then hydrogen-bonds and metal-coordinates to the exposed mineral oxide underneath. Measured directly with a surface forces apparatus, the purified protein turned out to be the strongest interfacial adhesive the mussel makes, beating even the biotin-streptavidin pair that biochemists use as a byword for tight binding (Danner 2012, https://doi.org/10.1021/bi3002538).

The human stakes are surgical. A glue that works on wet, moving, bleeding tissue would replace sutures and staples in places they do not belong, and companies have chased it for two decades: recombinant mussel adhesive protein is already sold as a cell-culture coating and a hydrogel. But no mammal has been engineered to make it, and the reason is the same chemistry that makes it work. A reduced catechol is a transient state. The mussel protects it behind an acidic, oxygen-poor secretion; a human dermis offers pH 7.4 and plenty of oxygen, which turns the sticky reduced form into cross-linked, non-adhesive polymer and releases a reactive quinone along the way.
Short Description: Your skin secretes a protein varnish that bonds to wet rock, steel or bone underwater and holds, the same holdfast a mussel uses to stay on a surf-battered piling. Roughly 30 mol% of the protein's residues are the catechol amino acid DOPA, which shoves the water layer off a mineral surface and grips it directly; between mica plates a purified film reached an adhesion energy near -14 mJ/m2, four to five times the mussel's other interfacial protein and stronger than oriented biotin-streptavidin. Nothing has ever been engineered to secrete it from its own skin, but recombinant mussel adhesive protein is on sale today as a lab reagent through Sigma-Aldrich and AMSBIO. The catch is chemical: DOPA only sticks while it stays reduced, so the mussel builds its plaque inside an acidic reducing pocket, and at blood pH under normal oxygen it oxidises to dopaquinone and the grip collapses into inert bulk cross-linking.
Mechanism: Mussel foot protein 5 (Mefp-5) is a small protein of about 98 amino acids, intrinsically disordered and strongly cationic, deposited specifically at the interface between the adhesive plaque and the substrate. Roughly 30 mol% of its residues are 3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA), which the animal generates by tyrosinase-catalysed hydroxylation of tyrosine after the protein is translated. The catechol group of DOPA displaces the interfacial hydration layer that normally blocks bonding to a wet surface, then binds mineral oxides through bidentate hydrogen bonding and direct metal coordination. This only works while the catechol stays reduced, which the mussel enforces by secreting the plaque into an acidic, reducing microenvironment; oxidation to dopaquinone switches the chemistry from interfacial adhesion to bulk cohesive cross-linking, so the same residue that provides the grip destroys it once oxidised. Phosphoserine residues supply a second, independent mineral-binding motif alongside the catechols.
Achievements (effect sizes): The central measurement is a direct one. Working with native protein purified from mussel feet, Danner and colleagues placed a film of Mefp-5 between two atomically flat mica surfaces in aqueous solution and pulled them apart in a surface forces apparatus, recording an adhesion energy approaching E(ad) = ~-14 mJ/m(2) (Danner 2012, https://doi.org/10.1021/bi3002538). The same study set that value in context by measuring the other interfacial mussel foot protein under identical conditions: Mefp-5 exceeded the adhesion energy of Mefp-3 by a factor of 4-5, and the authors note it is also greater than the adhesion measured between highly oriented monolayers of biotin and streptavidin, a protein-ligand pair normally treated as a benchmark for tight binding (https://doi.org/10.1021/bi3002538). Two things about these numbers matter for reading the card honestly. They are symmetric mica-on-mica surface energies rather than lap-shear strengths on tissue, so they cannot be quoted as a bond strength a surgeon would feel; and they were obtained with native protein carrying its full complement of DOPA, not with unmodified recombinant protein, which is markedly less adhesive until the catechols are installed.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (purified-protein biophysics replicated across labs; recombinant product sold commercially; no in vivo mammalian expression)
Translational Gaps: No mammal has been engineered to secrete mussel foot protein 5 from its own epidermis, so the entire skin-as-glue framing rests on purified-protein biophysics rather than on any animal experiment. Recombinant production does not by itself give you an adhesive: the bacterium must also be given a tyrosinase, or the purified protein must be treated in vitro, because unmodified recombinant Mefp-5 lacking DOPA is markedly less adhesive than the native molecule. The headline -14 mJ/m(2) figure was measured between two identical mica surfaces in a surface forces apparatus, which means nobody has converted it into a lap-shear or peel strength on living tissue, and a card reader should not assume the two are interchangeable. The oxidation problem also remains unsolved in a body: any tissue-facing application has to hold the catechols reduced at physiological pH and oxygen tension long enough for them to bond.
Key References (DOIs): Danner Biochemistry 2012 https://doi.org/10.1021/bi3002538
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: A structural mislabelling is easy to make here and worth stating plainly. Protein Data Bank entry 7QAB is an NMR structure of Pvfp-5b, the homologous foot protein 5 of the green mussel Perna viridis, and it is not a structure of Mytilus edulis Mefp-5; it must not be presented as one. An AlphaFold model does exist for UniProt Q8WTE8 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q8WTE8), but because the protein is intrinsically disordered by nature the model is low-confidence by construction rather than by accident, and computed disorder for this sequence runs to 75.5%. On availability: recombinant mussel adhesive protein is a purchasable reagent today rather than a therapeutic. Kollodis BioSciences (https://www.kollodis.com) produces it in a proprietary Escherichia coli system and sells it under the MAPTrix trademark as coating solutions, extracellular-matrix-mimetic reagents and 3D culture hydrogels, resold through Sigma-Aldrich and AMSBIO, with supplier datasheets listing a ~24,000 Da recombinant protein supplied at 0.2, 0.5 or 1.0 mg/mL (https://www.sigmaaldrich.com/US/en/product/sigma/161052k). It is a research-use reagent and not an approved drug or device, and no registered clinical trial administers mussel foot protein to humans. Note also that this route to adhesion is chemically opposite to the gecko route already in this library: setal beta-keratin sticks by dry van der Waals contact and fails underwater, whereas Mefp-5 forms actual chemical bonds to a wet surface.

Narrative: In the years after the Chernobyl accident, biologists found black fungi growing on the ruined reactor walls, in a place where almost nothing should have been able to make a living. These fungi are loaded with melanin, and they appeared not merely to tolerate the gamma field but to prefer it. In 2007 Ekaterina Dadachova and colleagues proposed an explanation with genuinely startling implications: radiosynthesis, in which a fungus harvests energy from ionizing radiation the way a plant harvests sunlight (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0000457). A follow-up experiment flown to the International Space Station in 2020 found that Cladosporium sphaerospermum grew faster in orbit than on the ground and that its biomass measurably reduced the radiation passing through it (https://doi.org/10.1101/2020.07.16.205534, published as https://doi.org/10.3389/fmicb.2022.877625). Hamster ovary cells transfected with a tyrosinase gene make their own eumelanin and survive gamma irradiation and UVA better than their unpigmented parents, although the same pigment makes them more vulnerable to UVC (https://doi.org/10.1002/em.1074). The radiotrophy claim itself is still contested. Critics argue that ordinary passive shielding plus relief from oxidative stress accounts for everything observed, without requiring a new form of metabolism, and the authors of the space-station study themselves retreated to the weaker word radioadaptive. What melanin unquestionably does is absorb radiation and scavenge reactive oxygen species; whether it does anything more exotic than that remains unsettled almost two decades after the proposal. In a human body the same chemistry would cut both ways. Pigmented human melanomas are among the most radioresistant tumours in the clinic, which is a blunt reminder that a molecule good at protecting cells from radiation is equally good at protecting the cells you most want radiation to kill.
Short Description: Cells given a working tyrosinase gene build eumelanin, a dense dark polymer that both absorbs incoming radiation and quenches the free radicals it generates before they cut DNA. A Chernobyl-derived black fungus carrying this pigment grew 1.21-fold faster aboard the International Space Station than on the ground, and a lawn of it only 1.7 mm thick cut the radiation reaching a detector beneath it by 2.17%. The pigment pathway has only ever been switched on in fungi and in hamster ovary cells; no mammal carries the fungal melanin route, and mice in the radioprotection experiments received injected melanin nanoparticles rather than a gene. The same pigmented hamster cells became measurably easier to kill with UVC even as they resisted gamma rays, and melanin is part of why pigmented human melanomas shrug off radiotherapy.
Mechanism: Melanin is not a conventional protein but an irregular, heavily conjugated polymer built from indolequinone subunits. Two of its actions are well established and uncontroversial. First, it shields passively: the polymer is physically dense and electron-rich, so it attenuates photons and charged particles that would otherwise reach DNA. Second, it scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS), intercepting the hydroxyl radicals and superoxide that ionizing radiation generates in water and that do most of the actual damage to the genome. The contested third action is radiosynthesis. Dadachova and colleagues reported that irradiating melanin shifts its electron spin resonance (ESR) signal, consistent with a change in electronic structure, and that irradiated melanin gained a four-fold greater capacity to reduce NADH than unirradiated melanin, which would place it in the role of an electron-transfer agent coupling radiation energy to metabolism (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0000457). Building the pigment is itself a multi-component job rather than a single gene: eumelanin synthesis needs tyrosinase plus its copper cofactor, the related enzymes TRP1 and TRP2, and melanosome trafficking machinery to keep the reactive intermediates contained. In the hamster-cell experiments tyrosinase alone was sufficient to produce eumelanin without TRP1 or TRP2, and the resulting pigment protected against gamma rays and UVA but sensitised the cells to UVC (https://doi.org/10.1002/em.1074).
Achievements (effect sizes): Dadachova and colleagues reported in 2007 that melanized Wangiella dermatitidis and Cryptococcus neoformans cells held in an ionizing radiation field roughly 500 times higher than background grew significantly faster than non-irradiated melanized cells or irradiated albino mutants, showing higher colony-forming unit counts, more dry biomass and three-fold greater incorporation of carbon-14-labelled acetate; irradiation also shifted melanin's electron spin resonance signal and produced a four-fold increase in its capacity to reduce NADH (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0000457).
