It recognises the nick, coats the lesion with a cooperative protein layer, and physically prevents a single-strand cut from opening into a double-strand break — no repair chemistry and no ATP hydrolysis required. Purified enzyme cut the rate of double-strand breakage roughly eight-fold at 90 C, and deleting it from Pyrococcus furiosus makes the archaeon unable to grow at 95 C or 100 C. This has only ever been done in archaea and in a test tube; nobody has expressed reverse gyrase in a eukaryote of any kind. Below the threshold it buys nothing while still costing something: a Thermococcus knockout grows fine at 90 C, and at 37 C the enzyme would burn ATP and impose positive supercoiling that runs opposite to the negative supercoiling human topoisomerases maintain for transcription and replication.
Mechanism: Reverse gyrase is a topoisomerase IA domain fused to a helicase-like adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase) domain, 1,214 amino acids and about 140 kDa in Pyrococcus furiosus. Its namesake activity is the introduction of POSITIVE supercoils into closed circular DNA, the opposite of what bacterial gyrase does. The thermoprotective function, however, is separable from supercoiling. The enzyme recognises nicked DNA, recruits a cooperative coat of protein molecules onto the lesion, and then acts as a physical splint that stops a single-strand nick from propagating into a double-strand break; at the same time it prevents denatured stretches of DNA from aggregating inappropriately and promotes their correct re-annealing. This chaperone-like protection requires no ATP hydrolysis and is independent of the positive-supercoiling activity, so the two functions can be uncoupled experimentally. Nothing in this description is repair: no base is excised, no phosphodiester bond is remade to restore a lost nucleotide. The enzyme prevents damage from getting worse rather than reversing damage already done.
Achievements (effect sizes): The mechanistic result is a straight in vitro measurement. Purified reverse gyrase incubated with DNA at 90 C “reduces the rate of double-stranded DNA breakage approximately 8-fold at 90 degrees C” relative to a protein-free control, and the authors report that this activity does not require ATP hydrolysis and is independent of the enzyme's positive-supercoiling activity (Kampmann 2004, https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkh683). Genetics in living archaea then bracketed when the protection actually matters. Deleting the gene from Pyrococcus furiosus, an organism whose optimal growth temperature is 100 C, showed that “the gene is required for growth at 95 degrees C, as well as at 100 degrees C”, leading the authors to conclude that a temperature threshold above 90 C exists above which reverse gyrase is absolutely necessary (Lipscomb 2017, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-017-0929-z). The boundary condition comes from a different genus: in Thermococcus kodakaraensis KOD1, whose optimum is 85 C, “the disruption of the reverse gyrase gene did not lead to a lethal phenotype at 90 degrees C”, although positive-supercoiling activity present in the host strain was absent from the disruptant and growth retardation became more striking as temperature rose (Atomi 2004, https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.186.14.4829-4833.2004). A third laboratory, a third organism and a third method extended the phenotype to chemical DNA damage: knocking down topR1 by endogenous type III-B CRISPR-Cas messenger-RNA interference in the thermoacidophilic crenarchaeon Sulfolobus islandicus and challenging the cells with the alkylating agent methyl methanesulfonate showed that “the survival rate of pKD-topR1/E233S1 was about four times lower than pSeSD1/E233S1 during 1.3 and 2 mM MMS treatment and about 90 times lower during 2.6 mM MMS treatment” (Han 2017, https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms18071340).
Highest Evidence Tier: T3 (in vitro biochemistry plus loss-of-function genetics in three archaeal species from independent laboratories; no heterologous gain-of-function in any eukaryote)
Translational Gaps: Every quantified result in this record is either purified-enzyme biochemistry or loss of function in an archaeon. Nobody has expressed reverse gyrase in a mesophilic eukaryote and then measured thermotolerance, so the gain-of-function direction this card frames has never been tested in the direction it is framed. Delivery is a second obstacle with a hard number attached: the protein is 1,214 amino acids in Pyrococcus furiosus and 1,711 in Thermococcus kodakarensis, which puts its coding sequence near the practical ceiling for packaging into a single adeno-associated viral vector. There is also a plausible mechanistic conflict that has not been experimentally examined: human topoisomerases maintain negative supercoiling to support transcription and replication, and an enzyme that adds positive supercoils would be working against them. Whether a human cell tolerates that has not been measured in any system.
Key References (DOIs): Kampmann Nucleic Acids Research 2004 https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkh683 | Lipscomb Extremophiles 2017 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-017-0929-z | Atomi Journal of Bacteriology 2004 https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.186.14.4829-4833.2004 | Han International Journal of Molecular Sciences 2017 https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms18071340
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The apparent contradiction in the titles is real and worth putting on the wall rather than smoothing over. One paper is titled to say reverse gyrase is not a prerequisite for hyperthermophilic life (https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.186.14.4829-4833.2004) and another that it is essential for microbial growth at 95 C (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-017-0929-z). Both conclusions hold, because they were reached in different organisms at different temperatures, and read together they define a threshold near 90 C: disrupting the gene in Thermococcus kodakaraensis is survivable at 90 C, whereas the Pyrococcus furiosus gene is required at 95 C and 100 C. Structural depiction requires care. The deposited structures 4DDT (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/4DDT), 3P4X (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/3P4X) and 3OIY (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/3OIY) are all of the Thermotoga maritima homologue, UniProt O51934 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/O51934); no experimental structure of the Pyrococcus enzyme (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P95479) exists, so any image of it is an AlphaFold prediction and should be labelled as one. There are no clinical trials and no commercial product. The enzyme's practical uses today are as a research reagent and as the definitive phylogenetic marker for hyperthermophily. Supporting loss-of-function evidence now spans three archaeal genera and three independent methods — gene disruption in Thermococcus, deletion in Pyrococcus, and CRISPR interference in Sulfolobus (https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms18071340) — which is unusually broad for a gene with no eukaryotic data at all.

Narrative: The silver spinyfin (Diretmus argenteus) has the most complex visual system of any vertebrate — 38 rod opsin genes where most fish have one. By expressing multiple tuned rhodopsins in its retina, each absorbing a slightly different wavelength, the spinyfin can distinguish colors in the near-total darkness of the deep ocean using only rod photoreceptors. This breaks the textbook rule that rod cells cannot do color vision.
Short Description: Rod cells normally sense only dim light, not color, but this deep-sea fish split its rods into over a dozen types, each tuned to a different blue wavelength. Its most extreme variant, RH1-1, absorbs light at just 444 nm, the bluest rod pigment ever found in a vertebrate. Gene therapy already restores one rhodopsin gene in humans (Luxturna); this fish runs 14 of 38 duplicated copies at once. No lab has tried a multi-opsin version in mammals, so it stays deep-sea biology only.
Mechanism: Through tandem duplication of the RH1 (rhodopsin) gene, the spinyfin expresses 14+ rod opsins tuned to wavelengths from 444-519 nm. Key spectral tuning sites (including positions 83, 122, 261, 292) carry substitutions that shift absorption peaks. Co-expression of differently tuned opsins in separate rod populations enables wavelength discrimination without cone cells.
Achievements (effect sizes): The most blue-shifted rod photopigment known (RH1-1, ~444 nm) was characterized from spinyfin. 14 of 38 RH1 genes are expressed in adult retina. Three independent deep-sea fish lineages evolved expanded RH1 repertoires convergently.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3
Translational Gaps: Rod opsin engineering for human therapy is speculative. Retinal gene therapy for single genes is feasible (Luxturna), but multi-opsin systems are far more complex. Basic science value is primary.
Key References (DOIs): https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aav4632
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Breaks the vertebrate 'one rod opsin' rule. Three independent evolutionary origins of multi-RH1 systems in deep-sea fish.

Narrative: Deer antlers are the fastest-growing bone in the animal kingdom — up to 2 cm per day. S100A10 (annexin A2 ligand) is a calcium-binding protein highly enriched in the antler growth zone that accelerates osteoblast proliferation and bone mineralization. Stanford researchers showed that antler progenitor cells can stimulate bone repair in mice, with S100A10 as a key driver of this extraordinary growth rate.
Short Description: On osteoblast surfaces it partners with annexin A2 to boost calcium flux, pushing bone cells to multiply and mineralize fast. Deer antler bone grows over 20 kg a year at up to 2 cm a day, driven by this protein in the growth zone. So far it's only worked in mice, where implanted antler progenitor cells sped up fracture healing. Rapid bone growth carries an untested cancer risk in humans, and the antler's other growth factors this gene alone may not replace.
Mechanism: S100A10 forms a complex with annexin A2 on osteoblast surfaces, enhancing calcium signaling and plasminogen activation. In antler periosteum, it is dramatically upregulated during the rapid growth phase, promoting progenitor cell proliferation, extracellular matrix deposition, and accelerated mineralization through enhanced calcium flux.
Achievements (effect sizes): Antler-derived progenitor cells implanted in mice accelerated bone fracture healing. S100A10 is among the most differentially expressed genes in antler growth zones. Deer antlers regenerate 20+ kg of bone annually with zero cancer risk.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4
Translational Gaps: Antler growth involves a complex niche of progenitor cells, growth factors, and vascular networks. S100A10 alone may be insufficient. Cancer risk from stimulating rapid bone growth in humans needs evaluation.
Key References (DOIs): https://doi.org/10.1126/science.add0488
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Paired with UHRF1 (epigenetic regulator) from same Stanford deer antler study.

Narrative:
Syntrichia caninervis is a desert moss and probably the toughest multicellular organism in this library. Li and colleagues reported in 2024 that it recovers photosynthetic and physiological activity within seconds of rehydration after losing more than 98% of its cellular water, regenerates after three or five years at -80 degrees C and after 15 or 30 days in liquid nitrogen, has an estimated gamma-radiation LD50/1h of about 5,000 Gy in the dry state against about 2,000 Gy when hydrated, and survives simulated Mars conditions with its capacity to regenerate intact (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2024.100657). None of that is attributed to this gene, and the honest version of the story keeps the organism and the enzyme apart.

What the gene does is narrower and much better measured. Every one of those insults - drying, salinity, ionising radiation - peroxidises membrane lipids, and peroxidised lipids break down into reactive aldehydes such as malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal that then attack proteins and DNA. ScALDH21 is a single-copy aldehyde dehydrogenase from a family found only in mosses, and it oxidises those aldehydes to their corresponding acids. A group at the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography in Urumqi cloned it, put it into tobacco (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.plaphy.2015.07.001), then into upland cotton, and took the cotton all the way to a field trial under water withholding, where the transgenic plants outyielded controls without losing fibre quality (https://doi.org/10.1007/s11032-015-0422-2).

This is the least theatrical kind of stress resistance and possibly the most useful. It is not a shield and not a radical scavenger: it is a mop for the damage products that get past both, which is why it works on drought, salt and oxidative stress with the same chemistry. In a human body the same logic would apply to any tissue that peroxidises its own membranes under load - and so would the complication that the aldehyde being mopped up is also a messenger.
Short Description: Drought, salt and radiation all burn membrane lipids, and the burning leaves reactive aldehydes behind that crosslink proteins and DNA; this enzyme oxidises them into harmless acids first. Cotton engineered with it accumulated roughly 11.8-304% more proline than non-transgenic cotton under drought, carried less lipid-peroxidation aldehyde, and in the field grew taller, set larger bolls and yielded more fibre with no loss of fibre quality. It comes from a desert moss that regains photosynthesis seconds after rewetting from the loss of over 98% of its water and survives simulated Mars conditions - whole-organism feats, not this gene's. It has only ever been expressed in plants, tobacco and cotton, with field trials in China and no commercial cultivar. The cost is that it consumes the signal along with the poison: 4-hydroxynonenal is how a cell detects oxidative attack, and the same chemistry in a human belongs to ALDH2, the liver enzyme that clears acetaldehyde after alcohol.
Mechanism: ScALDH21 is an aldehyde dehydrogenase of 483 amino acids and roughly 53 kDa that depends on the oxidised nicotinamide cofactor NAD(P)+, and it belongs to aldehyde dehydrogenase family 21 - a family unique to mosses and represented there by a single-copy gene. When drought, high salinity or ionising radiation peroxidise membrane lipids, the damaged lipids release reactive electrophilic aldehydes: malondialdehyde (MDA), 4-hydroxynonenal and related lipid-derived carbonyls, all of which form covalent adducts with proteins and with DNA. The enzyme oxidises these aldehydes to their corresponding carboxylic acids, removing the electrophile and regenerating the reduced cofactor NAD(P)H. That places it downstream of the antioxidant enzymes rather than alongside them: it is chemical detoxification of a damage product, not radical scavenging and not physical shielding, so it clears the damaging species that survive after superoxide dismutases, catalases and peroxidases have already acted.
Achievements (effect sizes): Aldehyde dehydrogenase 21 from the desert moss Syntrichia caninervis was first moved into tobacco, where transgenic plants challenged with drought and salt stress displayed higher germination ratios, higher root lengths, greater fresh weight, higher proline accumulation, lower malondialdehyde (MDA) contents and stronger photosynthetic capacities, as well as higher activities of antioxidant enzymes, and detached leaves from those plants lost water more slowly than non-transgenic leaves (Yang 2015, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.plaphy.2015.07.001). In upland cotton the same transgene produced an agronomic result rather than a purely physiological one: transgenic cotton accumulated approximately 11.8-304% more proline than did non-transgenic cotton under drought stress, made a lower concentration of lipid-peroxidation-derived reactive aldehydes, kept higher peroxidase activity under oxidative stress and lost less of its net photosynthetic rate. Under field conditions the transgenic cotton showed greater plant height, larger bolls, and greater cotton fiber yield than non-transgenic cotton, but no significant difference in fiber quality, which led the authors to conclude that overexpression can greatly improve drought tolerance without costing yield or quality (Yang 2016, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11032-015-0422-2). A salt-stress time course on the transgenic line L96 confirmed the underlying chemistry, since hydrogen peroxide and MDA contents were decreased in the L96 line compared to non-transgenic cotton at all time points across 0, 2 and 5 days of 150 mM sodium chloride, while proline content and phenylalanine ammonia-lyase activity ran significantly higher (Yang 2023, https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms24065822).
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (transgenic gain-of-function in two crop species with field-scale agronomic endpoints; single primary lab lineage)
Translational Gaps: Every gain-of-function experiment is in a plant - tobacco and cotton - and no animal or mammalian cell has ever expressed this enzyme, so nothing is known about how a high-capacity moss aldehyde dehydrogenase behaves in a tissue that already runs a full complement of human aldehyde dehydrogenases. The primary work also comes from one laboratory lineage, so independent replication is still owed. A second gap is attributional rather than experimental: the source organism's spectacular tolerances, including the roughly 5,000 Gy dry-state gamma LD50/1h, the regeneration after five years at -80 degrees C and the survival of simulated Mars conditions, are properties of the whole moss and are not credited to this gene by the paper that reports them (Li 2024, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2024.100657), so a visitor buying this card is buying the measured aldehyde-clearance phenotype and not the moss.
Key References (DOIs): Yang Molecular Biology Reports 2012 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11033-011-1017-6 | Yang Plant Physiology and Biochemistry 2015 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.plaphy.2015.07.001 | Yang Molecular Breeding 2016 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11032-015-0422-2 | Yang International Journal of Molecular Sciences 2023 https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms24065822 | Li The Innovation 2024 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2024.100657
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The sequence identifier needs a caveat: no UniProt entry maps cleanly onto ScALDH21, and the protein is deposited in GenBank instead, as ACT10822 and ACT10823 at 483 amino acids from Syntrichia caninervis (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/protein/ACT10823), consistent with the 483-amino-acid, 53 kDa protein reported when the gene was cloned (Yang 2012, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11033-011-1017-6). No experimental structure exists. Commercially, transgenic ScALDH21 cotton has been through greenhouse and field trials in China as a drought-tolerance trait, but no commercial cultivar release has been reported, and there is no clinical relevance and no registered trial of any kind. The organism-level numbers reported by Li 2024 are verified in that paper's full text and belong to the moss rather than to the transgene (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2024.100657); mixing the two would be the easiest way to overstate this card. Within this library the entry is deliberately distinct from the desiccation genes such as CAHS D, PvLEA and trehalose synthase, which work by physically vitrifying or gelling the cytoplasm - this one is an enzyme that destroys a chemical, with no shielding role at all.

Narrative: The electric eel generates 860 volts by stacking thousands of modified muscle cells — electrocytes — that discharge in unison. The molecular machinery is a teleost-specific duplicate of the muscle sodium channel, scn4aa, which lost its original job in muscle and was repurposed to fire on demand inside the electric organ. It's a beautiful case of evolutionary tinkering. In 2018, Harold Zakon's group took five amino-acid changes from an Apteronotus knifefish and engineered them into a human cardiac sodium channel expressed in frog eggs. The resulting human channel generated a large, physiologically relevant persistent sodium current without needing the usual accessory proteins. But the 860-volt discharge isn't a protein — it's an anatomical design, the electrical equivalent of batteries wired in series across five thousand cells. No mammalian cell or mouse makes its own electricity. The hydrogel 'artificial electric organs' that periodically make the press are pure materials science: zero genes, 110 volts, impressive engineering, no biology.
Short Description: Muscle cells stack into electrocytes that fire together, and a duplicated gene, scn4aa, gets retooled to trigger discharge instead of contraction. In 2018 five knifefish amino acids spliced into a human heart sodium channel produced a large persistent current in frog eggs, no accessory proteins needed. The eel's 860-volt shock is anatomy, cells wired in series, never reproduced in a mammalian cell or mouse. The knifefish organ itself actually runs on a different paralog, scn4ab1.
Mechanism: Teleost-WGD Nav paralog; lost muscle expression, compartmentalized to electrocytes; positively selected substitutions in inactivation gate / S4–S5 linker; electric organ voltage arises from STACKED series of electrocytes firing via Nav channels.
Achievements (effect sizes): Zakon 2006 PNAS: convergent muscle-expression loss + positive selection. Gallant 2014 Science: eel genome + muscle-vs-EO transcriptomics. Traeger 2015 BMC Genomics: Nav isoform quantification. Thompson 2018 PLoS Biol: Apteronotid 5-residue D4 S4–S5 linker substitutions engineered into HUMAN hNav1.5 backbone, expressed in Xenopus oocytes → large persistent Na+ current (INaP) gain-of-function, independent of auxiliary beta-subunits. Native eel protein was NOT expressed in mammalian cells. Whole-animal E. voltai >860 V is ANATOMICAL (stacked electrocytes). Schroeder 2017 Nature "artificial electric organ" is hydrogel (110 V, ~27 mW/m2), zero genetic content.
Highest Evidence Tier: T2–T3 (Xenopus oocyte on human backbone)
Translational Gaps: No mammalian cell/mouse bioelectrogenesis; electrocyte developmental program un-transferred.
Key References (DOIs): Zakon PNAS 2006 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0600160103 | Thompson PLoS Biol 2018 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.2004892 | Schroeder Nature 2017 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature24670
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Voltage = MULTICELLULAR ARCHITECTURE, not single gene. Channel identity is actually scn4ab1 in Apteronotids (not scn4aa) — complicating "universal electric-organ gene" narrative. Apteronotids retain muscle scn4aa. Artificial organs (Schroeder 2017) sidestep biology entirely.

Manipulation: Human centenarian haplotype knock-in (two linked coding substitutions, N308K + A313S)
Narrative:
Nir Barzilai's Longevity Genes Project has spent years sequencing Ashkenazi Jewish centenarians, a population whose relative genetic homogeneity makes rare enrichments easier to spot. One of the things it turned up was a two-residue variant of SIRT6, a chromatin enzyme that sits at the centre of comparative-biology explanations for why some mammals live longer than others. Vera Gorbunova and Andrei Seluanov's laboratory at Rochester, who study exactly that question, took the allele into cells to find out what it actually does.

What it does is retune the enzyme. SIRT6 has two catalytic modes — it removes acetyl groups from histones, and it transfers ADP-ribose onto proteins. The centenarian version shifts the balance: nearly twice the maximal ADP-ribosylation activity, and weaker deacetylation. That shift lands on two specific partners. It ribosylates KAP1, the scaffold protein through which SIRT6 keeps LINE1 retrotransposons — the parasitic sequences that copy themselves around the genome and break loose as we age — packed away in heterochromatin. And it binds lamin A/C, the nuclear-envelope protein, more tightly and ribosylates it more. Cells carrying the variant sealed double-strand breaks faster by both major repair pathways and sat at half the baseline DNA-damage load. Cancer cell lines forced to express it survived worse and killed themselves more readily.

This card is the library's only human centenarian-derived allele, and it is honest about what that is worth. The population signal that led to it is genuinely underpowered — 1% of centenarians against 0.5% of controls, which is a doubling in frequency but nowhere near statistical significance in a cohort of a thousand people. Every functional result is in cultured human cells or purified protein. No mouse carries this allele, so no lifespan, healthspan or tumour-incidence number exists for it. It is a mechanistically legible story anchored to a statistically weak observation — which is the honest state of most human longevity genetics.
Short Description: Swaps two amino acids in a chromatin enzyme for the version carried by Ashkenazi centenarians, and the cell holds its jumping genes down harder, seals broken DNA faster, and kills its own cancer cells more readily. Human cells carrying the centenarian version repaired double-strand breaks 2.5-fold better by non-homologous end joining and 2-fold better by homologous recombination, and carried 50% fewer resting DNA-damage foci. Nothing is being developed: there is no company, no trial, and no animal has ever been made carrying this allele. The variant is a trade rather than an upgrade — it gains ADP-ribosylation activity but the paper reports weaker deacetylase activity, so every histone mark through which this enzyme governs glycolytic and inflammatory gene expression is served less well. The human evidence is thin on its own terms: the allele appeared in 1% of centenarians versus 0.5% of controls at P = 0.3.
Mechanism: SIRT6 is a 355-amino-acid enzyme with two catalytic activities: it is a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)-dependent deacylase, removing acetyl groups from histones, and a mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase, transferring ADP-ribose onto protein substrates. The centenarian allele carries two linked substitutions, N308K and A313S, in the flexible C-terminus, and it trades one activity for the other: weaker deacetylase activity but stronger mono-ADP-ribosyl (mADPr) activity across a range of NAD+ concentrations and substrates. The gain lands on two specific partners. Enhanced mADPr activity drives ribosylation of KAP1, the heterochromatin scaffold through which SIRT6 silences long interspersed nuclear element 1 (LINE1) retrotransposons, and it strengthens the physical interaction with lamin A/C (LMNA), which is itself ribosylated more heavily. The consequences are tighter LINE1 repression and faster repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Notably, none of this comes from a structural change: the variant protein shows no difference in folding or thermal stability, so the effect is a redistribution of catalytic preference rather than a stability or expression effect.
Achievements (effect sizes): Expressing equivalent amounts of the centenarian allele against wild-type SIRT6 in reporter assays, centSIRT6 stimulated non-homologous end joining 2.5-fold and homologous recombination 2-fold more than the wild-type protein, and in cumate-inducible fibroblasts the basal level of γH2AX foci — the standard marker of unrepaired double-strand breaks — was reduced by 50% relative to either single-substitution allele or wild-type SIRT6 (Simon 2022, https://doi.org/10.15252/embj.2021110393). The variant also proved more hostile to transformed cells: two cancer cell lines expressing centSIRT6 yielded around 2-fold fewer adherent surviving cells than the same lines expressing wild-type SIRT6, and the centenarian allele triggered at least 2-fold higher levels of apoptosis in those lines (Simon 2022, https://doi.org/10.15252/embj.2021110393). The enzymology matches the phenotype: in a biotin-labelled NAD+ assay, centSIRT6 displayed almost 2-fold higher maximal mono-ADP-ribosylation activity, and the same trend of enhanced activity held as NAD+ was titrated (Simon 2022, https://doi.org/10.15252/embj.2021110393). The human anchor is the weakest link in the chain and should be read as such: targeted sequencing of the SIRT6 locus in 450 Ashkenazi Jewish centenarians and 550 Ashkenazi individuals without a family history of exceptional longevity found the missense variant at twice the allele frequency in centenarians (1%) compared with controls (0.5%), but the authors state plainly that they lacked the power to detect statistically significant differences (P = 0.3), while a follow-up GnomAD analysis placed the allele in the top 5th percentile of SNPs enriched in people over 75 (Simon 2022, https://doi.org/10.15252/embj.2021110393).
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (human cell functional characterisation across multiple orthogonal assays, anchored to an underpowered centenarian cohort enrichment; no in vivo mammalian test of this specific allele)
Translational Gaps: No animal has ever been made carrying centSIRT6, so no lifespan, healthspan or tumour-incidence endpoint has been measured for this allele in a living organism — every functional result comes from cultured human cells or purified protein. There is no clinical trial and no company developing it, which means there is also no delivery strategy: installing two linked coding substitutions across the tissues of an adult human would require precise editing at a scale nobody has attempted. Because the two substitutions travel together in the human haplotype and were tested together, the individual contribution of N308K and of A313S remains unresolved, so a designer cannot tell which one to install if only one is achievable. Finally, the trade in catalytic modes has not been characterised at the whole-organism level: nobody has measured what weaker deacetylase activity does to glycolytic and inflammatory gene expression in a living animal.
Key References (DOIs): Simon The EMBO Journal 2022 https://doi.org/10.15252/embj.2021110393 | Simon The EMBO Journal 2023 https://doi.org/10.15252/embj.2022113326
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The 2022 EMBO Journal paper (https://doi.org/10.15252/embj.2021110393) is the primary record and the source of every number here; an erratum was published in 2023 (https://doi.org/10.15252/embj.2022113326), and the 2022 DOI is the one to cite for the effect sizes. Two pieces of the surrounding evidence are weaker than they look and are recorded here so nobody overstates them. The expression quantitative trait locus rs350845, which is linked to higher SIRT6 levels, was only nominally significant for longevity (P = 0.049). And SIRT6 overexpression does extend lifespan in Drosophila and in mouse according to the paper's own citations, but that is a dose-based intervention on a different axis — more enzyme — whereas this card is a coding variant that changes which reaction the same amount of enzyme prefers, so the overexpression lifespan data cannot be transferred to this allele. There is no commercial route to this variant: it is academic only, with no trial, no company and no consumer access. The tradeoff is intrinsic rather than incidental — the paper reports that centSIRT6 displayed weaker deacetylase activity while gaining mono-ADP-ribosylation activity, so the histone H3K9 and H3K56 acetylation marks through which SIRT6 governs glycolytic and inflammatory gene expression are served less well in exchange for the genome-maintenance gain (https://doi.org/10.15252/embj.2021110393).

Narrative:
Insulin is stored as a zinc-stabilised crystal. Inside every secretory granule of a pancreatic beta cell, a transporter called ZnT8 pumps zinc ions in, and the zinc packs six insulin molecules into a compact hexamer ready for release. The obvious prediction is that breaking the pump would be bad for you. The field made that prediction, and human genetics contradicted it.

In 2014 a consortium sequenced or genotyped around 150,000 people across five ancestry groups, collected twelve rare variants that truncate the ZnT8 protein, and analysed them together. Carriers had 65% less type 2 diabetes. Non-diabetic Icelandic carriers of a frameshift allele ran lower glucose. Eleven years later a Pakistani biobank of 145,037 sequenced participants pushed the experiment to its limit: because a truncating variant is enriched in South Asian populations, the cohort contained eighteen people with two broken copies — complete human knockouts of the zinc pump, walking around. They were the most protected group of all, with a recessive odds ratio of 0.34, and when they were recalled for oral glucose tolerance tests the physiology was legible in a way epidemiology rarely is: glucose fell with gene dose while insulin rose, independent of body mass index.

Two things make this card unusual. The first is that it is a knockout you would want, discovered by looking at people instead of at mice — and mouse knockouts of the same gene gave heterogeneous results that did not agree with the human finding, so the model organism actively misled the field. The second is the corporate fingerprint on the author list: Novartis, AstraZeneca, Regeneron and Astellas are all on these papers, and the 2025 study concludes in as many words that inhibiting this transporter, up to and including complete knockout, may be a way to treat type 2 diabetes. Nobody has announced a drug. Somebody is almost certainly looking for one.
Short Description: Breaks the zinc pump that loads the insulin granules inside pancreatic beta cells, and the beta cell answers by releasing more insulin for the same glucose load. Eighteen people carrying no functional copy at all have now been found and called back for testing: their type 2 diabetes risk is about a third of everyone else's (recessive odds ratio 0.34), while single-copy carriers show a 65% reduction. Nobody sells an inhibitor — AstraZeneca, Regeneron and Novartis all co-authored the human knockout paper, but no clinical candidate has been disclosed. The protein is also the autoantigen behind ZnT8 autoantibodies, detected in 42.3% of newly diagnosed type 1 diabetic children in one Tunisian cohort, so deleting it removes a molecule that the immune system in autoimmune diabetes is already attacking. Mouse knockouts of the same gene disagreed with the human result, so the usual model organism is no help here.
Mechanism: SLC30A8 encodes ZnT8, a 369-amino-acid proton-coupled zinc antiporter that concentrates Zn2+ ions into the insulin secretory granules of the pancreatic beta cell, where zinc crystallises insulin into hexamers. Protein-truncating alleles produce an unstable ZnT8 protein and therefore less granule zinc. This runs counter to the prior model, which held that reduced zinc transport should raise diabetes risk. Instead, human haploinsufficiency and complete knockout both raise glucose-stimulated insulin secretion: recall-by-genotype oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTTs) show a gene-dose-dependent fall in glucose alongside elevated insulin, with the corrected insulin response and the disposition index preserved and the effect independent of body mass index. The proposed explanation is that lower granule zinc reduces first-pass extraction of insulin by the liver, and/or alters the kinetics with which insulin crystallises and redissolves, so more of each secretory pulse reaches the periphery. That link between granule zinc and the secretory phenotype is still inferred from the human physiology rather than demonstrated mechanistically.
Achievements (effect sizes): Sequencing or genotyping of roughly 150,000 individuals across five ancestry groups identified twelve rare protein-truncating variants in SLC30A8. Analysed collectively, carriers had a 65% reduced risk of type 2 diabetes (P = 1.7 × 10^-6), and non-diabetic Icelandic carriers of the p.Lys34Serfs*50 frameshift had reduced glucose levels (-0.17 standard deviations, P = 4.6 × 10^-4) (Flannick 2014, https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.2915). The result was then pushed to complete human knockout in the Pakistan Genome Resource biobank, where 145,037 whole-exome or whole-genome sequenced participants yielded 1,024 heterozygotes for loss-of-function variants and 18 people with no functional ZnT8 at all, including homozygotes for the South-Asian-enriched Gln174Ter allele. The additive odds ratio for type 2 diabetes was 0.62 (95% CI 0.53, 0.72; p = 1.1 × 10^-9) and the recessive odds ratio was 0.34 (95% CI 0.12, 0.93; p = 0.04). Recalling carriers by genotype for oral glucose tolerance testing showed a gene-dose-dependent reduction in glucose with elevated insulin, which is the physiological signature the genetics predicted (Lamarche 2025, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00125-025-06530-3).
Highest Evidence Tier: T8 (human loss-of-function genetics at two independent scales — around 150,000 people across five ancestries in 2014, and 145,037 sequenced participants including 18 confirmed complete knockouts with recall-by-genotype physiology in 2025)
Translational Gaps: No ZnT8 inhibitor has entered the clinic, so there is currently no way to acquire this phenotype other than being born with it. The eighteen complete human knockouts are a small group, and they have not been followed in detail for effects on bone, retina and the other tissues where zinc handling matters, which is where a systemic inhibitor would most plausibly cause trouble. The mechanism that connects reduced granule zinc to higher insulin secretion is still inferred from human physiology rather than demonstrated, and until it is, a drug developer cannot say which step to hit or predict what happens outside the beta cell. The only registry records that mention this gene use it as a genotype covariate rather than administering anything, so no dose, schedule or safety window exists to reason from.
Key References (DOIs): Go-T2D Consortium Nature Genetics 2014 https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.2915 | Lamarche Diabetologia 2025 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00125-025-06530-3
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: This target reverses the direction the field originally predicted: earlier functional work suggested that reduced zinc transport should increase type 2 diabetes risk, and the human genetics contradicted it (https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.2915). The model organism disagrees too — mouse Slc30a8 knockouts showed phenotypic heterogeneity that did not match the human result, which is worth stating plainly because it means rodent work cannot be used to support or refute this card. Registry searches for SLC30A8 return type 1 diabetes autoantibody screening and antipsychotic-induced metabolic syndrome studies; the closest hit, a mechanistic study of TCF7L2 and SLC30A8 in antipsychotic-induced metabolic syndrome (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02093858), runs in the opposite direction from this library's framing and merely measures the gene as a covariate, so it should not be read as clinical support. There is a real immunological caveat: ZnT8 is the autoantigen behind ZnT8 autoantibodies, which were detected in 66 of 156 (42.3%) newly diagnosed type 1 diabetic children in one Tunisian cohort, 6 of those (9%) positive for ZnT8 antibodies as their only humoral marker — and how a null allele interacts with type 1 diabetes autoimmunity has not been studied. Corresponding-author affiliations on the knockout paper span Novartis, AstraZeneca, Regeneron and Columbia, consistent with active industry interest but no disclosed clinical candidate (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00125-025-06530-3).

Narrative:
A planarian flatworm cut into 200 pieces will regenerate into 200 whole worms, each with a working brain. The engine of this feat is a population of adult stem cells called neoblasts, maintained by the smedwi genes, which are relatives of the germline PIWI family found across animals. Knocking down smedwi-2 or smedwi-3 with RNA interference causes complete regeneration failure, and the worm dissolves (Reddien 2005, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1116110; Palakodeti 2008, https://doi.org/10.1261/rna.1085008).

In mammals the PIWI-family genes are confined to germ cells, and knocking out all of them leaves mice with no obvious defect in the rest of the body. When mammalian tumours accidentally switch PIWI on in their non-germline cells, the result is uniformly bad news: colorectal, gastric and pancreatic cancers all weaponise ectopic PIWI to drive proliferation and metastasis. Every time evolution or a laboratory has reached for this pathway outside the germline in a mammal, the outcome has been cancer rather than regeneration. The chasm between planarian pluripotency and human tissue repair is one of the deepest in enhancement biology.
Short Description: A population of adult stem cells called neoblasts, kept functional by the smedwi genes, lets a flatworm cut into 200 pieces regrow 200 whole worms, each with a working brain. Silence smedwi-2 with RNA interference and regeneration fails completely; the animal lyses within about 12 days. No laboratory has ever moved this pathway into a mammal for repair, and every published case of a mammalian body switching the equivalent PIWIL genes on outside the germline is a tumour — colorectal, gastric and pancreatic cancers all use it to proliferate and metastasise. Mice lacking all their PIWI genes develop normally, so mammalian bodies do not need this switch at all. The tradeoff is that the only known mammalian phenotype for turning it on is cancer.
Mechanism: PIWI proteins bind a class of small non-coding RNAs called PIWI-interacting RNAs, or piRNAs, and use them as guides to silence transposable elements before those elements can insert themselves into the genome. In planarians this silencing is what keeps the neoblast population genomically stable and therefore pluripotent, so the PIWI-piRNA system is not merely a defence mechanism but the maintenance system for whole-body regenerative capacity.
Achievements (effect sizes):
Reddien and colleagues showed that RNA interference against smedwi-2 causes complete regeneration failure in the planarian Schmidtea mediterranea, with the animals lysing at approximately day 12 (Reddien 2005, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1116110). Palakodeti and colleagues extended this to smedwi-3, where knockdown produced lysis at approximately day 22, and demonstrated that both genes are required for piRNA expression (Palakodeti 2008, https://doi.org/10.1261/rna.1085008). Neoblasts make up roughly 20% of the adult planarian's cells, and the animal can regenerate a complete body from less than 1% of its original tissue.

The mammalian picture is entirely different. The mammalian PIWI-like genes PIWIL1 through PIWIL4 are restricted to the germline, and mice in which all of them are knocked out show no somatic phenotype. Where ectopic somatic PIWIL1 has been documented, it has been in cancer. In colorectal cancer PIWIL1 is ectopically activated with accompanying promoter demethylation, and the protein assembles a functional piRNA-loaded complex in the perinuclear region of the cell (Sellitto 2019, https://doi.org/10.3390/cells8111390). In gastric cancer, knocking out PIWIL1 drastically reduces proliferation, migration, metastasis and tumorigenesis, and the effect survives abolition of piRNA binding, so it is piRNA-independent (Shi 2020, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2008724117). In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, PIWIL1 acts without piRNAs as a co-activator of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, which then degrades the cell-adhesion protein Pinin and thereby enhances metastasis (Li 2020, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41556-020-0486-z). In all three cancers the gain of function is oncogenic — increased proliferation, migration and metastasis — and it operates through a piRNA-independent co-activator role rather than through transposon silencing. No transfer of smedwi into mammalian cells for regenerative purposes has ever been published.
Highest Evidence Tier: T1 (planarian LOF); T4–T6 for mammalian PIWIL ectopic expression but ONLY in oncogenic direction
Translational Gaps: The whole-body regeneration gap has never been bridged in a mammal, and this gene does not obviously bridge it. Transferring a single gene cannot reconstitute the piRNA biogenesis apparatus that PIWI proteins depend on — the processing enzymes, the piRNA clusters and the nuage compartment would all have to be built alongside it. There is no animal model in which smedwi expression has produced regeneration, so there is no dose, route or tissue target to translate.
Key References (DOIs): Reddien Science 2005 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1116110 | Palakodeti RNA 2008 https://doi.org/10.1261/rna.1085008 | Sellitto Cells 2019 https://doi.org/10.3390/cells8111390 | Shi Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 2020 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2008724117 | Li Nature Cell Biology 2020 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41556-020-0486-z
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave:
The critical translation barrier here is not technical difficulty but direction of effect. Every mammalian somatic PIWIL gain-of-function published to date is oncogenic rather than regenerative, across colorectal, gastric and pancreatic cancer. That is not a gap in the evidence; it is evidence pointing the other way.

Mice lacking all three PIWI genes are normal, which tells us the pathway is not rate-limiting for anything the mammalian body does outside the germline. Read together with the cancer literature, the most parsimonious interpretation is that the mammalian soma deliberately excludes this pathway, and that the exclusion is itself a tumour-suppressive adaptation. There is no mammalian precedent for PIWI-driven regeneration to build on.

Narrative:
For 20 years SOD2 was the poster child for the free-radical theory of ageing. The logic was clean: superoxide leaks from the respiratory chain, superoxide damages everything it touches, and manganese superoxide dismutase is the enzyme that removes it inside the mitochondrion. More of the enzyme should therefore mean less damage and a longer life. It did not work out that way. When several laboratories built mice that produced roughly twice the normal amount of the enzyme across their whole lives, the mice lived exactly as long as their controls. Oxidative damage did drop and paraquat tolerance did improve, but the ageing clock did not move (Jang 2009, https://doi.org/10.1093/gerona/glp100).

The results that followed were more awkward still. Deleting the equivalent gene in nematode worms extended their lifespan rather than shortening it (Van Raamsdonk 2009, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000361). Naked mole-rats, held up for years as living proof that high antioxidant capacity buys longevity, turn out to carry substantial oxidative damage of their own (Andziak 2006, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1474-9726.2006.00237.x). The honest conclusion from 20 years of mouse work is that topping up a single antioxidant enzyme does not move ageing, because the rest of the antioxidant network compensates for the change. SOD2 remains genuinely essential for survival — animals lacking it entirely do not live — but it is not a lever you can pull on lifespan.
Short Description: Inside mitochondria this enzyme intercepts superoxide, the reactive by-product of respiration, and converts it to the less aggressive hydrogen peroxide before it can damage lipids and DNA. Mice engineered to make roughly twice the normal amount across their entire lives showed less lipid peroxidation and better resistance to the herbicide paraquat, and lived exactly as long as controls in a cohort of 97 animals. No clinic and no trial uses this today; it is mouse data, and two decades of it point the same way. Deleting the equivalent gene in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans extends lifespan rather than shortening it. Overexpression also drives p53-dependent senescence in human colorectal cancer cells, which is the opposite of what a longevity intervention should do.
Mechanism: SOD2 encodes manganese superoxide dismutase, a matrix enzyme that catalyses the dismutation of the superoxide radical anion to hydrogen peroxide and molecular oxygen. Because superoxide is generated continuously by electron leak from the respiratory chain, the enzyme sits at the point where mitochondrial reactive oxygen species are first produced, and its product, hydrogen peroxide, is then cleared downstream by catalase and the glutathione and peroxiredoxin systems. The enzyme is therefore the first step in a network rather than a standalone defence, which is the central reason increasing it in isolation changes so little.
Achievements (effect sizes):
The definitive negative result comes from two coordinated mouse studies. Jang and colleagues overexpressed manganese superoxide dismutase roughly twofold in C57BL/6 mice across the whole lifespan and measured mitochondrial function, oxidative damage, lifespan and end-of-life pathology in a cohort of 97 animals. Lipid peroxidation fell and paraquat resistance improved, but there was no lifespan extension and no change in age-related pathology (Jang 2009, https://doi.org/10.1093/gerona/glp100). Pérez and colleagues extended the test across the whole family of major antioxidant enzymes, generating transgenic mice overexpressing copper-zinc superoxide dismutase, catalase, and combinations of copper-zinc superoxide dismutase with either catalase or manganese superoxide dismutase, and concluded that overexpressing these enzymes is insufficient to extend lifespan in mice (Pérez 2009, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1474-9726.2008.00449.x).

One positive report exists and has not been replicated. Hu and colleagues, working in a smaller cohort of 54 animals, found that overexpressing the enzyme had no effect on hippocampal long-term potentiation or memory formation in young mice and did not rescue age-related impairment in old ones, but did reduce mitochondrial superoxide in hippocampal neurons and did extend lifespan; the record gives the effect as a 4 percent increase in mean and an 18 percent increase in maximum lifespan (Hu 2007, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nlm.2006.10.003).

The loss-of-function side is equally instructive. Mice heterozygous for Sod2 carry 50 percent of normal enzyme activity in every tissue throughout life and accumulate significantly elevated 8-oxo-2-deoxyguanosine in nuclear DNA along with a higher incidence of cancer, yet their lifespan is unchanged (Van Remmen 2003, https://doi.org/10.1152/physiolgenomics.00122.2003). Halving the enzyme raises damage and tumour burden without accelerating ageing, which is hard to reconcile with the free-radical theory in its simple form.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (multiple cohorts)
Translational Gaps: This is not a viable stand-alone longevity target and the mouse literature says so directly. Any credible attempt would have to be combinatorial — pairing SOD2 with a downstream peroxide sink such as catalase targeted to the mitochondrion, so that the hydrogen peroxide the enzyme produces is actually removed rather than handed to the existing network. The roughly twofold overexpression tested in mice may also sit below whatever threshold would matter, and no study has established what that threshold is or whether a higher one is tolerable.
Key References (DOIs): Jang The Journals of Gerontology Series A 2009 https://doi.org/10.1093/gerona/glp100 | Pérez Aging Cell 2009 https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1474-9726.2008.00449.x | Andziak Aging Cell 2006 https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1474-9726.2006.00237.x | Van Raamsdonk PLoS Genetics 2009 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000361 | Van Remmen Physiological Genomics 2003 https://doi.org/10.1152/physiolgenomics.00122.2003 | Hu Neurobiology of Learning and Memory 2007 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nlm.2006.10.003 | Behrend Molecular and Cellular Biology 2005 https://doi.org/10.1128/MCB.25.17.7758-7769.2005
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave:
This entry is included because it is strongly contradicted as a longevity target, and the contradictions are more valuable than the original hypothesis was.

The Van Remmen and Richardson consortium, which ran the largest coordinated test of the free-radical theory in mammals, concluded that the major antioxidant enzymes are insufficient to extend lifespan (Pérez 2009, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1474-9726.2008.00449.x). That is a null result from the group best positioned to find a positive one.

Deleting sod-2 in Caenorhabditis elegans extends lifespan (Van Raamsdonk 2009, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1000361). This is not a weaker effect in the same direction, it is the opposite direction in a genetically tractable animal, and any model of how mitochondrial superoxide relates to ageing has to accommodate it.

The naked mole-rat argument fails on its own terms. The longest-living rodent known, at more than 28.3 years, carries high levels of accrued oxidative damage alongside its high manganese superoxide dismutase (Andziak 2006, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1474-9726.2006.00237.x). High enzyme levels in a long-lived species therefore cannot be read as mechanistic evidence that the enzyme causes the longevity.

Overexpression carries an active risk rather than merely failing to help. Raising manganese superoxide dismutase in HCT116 human colorectal cancer cells slowed growth by inducing cellular senescence, upregulating p53 and its transcriptional target p21, and knocking down p53 by RNA interference rescued the phenotype (Behrend 2005, https://doi.org/10.1128/MCB.25.17.7758-7769.2005). A p53-dependent senescence programme is precisely what a longevity intervention is supposed to avoid triggering.

Two caveats cut the other way and should be kept. The roughly twofold overexpression used in the mouse studies may fall below the threshold at which anything happens, and the antioxidant network downstream of the enzyme compensates for changes in its activity, so a single-enzyme manipulation may be buffered before it reaches any phenotype.

Narrative:
Pyrococcus furiosus lives on hydrothermal vents at around 100 degrees C and is a strict anaerobe, which makes oxygen a chronic hazard rather than a resource. Whenever vent water mixes with the oxygenated ocean the archaeon meets the superoxide anion - the same radical aerobes generate as a by-product of breathing. Aerobes handle superoxide with superoxide dismutase, which turns two radicals into one molecule of oxygen and one of hydrogen peroxide. For an anaerobe that solution is absurd, because it manufactures the very gas the organism is trying to avoid. In 1999 Francis Jenney and Michael Adams at the University of Georgia described the alternative: a small iron enzyme that reduces superoxide to hydrogen peroxide using an electron pulled from NAD(P)H, releasing no oxygen at all (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.286.5438.306). They also found it working far outside its own thermal niche, active 80 degrees C below the archaeon's growth optimum - an enzyme from a boiling spring that still turns over at room temperature.

Amy Grunden's group at North Carolina State University then asked whether an enzyme from a vent archaeon could be handed to a plant. It could. Thale cress carrying the archaeal gene resisted heat, high light and chemically imposed oxidative stress (https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.109.145409), and a later experiment moved it into bunchberry dogwood, a woody perennial, where transgenic plants stayed green through a heat ramp that withered most of their non-transgenic siblings (https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2016.00026). For a visitor building a body, the interesting part is what this is not. It is not a better version of a human antioxidant enzyme; it is a different chemical answer to the same problem, invented by an organism that has never breathed. Installing it means taking the anaerobe's bargain - nothing is oxidised back into oxygen, but every radical you clear arrives downstream as peroxide for something else to finish.
Short Description: Superoxide, the radical your own respiration leaks every second, gets stripped out by a borrowed archaeal enzyme that reduces it to hydrogen peroxide instead of dismutating it, so no oxygen gas is regenerated on the way. The donor enzyme stays catalytically active 80 degrees C below the 100 degrees C growth optimum of the boiling-vent archaeon it came from, so it does not quit when a tissue overheats. Plants carrying it held photosystem II efficiency at 0.590 after a four-day ramp to 40 degrees C, where non-transgenic plants collapsed to 0.335 and fewer than 20% recovered at all. It has only ever been put into plants - thale cress and bunchberry dogwood - with no animal or mammalian-cell expression anywhere and no clinical trials. The catch is the product: every radical cleared becomes a peroxide molecule, so liver and red blood cells, which already run their catalase near saturation, would swap a superoxide load for a peroxide one.
Mechanism: Superoxide reductase (SOR) is a small non-haem enzyme of 124 amino acids built around a single iron atom held in a square-pyramidal site by four histidines and one cysteine. It carries out a one-electron reduction of the superoxide anion to hydrogen peroxide, taking that electron from NAD(P)H - the cell's reduced nicotinamide cofactor - delivered through the small iron-containing carrier rubredoxin and an NAD(P)H:rubredoxin oxidoreductase. The chemistry is the mirror image of superoxide dismutase (SOD), which disproportionates two superoxide anions into molecular oxygen plus hydrogen peroxide. SOR instead consumes an external electron and never regenerates oxygen, and for a strict anaerobe that distinction is the entire point. Because SOR is a foreign protein, its expression is also not held down by the host's own regulatory ceiling on how much cytosolic superoxide dismutase it will tolerate, and it acts in the cytosol rather than the mitochondrial matrix.
Achievements (effect sizes): Purified superoxide reductase from Pyrococcus furiosus, together with its rubredoxin and NAD(P)H:rubredoxin oxidoreductase partners, was shown to be catalytically active 80 degrees C below the 100 degrees C optimum growth temperature of the archaeon, which is what makes the enzyme usable in a mesophilic host at all (Jenney 1999, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.286.5438.306). When the gene was first moved into a plant, Arabidopsis thaliana lines producing SOR showed enhanced tolerance to heat, light and chemically induced reactive oxygen species, and that tolerance tracked with a delayed rise in reactive-oxygen-sensitive transcripts and a fall in ascorbate peroxidase activity (Im 2009, https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.109.145409). The enzyme was then carried into the woody perennial bunchberry dogwood, Cornus canadensis, as a green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusion. After a four-day heat ramp holding 24 hours each at 30, 35, 37 and 40 degrees C, all of the GFP-SOR transgenic plants quickly recovered, but fewer than 20% of the non-transgenic plants recovered. Chlorophyll fluorescence put a number on the protection: at 40 degrees C the maximum quantum yield of photosystem II (Fv/Fm) was 0.335 in wild-type plants against 0.590 in SOR plants, while the two lines were indistinguishable at the 22 degrees C control (0.802 and 0.805) (Geng 2016, https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2016.00026).
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (heterologous gain-of-function in two transgenic plant species plus independent enzyme characterisation; both plant studies from one lab lineage, no animal data)
Translational Gaps: Both gain-of-function studies are in plants, and both trace to the same laboratory lineage at North Carolina State University, so no independent group has reproduced the phenotype and nobody has expressed superoxide reductase in a mammalian cell or in an animal of any kind. Turnover also depends on partners the host does not have: the iron centre must be re-reduced by rubredoxin and an NAD(P)H:rubredoxin oxidoreductase, and the plant experiments relied on endogenous reductants standing in for the archaeal pair. Whether a mammalian cytosol can recycle that iron centre fast enough for the enzyme to matter has never been tested. Because the reaction product is hydrogen peroxide rather than water, a human application would additionally have to show that the receiving tissue's catalase and peroxidases can absorb the extra peroxide flux instead of simply relocating the oxidative burden.
Key References (DOIs): Jenney Science 1999 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.286.5438.306 | Im Plant Physiology 2009 https://doi.org/10.1104/pp.109.145409 | Geng Frontiers in Plant Science 2016 https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2016.00026
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Three experimental structures of the Pyrococcus furiosus enzyme have been solved - Protein Data Bank entries 1DO6, 1DQI and 1DQK (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1DO6) - and the mononuclear iron site coordinated by four histidines and one cysteine looks nothing like the copper-zinc or manganese sites of the superoxide dismutases, which makes this a clear contrast card in a 3D viewer; the sequence reference is UniProt P82385 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P82385). At 124 amino acids it is among the smallest functional units in the library and is trivially deliverable in any vector. There are no clinical trials and no registry records; the enzyme is being developed as an abiotic-stress trait for crops and no commercial line has been released. One finding cuts against a simple more-antioxidant-is-better reading: the transgenic dogwood plants blunted the normal proline stress response, so the host lost part of the reactive-oxygen signal it uses to mount its own defence (Geng 2016, https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2016.00026). This entry should not be confused with the library's SOD2 card, which is a manganese dismutase in the mitochondrial matrix that regenerates oxygen; SOR is a cytosolic iron reductase that consumes NAD(P)H and makes none.

Manipulation: Knockout / antibody neutralisation (anti-USAG-1 monoclonal, humanised as TRG035) / local siRNA knockdown
Narrative:
Most mammals get two sets of teeth and then stop, and the stopping is active rather than passive. Underneath the permanent dentition many species carry a rudimentary successional tooth germ — a third set that begins to form and is then deliberately killed off by apoptosis. Humans occasionally fail to kill it, which is where supernumerary teeth come from. In 2007 a Kyoto group found the brake: mice lacking USAG-1, a small secreted protein better known to the kidney literature, kept their rudimentary germ and erupted an extra tooth (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbrc.2007.05.148).

What makes this a candidate for a body rather than a curiosity is that the brake can be released with a drug. USAG-1 works outside the cell, mopping up bone morphogenetic proteins and blocking a Wnt co-receptor, which means an antibody can neutralise it without touching the genome. In 2021 the group screened a panel of monoclonals and found that the ones binding the BMP-facing surface reproduced the knockout phenotype outright: a single systemic dose generated whole teeth in wild-type mice, and in a strain engineered to have missing molars it reversed the agenesis dose-dependently (https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abf1798). They then moved to the ferret, which unlike a mouse has two tooth generations and a human-like dental pattern, and grew an extra maxillary incisor sitting behind the permanent teeth.

The clinical stakes are real and narrow. Roughly the target population is children with severe congenital tooth agenesis, who currently face implants and prosthetics for life; Toregem BioPharma's humanised antibody TRG035 carries Japanese orphan designation for that indication and is in Phase 1 safety testing in healthy adults, with commercialisation targeted around 2030. What nobody can yet do is aim it. The antibody instructs a jaw to grow a tooth; it does not say where, and in the mouse maxilla the answer came back as fused enlarged molars. And because the same protein restrains BMP-7 in the kidney and closely resembles sclerostin, releasing it systemically pulls on bone mass and renal signalling at the same time as it pulls on teeth.
Short Description: Switch off a single inhibitor protein and the dormant tooth buds you were born with — the 'third dentition' that normally dies away in the jaw — wake up and erupt as a real extra tooth with enamel, dentine and a root. One systemic dose of a blocking antibody was enough to generate a whole tooth in mice, and it rescued the missing molars of a tooth-agenesis strain in which 75% of animals otherwise had mandibular hypodontia. The same antibody grew a third-dentition incisor in ferrets, which have human-like two-generation teeth, but only at five times the concentration, across three injections and under immunosuppression. A humanised version, TRG035, holds Japanese orphan-drug designation for severe congenital hypodontia and is in Phase 1 in healthy adults. The protein is not dental: it is expressed most highly in the kidney, it is a close relative of the bone-mass regulator sclerostin, and in the mouse maxilla it produced fused enlarged molars instead of separate extra teeth.
Mechanism: USAG-1 (uterine sensitization-associated gene-1, also called sclerostin domain-containing protein 1 and encoded by SOSTDC1) is a 206-amino-acid secreted antagonist of the DAN family. It binds bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs) directly and also binds the Wnt co-receptor LRP5/6, so it suppresses both signalling arms in the dental epithelium and mesenchyme. In wild-type mammals that suppression drives apoptotic elimination of the rudimentary successional tooth germ, which is what caps tooth number at two generations. Deleting USAG-1 rescues the germ from apoptosis and it erupts as a supernumerary tooth. Antibodies that block the BMP-binding face specifically — clones #37 and #57 — reproduce the knockout phenotype, and epitope mapping placed #37 on the ten-residue segment VNDKTRTQRI within Q129-EWRCVNDKTRTQRIQLQCQ-148. Antibodies that block only the Wnt/LRP5/6 arm do not generate whole teeth, so BMP derepression is the operative mechanism. Cells positive for phosphorylated SMAD1/5/8 appear in the pulp of the induced tooth, confirming that BMP signalling is running inside the regenerated organ (https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abf1798).
Achievements (effect sizes): Crossing the USAG-1 knockout onto a mouse strain deficient in ectodysplasin A1 (EDA1), which causes congenital tooth agenesis, rescued the missing teeth: 75% of the female USAG-1+/+/EDA1−/− and male USAG-1+/+/EDA1+/− mice had molar hypodontia in the mandible, whereas the USAG-1/EDA1 double knockout mice had normal teeth, hyperdontia, or fused mandibular molars when scored in dry skulls at eight months (https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abf1798). Pharmacology reproduced the genetics: a single systemic administration of a neutralizing antibody can generate a whole tooth, with antibody #37 reversing hypodontia at a high rate and in a dose-dependent manner and antibody #57 inducing supernumerary teeth in wild-type mice at a high rate and a dose-dependent manner (https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abf1798). The effect crossed into a non-rodent with two tooth generations: in postnatal ferrets injected intraperitoneally with 16 or 80 µg/g of antibody #37 and imaged by three-dimensional micro-computed tomography at thirteen weeks, the authors report that we observed supernumerary tooth formation in maxillary incisor like the third dentition, although a five times higher concentration, three administrations of antibody #37, and immunosuppression were required, and the induced incisor sat lingual to the permanent teeth with a shorter root (https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abf1798). A local nucleic-acid approach fell short of a whole tooth: Usag-1 mRNA levels were reduced by ~50% with Usag-1 Stealth siRNAs #304 and #903, and growing explants were observed (42.3%) following topical application of Usag-1 #304 siRNA, versus an incidence of no tooth formation of 66.7% following Runx2 siRNA treatment and 33.3% in the negative-control group (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-93256-y).
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (mouse genetic rescue + antibody pharmacology, replicated in a non-rodent diphyodont (ferret), humanised candidate TRG035 with Japanese orphan designation and a Phase 1 underway)
Translational Gaps: Nobody has grown a tooth in a person. The Japanese Phase 1 is a safety study in healthy adults, so no human efficacy data of any kind has been published, and the whole approach presumes that a patient actually still carries a dormant successional tooth bud for the antibody to act on. The authors infer that such buds exist from an analysis of 78 patients with supernumerary teeth rather than from imaging quiescent germs in the children they intend to treat, which is why the same group is now developing magnetic-resonance and computed-tomography biomarkers capable of finding pre-calcified tooth germs in two- to five-year-olds. Positional control is entirely absent: the antibody tells a jaw to grow a tooth but cannot tell it where, and in the mouse maxillary molar region the result was fused enlarged molars rather than separate teeth. Because the target restrains BMP-7 in the kidney and resembles sclerostin closely enough that one antibody cross-reacted with it, a systemic dose has to be shown not to move bone mass or renal BMP tone before it can be given to children.
Key References (DOIs): Murashima-Suginami Science Advances 2021 https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abf1798 | Mishima Scientific Reports 2021 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-93256-y | Murashima-Suginami Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications 2007 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbrc.2007.05.148 | Takahashi Journal of Oral Biosciences 2024 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.job.2024.10.002
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The clinical candidate is TRG035, a humanised anti-USAG-1 antibody from Toregem BioPharma, a Kyoto University spin-out. There is no ClinicalTrials.gov record for it — the trial is registered in Japan through jRCT — so no NCT number should be attached to this gene. The 2024 Journal of Oral Biosciences paper states that the Phase 1 protocol framework has been finalised (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.job.2024.10.002), and the 2026 paper from the same group names TRG035 explicitly as the humanised anti-USAG-1 antibody in development; manufacturing is with WuXi Biologics per company communications, and the company's stated commercialisation target is around 2030 in the rare-disease indication (https://toregem.co.jp/en/). The safety picture in the mouse work is not uniformly clean: three of the five antibodies raised in that study, clones #12, #16 and #48, caused low offspring birth and survival rates, and antibody #57 cross-reacted with sclerostin (SOST) expressed in HEK293 cells (https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abf1798). The phenotype is also not tidy even when it works, since the same paper reports fused mandibular molars alongside normal teeth and hyperdontia in the rescued double knockouts. The reference accession used here, A0A8U0MID0, is the reviewed ferret (Mustela putorius furo) SOSTDC1 entry, chosen to match the species in which third-dentition teeth were actually produced (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A8U0MID0/entry); most of the other experiments in that paper were done in mouse, whose Sostdc1 is Q9CQN4. Nothing is on sale.

Narrative: Bats coexist with Ebola, SARS, and Nipah without dying of any of them — a trick that depends on running their immune systems differently. Every bat species examined has a single critical substitution in its STING protein (the S358 residue becomes something else), and this dulls the screaming cytokine response that kills humans infected with these viruses. When Lin-Fa Wang's group in 2018 reverted the bat residue back to human S358 in bat cells, the full interferon blowtorch switched back on. In 2024, Yu-Ping Xiao's team made the first knock-in mouse carrying the bat MdSTING variant; aged female mice (not males — nobody knows why yet) had less inflammation and less tissue damage than wild-type littermates. Lifespan wasn't measured, cohorts were small, and STING also helps suppress tumors, so dampening it has an obvious downside. But as a target for inflammaging — the chronic low-grade inflammation that drives aging — it's one of the cleanest leads in the field.
Short Description: Bats run a deliberately softened viral alarm, damping the interferon storm that does much of the damage in infection rather than the virus itself. All 30 bat species tested lack the S358 site that switches this alarm to full volume. Knock-in mice carrying the bat version reached old age with fewer inflammatory signals, but only females, in a cohort of 5 to 9 with no lifespan measured. The same alarm hunts early tumours, and that tradeoff is untested.
Mechanism: Bat STING lacks canonical S358 TBK1-phosphorylation site (30/30 bat species tested); dampens IRF3 docking and type-I IFN induction.
Achievements (effect sizes): Xie 2018 Cell Host Microbe: R. sinicus STING X358S revertant in HEK293T → significantly restored IFN-β luciferase (multi-fold) and ISG/HSV-1 activity; human STING S358A reduces IFN-β. Consistent in PakiT03 bat cell line. Wang/Zhou 2024 Zool Res: FIRST MdSTING knock-in C57BL/6 mice; splenocytes dampened IFN to cGAMP; 3-year longitudinal blood transcriptomics: aged FEMALE (not male) MdSTING-KI mice had lower pro-inflammatory cytokines/chemokines, less immunopathology, less neutrophil recruitment vs WT; cohort small (n=5–9); no lifespan endpoint reported.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (knock-in mouse, 2024) + T6 (HEK293 mutagenesis, 2018)
Translational Gaps: Survival data; primary human immune-cell studies; no human genetics linking hypomorphic STING to longevity (HAQ/AQ/R232H have complex context-dependent effects).
Key References (DOIs): Xie Cell Host Microbe 2018 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chom.2018.01.006 | Wang Zool Res 2024 https://doi.org/10.24272/j.issn.2095-8137.2024.030
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Sex-dependent effect unexplained; dampened ≠ abolished; STING has anti-tumor surveillance role — tradeoff untested. Constitutive IFN-α in P. alecto coexists with dampened STING (Zhou 2016) — rebalanced, not simply suppressed, system not recapitulable via S358 alone.

Narrative: Humboldt squid sucker ring teeth are among the hardest wholly organic structures in nature — rivaling the hardness of the strongest synthetic polymers without any mineral content. Suckerins are the modular proteins responsible, self-assembling into nanoconfined beta-sheet networks that create a material as hard as human tooth enamel from protein alone. This is nature's answer to engineering hard materials without metals or ceramics.
Short Description: Squid teeth-like proteins lock into nanoscale beta-sheet networks, forming a purely organic material without any mineral content. This self-assembled armor reaches 5 GPa hardness, matching tough synthetic engineering polymers. A biotech startup, Tandem Repeat Technologies, is already commercializing squid-inspired protein coatings and 3D-printable bioinks from it. The gap is scale: nobody has grown recombinant suckerin beyond lab-dish quantities, so implant-grade sheets don't exist yet.
Mechanism: Suckerins contain repetitive glycine-rich and alanine-rich modular domains that self-assemble into nanoconfined beta-sheet structures within an amorphous matrix. This nanocomposite architecture achieves hardness of ~5 GPa and stiffness of ~8 GPa — matching synthetic engineering polymers — through purely protein-based hierarchical organization.
Achievements (effect sizes): Recombinant suckerin-based films achieve hardness of 5 GPa. Suckerin-based 3D-printable bioinks and coatings have been demonstrated. Tandem Repeat Technologies commercializing squid-inspired protein materials.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4
Translational Gaps: Scaling recombinant suckerin production beyond lab quantities. Long-term durability under physiological conditions for medical applications. Regulatory pathway for structural biomaterial implants.
Key References (DOIs): https://doi.org/10.1021/nn502149u
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Fully organic structural material with no mineral reinforcement. Tandem Repeat Technologies (Melik Demirel) developing commercial applications.

Narrative: Budgerigars and many birds see ultraviolet light that is completely invisible to humans — their world is painted with colors we cannot imagine. The molecular basis is strikingly simple: a single photoreceptor protein called SWS1 (short-wavelength sensitive opsin 1) that detects wavelengths around 365 nm, deep into the UV. Humans have a close ortholog, OPN1SW, which detects violet light at 420 nm — just 55 nm away. The difference comes down to just 2–3 amino acid positions near the retinal chromophore binding pocket: sites 86 and 90. Van Hazel and colleagues showed in 2013 that mutating C86F and S90C in the bowerbird SWS1 was sufficient to shift spectral sensitivity from UV to violet, or vice versa. The human blue cone pigment sits on the same protein scaffold. In principle, introducing the UVS-conferring residues (Cys86, paired with Ala or Cys90) into human OPN1SW could retune existing blue cones to detect UV light. No mammalian in-vivo test has been attempted, but the spectral tuning mechanism is thoroughly characterized through site-directed mutagenesis in multiple avian species. The catch: the human lens filters out most UV below 400 nm, so even with a retuned opsin, lens modification would also be needed. Aphakic humans (lens removed for cataracts) do perceive UV, confirming the retinal pathway works.
Short Description: Blue cone receptors normally catch violet light at 420 nm, but swapping two amino acids at positions 86 and 90 retunes them to 365 nm, deep UV. That 55 nm shift comes from just two mutations next to the light-catching chromophore. It's only been done in bird cone proteins in a dish, never in a living mammal eye. Even if it worked, the human lens blocks over 99% of UV, so the eye would also need lens removal, raising macular degeneration risk from unshielded UV exposure.
Mechanism: SWS1 is a 7-transmembrane G-protein coupled receptor in cone photoreceptors. Spectral tuning between violet-sensitive (~420 nm) and UV-sensitive (~365 nm) variants is controlled by residues 86 and 90 adjacent to the retinal Schiff base. Cys86 and Ala/Cys90 confer UV sensitivity; Phe86 and Ser90 confer violet sensitivity.
Achievements (effect sizes): van Hazel 2013: C86F and S90C mutations individually shift SWS1 λmax by ~55 nm between UV and violet in bowerbird. Wilkie 1998: first cloning and expression of budgerigar UVS opsin, λmax 365 nm. Hunt 2007: comprehensive spectral tuning rules established across avian species.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3 (in-vitro expression systems + site-directed mutagenesis)
Translational Gaps: No mammalian in-vivo test of UV-shifted opsin. Human lens blocks most UV below 400 nm — opsin retuning alone insufficient. Potential phototoxicity from UV exposure to retinal tissue. No data on integration with existing trichromatic color processing in visual cortex.
Key References (DOIs): Wilkie Biochem J 1998 https://doi.org/10.1042/bj3300541 | van Hazel BMC Evol Biol 2013 https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2148-13-250 | Hunt Photochem Photobiol 2007 https://doi.org/10.1562/2006-06-27-IR-952
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The human lens absorbs >99% of UV-B and most UV-A below 400 nm, so a retuned cone opsin would detect almost nothing without lens modification.
